uni-bba-business-law.title: BBA · Business Law
uni-bba-business-law.description: Indian Contract Act 1872 (formation, capacity, free consent, void agreements, performance, discharge and remedies), special contracts (indemnity, guarantee, bailment, pledge, agency), Sale of Goods Act 1930, Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, and an overview of the Companies Act 2013, LLP Act 2008 and Consumer Protection Act 2019, with case-based problems. Study companion, not legal advice; topics commonly taught in Indian BBA programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Indian Contract Act: Nature and Formation of Contracts
courses.summary: Meaning and essentials of a valid contract under the Indian Contract Act, 1872; classification of contracts; offer, invitation to offer and acceptance, with rules of communication and revocation; and consideration, its exceptions and privity of contract, using landmark cases.
outcomes: State the essentials of a valid contract under section 10
Distinguish offer from invitation to offer and apply rules of acceptance
Determine when communication of offer and acceptance is complete
Explain consideration and its exceptions under section 25
Classify contracts as valid, void, voidable, illegal, express or implied

scenes.text: Ravi agrees over tea to sell his used laptop to Kiran for ₹25,000.
Next day he gets a better offer and refuses to sell to Kiran.
Is there an enforceable contract, even without paper? The Contract Act answers.

steps.title: Key definitions
steps.body:
- **Agreement** (s.2(e)): every promise and every set of promises forming consideration for each other.
- **Contract** (s.2(h)): an agreement enforceable by law.
So: all contracts are agreements, but not all agreements are contracts.

steps.title: Essentials (s.10 and general law)
steps.body:
1 Offer and acceptance
2 Intention to create legal relations
3 Lawful consideration
4 Capacity of parties
5 Free consent
6 Lawful object
7 Not expressly declared void
8 Certainty and possibility of performance
9 Legal formalities where required (writing, registration).

steps.title: Balfour v Balfour (1919)
steps.body: A husband's promise to pay his wife a monthly allowance was a domestic arrangement with no intention to create legal relations, so it was not enforceable. Commercial agreements are presumed to carry that intention.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
- By validity: **valid**, **void** (s.2(g), no legal effect), **voidable** (s.2(i), enforceable at the option of one party), **illegal**, **unenforceable**.
- By formation: express, implied, quasi-contract.
- By performance: executed, executory; unilateral, bilateral.

steps.title: Answering Ravi's case
steps.body: An oral agreement for sale of a laptop with consent, consideration and lawful object is a valid contract; oral evidence may be harder to prove, but writing is not required for such a sale.

activity.prompt: Classify each agreement

items.text: Sale of a car for ₹4 lakh between two adults freely
Agreement with a minor to buy a bike on credit
Contract signed under a threat of harm
Agreement to pay for an impossible act from the start

quiz.q: Which section lists what agreements are contracts?
quiz.why: Section 10 states that agreements are contracts if made by free consent of competent parties for lawful consideration and object, and not declared void.

quiz.q: A voidable contract is
options: enforceable at the option of one party
quiz.why: Section 2(i) defines it as enforceable at the option of one or more parties but not the others.

quiz.q: Balfour v Balfour concerned
quiz.why: Social and domestic arrangements are presumed not to create legal obligations.

scenes.text: A shop window shows a jacket marked ₹999.
Meena walks in and demands it at that price; the shopkeeper refuses.
Is the price tag an offer she accepted?

steps.title: Offer (s.2(a))
steps.body: When one person signifies to another willingness to do or abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other. Types: express/implied, specific/general, cross offers, counter offers, standing offers.

steps.title: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co (1893)
steps.body: An advertisement promising £100 to anyone who caught influenza after using the smoke ball as directed was a **general offer**; Mrs Carlill accepted by performing the conditions.

steps.title: Invitation to offer
steps.body: Price lists, catalogues, goods displayed in shops, tender notices and auction announcements are generally invitations to offer. The customer makes the offer; the seller may accept or reject. In Harvey v Facey (1893), quoting a lowest price was held to be information, not an offer.

steps.title: Lalman Shukla v Gauri Dutt (1913)
steps.body: A servant who traced a missing boy without knowing of the reward could not claim it: there can be no acceptance of an offer one does not know about.

steps.title: Lapse of offer
steps.body: By revocation, lapse of time, rejection or counter offer, death or insanity of offeror (if known to offeree before acceptance), non-fulfilment of a condition precedent.

activity.prompt: Offer or invitation to offer?

items.text: Reward ad for finding a lost dog
Letter: I will sell you my flat for ₹60 lakh

quiz.q: An advertisement offering a reward to anyone who finds a lost item is a
quiz.why: It is addressed to the world at large and can be accepted by anyone who performs the condition.

quiz.q: Goods displayed with price tags are generally
quiz.why: The customer offers to buy; the shopkeeper may accept or decline.

quiz.q: A counter offer
quiz.why: Varying terms amounts to rejection of the original offer and a fresh offer.

scenes.text: A Kolkata trader posts an offer to a Chennai buyer on 1 March.
The buyer posts acceptance on 5 March; it reaches Kolkata on 9 March.
On 7 March the trader telegrams a revocation. Is it too late?

steps.title: Rules of acceptance
steps.body: Acceptance (s.2(b)) must be absolute and unqualified (s.7), communicated, in the prescribed or a usual and reasonable manner, given by the offeree, before the offer lapses. Mere silence is not acceptance (Felthouse v Bindley, 1862).

steps.title: When communication is complete (s.4)
steps.body:
- Offer: when it comes to the knowledge of the offeree.
- Acceptance against proposer: when put in course of transmission so it is out of the acceptor's power.
- Acceptance against acceptor: when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer.

steps.title: Revocation (s.5)
steps.body: An offer may be revoked any time before communication of acceptance is complete against the proposer. An acceptance may be revoked any time before it is complete against the acceptor.

steps.title: Solving the letter case
steps.body: Acceptance was posted on 5 March, completing it against the trader. His 7 March revocation is too late; a contract exists. The buyer could revoke his acceptance only before 9 March, when it reached the trader.

activity.prompt: Match the event to when it is complete
pairs: When it reaches the offeree's knowledge
When posted, out of acceptor's power

quiz.q: 'I accept if you reduce the price by ₹500' is
quiz.why: Acceptance must be absolute; changing terms is a counter offer.

quiz.q: Felthouse v Bindley established that
quiz.why: An offeror cannot impose silence as acceptance on the offeree.

quiz.q: Acceptance posted 10 May, received 14 May. The proposer can revoke the offer until
options: before acceptance is posted on 10 May
quiz.why: Under section 5 the offer can be revoked only before acceptance is complete against the proposer, which happens on posting.

scenes.text: Uncle promises in writing to give his nephew ₹1 lakh out of love, and registers the document.
Later he changes his mind.
No consideration, but is it still enforceable?

steps.title: Definition (s.2(d))
steps.body: When, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains, or promises to do or abstain from doing something, such act, abstinence or promise is consideration. It may be past, present or future; it need not be adequate but must be real and lawful.

steps.title: Indian position on who may give consideration
steps.body: Consideration may move from the promisee **or any other person**. In Chinnaya v Ramayya (1882), a sister promised to pay an annuity to her uncle in return for property gifted by her mother; the uncle could enforce it though consideration came from the mother.

steps.title: Exceptions: no consideration, no contract (s.25)
steps.body:
An agreement without consideration is void except:
1 Made in writing and registered, out of natural love and affection between near relatives.
2 Promise to compensate for something done voluntarily for the promisor.
3 Written, signed promise to pay a time-barred debt.
Also: completed gifts, agency (s.185) and charitable subscriptions acted upon.

steps.title: Privity of contract
steps.body: Generally only parties to a contract can sue on it. Exceptions include trusts, family settlements, acknowledgement or estoppel, and assignment.

steps.title: The uncle's promise
steps.body: Written, registered, out of natural love and affection between near relatives: it falls under s.25(1) and is enforceable.

activity.prompt: Enforceable or void for lack of consideration?

items.text: Registered written promise to a son out of love
Oral promise to give a friend ₹10,000 for nothing
Signed written promise to pay a time-barred debt
Promise to pay a neighbour who voluntarily found your lost wallet

quiz.q: Under Indian law, consideration may move from
options: the promisee or any other person
quiz.why: Section 2(d) expressly includes 'the promisee or any other person'.

quiz.q: Inadequate consideration
options: does not by itself invalidate it if consent was free
quiz.why: Courts do not weigh adequacy, though it may be evidence on whether consent was free.

quiz.q: Which section lists exceptions to 'no consideration, no contract'?
quiz.why: Section 25 makes agreements without consideration void except in listed cases.

questions.why: The advertisement was an offer to the world accepted by performance.

questions.why: Without knowledge of the reward offer there was no acceptance.

questions.q: Quoting a minimum price in reply to an inquiry is
options: an invitation to offer or information
questions.why: Harvey v Facey held a price quotation is not an offer.

questions.q: Acceptance is complete as against the proposer when
options: it is posted and out of the acceptor's power
questions.why: Section 4 makes it complete against the proposer once in transmission.

questions.q: Two identical offers crossing in the post are
questions.why: Neither party knew of the other's offer, so there is no acceptance.

questions.q: Chinnaya v Ramayya illustrates
questions.why: Consideration from the mother supported the daughter's promise.

questions.q: A promise to pay a time-barred debt is enforceable if
questions.why: Section 25(3) requires a written promise signed by the debtor or agent.

questions.q: Which is generally an invitation to offer?
options: Letter offering to sell land at a price
questions.why: Catalogues invite customers to make offers.

questions.q: A contract fully performed by both parties is
questions.why: Executed contracts have nothing left to perform.

questions.q: Offer posted 1 June, acceptance posted 4 June, received 6 June. Acceptor's revocation is valid if it reaches the proposer
options: before or with the acceptance on 6 June
questions.why: Acceptance can be revoked before it is complete against the acceptor, that is, before it reaches the proposer.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Capacity, Free Consent and Void Agreements
courses.summary: Who is competent to contract (minors, unsound mind, disqualified persons), the elements that vitiate free consent (coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, mistake), lawful object, and agreements expressly declared void, including restraint of trade and wagering agreements.
outcomes: Apply section 11 and Mohori Bibee to minors' agreements
Distinguish coercion from undue influence and fraud from misrepresentation
Explain the effect of mistake of fact and of law
Identify agreements expressly declared void under sections 26–30
Advise on unlawful object and consideration under section 23

scenes.text: In the 1890s, Dharmodas Ghose, a minor, mortgaged his house to a moneylender for a loan.
Later he sued to cancel the mortgage. The lender wanted his money back.
The Privy Council's ruling still governs minors' contracts in India.

steps.title: Section 11
steps.body: Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject (18 under the Indian Majority Act, 1875, generally), is of sound mind, and is not disqualified by any law.

steps.title: Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose (1903)
steps.body: An agreement with a minor is **void ab initio**. The minor could not be made to repay the loan, and the mortgage was set aside.

steps.title: Rules on minors
steps.body:
- No estoppel against a minor who lied about age.
- Cannot ratify on attaining majority.
- Can be a promisee or beneficiary (e.g. receive a promissory note).
- Liable for **necessaries** supplied, but only from his property, not personally (s.68).
- Can be admitted to benefits of a partnership (Partnership Act s.30) but not be a full partner.
- Parents not liable unless they authorised the contract.

steps.title: Unsound mind and disqualified persons
steps.body: Section 12: a person of sound mind is one who can understand the contract and judge its effect on his interests. A usually unsound person may contract in lucid intervals; a usually sound person cannot while temporarily unsound (e.g. very drunk). Disqualified: alien enemies, insolvents in some respects, convicts while serving sentence, and foreign sovereigns/diplomats (subject to immunity).

activity.prompt: Can the creditor recover?

items.text: Price of necessary food supplied to a minor, from the minor's property
Loan given to a minor who lied about his age, from the minor personally
Price of luxury watch sold on credit to a minor
Contract made by a person of unsound mind during a lucid interval

quiz.q: An agreement with a minor is
quiz.why: Mohori Bibee held a minor's agreement void from the start.

quiz.q: For necessaries supplied to a minor, the supplier can recover
quiz.why: Section 68 makes the minor's property liable, not the minor personally.

quiz.q: A minor may
quiz.why: A minor can receive benefits under a contract, though he cannot be bound by it.

scenes.text: A threatens to harm B's son unless B sells his shop to A cheaply.
Elsewhere, a spiritual guru persuades an elderly follower to gift him all her land.
Both consents were not free, but for different reasons.

steps.title: Free consent (s.13, 14)
steps.body: Consent is agreeing upon the same thing in the same sense (consensus ad idem). It is free when not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake.

steps.title: Coercion (s.15)
steps.body: Committing or threatening to commit any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code, or unlawfully detaining or threatening to detain property, to cause any person to enter into an agreement. Since the criminal law has been replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, read the reference as being to acts forbidden by the criminal law. It can be by anyone, against anyone. Effect: contract **voidable** (s.19).

steps.title: Undue influence (s.16)
steps.body: Where one party is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses it to obtain an unfair advantage. Presumed relationships: real or apparent authority (employer–employee), fiduciary (guardian–ward, doctor–patient, spiritual adviser), mental distress. If the transaction appears unconscionable, burden shifts to the dominant party. Effect: voidable (s.19A); court may set aside on terms.

steps.title: Coercion vs undue influence
steps.body: Coercion uses physical or criminal force; undue influence uses mental pressure arising from a relationship. Coercion need not involve the parties' relationship.

activity.prompt: Match the case to the vitiating factor
pairs: Threat to burn a factory unless a contract is signed
Doctor obtains a patient's flat at a low price
Withholding someone's goods unlawfully to force a deal
Guru takes property from a devoted follower

quiz.q: A contract caused by coercion is
options: voidable at the option of the coerced party
quiz.why: Section 19 makes it voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.

quiz.q: Undue influence requires
options: a position to dominate the will and its use for unfair advantage
quiz.why: Section 16 focuses on domination of will within a relationship.

quiz.q: Which relationship is presumed to involve possible undue influence?
quiz.why: Fiduciary relationships such as doctor–patient raise the presumption.

scenes.text: A dealer rolls back a car's odometer from 90,000 km to 30,000 km.
Another seller honestly but wrongly says his car has never had an accident.
One is fraud, the other misrepresentation.

steps.title: Fraud (s.17)
steps.body: Acts by a party with intent to deceive: false suggestion of fact known to be untrue, active concealment, a promise made without intention to perform, any other deceitful act, or acts declared fraudulent by law. Mere silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak or silence is equivalent to speech. Effect: voidable; the victim may also claim damages.

steps.title: Misrepresentation (s.18)
steps.body: Innocent false statement believed true, breach of duty without intent to deceive, or causing a mistake innocently. Effect: voidable, but generally no damages. If the victim could have discovered the truth with ordinary diligence, the contract is not voidable (exception to s.19).

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body:
- **Bilateral mistake of fact** essential to the agreement → **void** (s.20), e.g. subject matter had already perished.
- **Unilateral mistake** → generally not voidable (s.22), except mistake as to identity or nature of document in some cases.
- **Mistake of Indian law** → no relief (s.21); mistake of foreign law treated as mistake of fact.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Do not call a bilateral mistake 'voidable'. Under s.20 the agreement is void.

activity.prompt: Match the situation to its effect
pairs: Both parties unaware cargo had sunk
No relief: mistake of Indian law

quiz.q: Silence is fraud when
options: there is a duty to speak
quiz.why: Under s.17 silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak or silence equals speech.

quiz.q: Both parties believe a horse is alive; it died yesterday. Agreement is
quiz.why: Section 20 makes agreements under bilateral mistake of essential fact void.

quiz.q: Misrepresentation differs from fraud mainly in
quiz.why: Fraud requires intent to deceive; misrepresentation is innocent.

scenes.text: A software engineer's contract says she cannot work for any rival anywhere in India for 2 years after leaving.
She resigns and joins a competitor.
Can her old employer stop her?

steps.title: Unlawful object or consideration (s.23)
steps.body: Unlawful if forbidden by law, would defeat any law, fraudulent, injurious to person or property, or immoral or opposed to public policy. Such agreements are void.

steps.title: Agreements expressly declared void
steps.body:
- s.26 restraint of marriage (of any person other than a minor).
- s.27 restraint of trade: void except sale of goodwill with reasonable local limits.
- s.28 restraint of legal proceedings (with exceptions for arbitration).
- s.29 uncertain agreements.
- s.30 wagering agreements.
- s.56 agreements to do impossible acts.

steps.title: Restraint of trade in practice
steps.body: Indian courts have generally held post-employment non-compete clauses void under s.27, while restrictions during employment and reasonable non-solicitation or confidentiality clauses are usually upheld. So the engineer's 2-year all-India restraint is likely void.

steps.title: Wagering
steps.body: A promise to pay money on an uncertain event in which neither party has any interest except the stake. Void, though not illegal in general; collateral transactions are not affected by the Contract Act alone. Insurance contracts, prize competitions involving skill, and commercial transactions are not wagers.

Bet on a cricket match result between friends

quiz.q: Which section declares agreements in restraint of trade void?
quiz.why: Section 27 voids restraints on lawful profession, trade or business, with the goodwill exception.

quiz.q: Wagering agreements are
quiz.why: Section 30 declares them void; they are not automatically illegal.

quiz.q: An insurance contract is not a wager because
options: the insured has an insurable interest
quiz.why: Insurable interest distinguishes insurance from betting.

questions.why: The exception to section 19 denies avoidance in that case.

questions.why: Section 21: ignorance of Indian law is no excuse.

questions.q: An agreement restraining legal proceedings is void under

questions.why: Neither party has an interest beyond the stake.

questions.q: A drunk person who cannot understand the contract at that time
questions.why: Section 12 tests ability to understand at the time of contracting.

questions.q: Agreement to sell goodwill with a covenant not to compete locally for a reasonable period is
options: valid under the exception to section 27
questions.why: Sale of goodwill is the statutory exception to section 27.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Contingent Contracts, Performance, Discharge, Quasi-Contracts and Remedies
courses.summary: Contingent contracts, who must perform and how, time as essence, modes of discharge including frustration under section 56 and novation, quasi-contracts under sections 68–72, and remedies for breach: damages under section 73 with Hadley v Baxendale, liquidated damages and penalties, specific performance, injunction and quantum meruit.
outcomes: Apply rules on contingent contracts
Identify the modes of discharge of a contract
Decide when supervening impossibility frustrates a contract
Explain the five quasi-contractual situations
Compute and classify damages for breach

scenes.text: A Mumbai importer agrees to buy cotton bales 'if the ship Sagar returns safely to port'.
The ship sinks in a storm.
The contract depended on an uncertain future event.

steps.title: Contingent contract (s.31)
steps.body: A contract to do or not to do something if some event collateral to the contract does or does not happen. Rules (s.32–36): enforceable only when the event happens; void if the event becomes impossible; contracts on an event not happening become enforceable when its happening becomes impossible; contingent on impossible events are void. Insurance and indemnity are common examples.

steps.title: Performance (s.37 onwards)
steps.body: Parties must perform or offer to perform. A valid **tender** must be unconditional, at proper time and place, of the whole obligation, with reasonable opportunity to inspect. Performance may be by the promisor, agent, legal representatives (unless personal skill involved), or a third person if accepted.

steps.title: Time as essence (s.55)
steps.body: If time is of the essence and the promisor fails to perform in time, the contract becomes voidable at the promisee's option. If time is not of the essence, the promisee may claim compensation but cannot avoid. In commercial contracts, time is often of the essence; in sales of immovable property it is generally presumed not to be unless expressly made so.

steps.title: Reciprocal promises
steps.body: Order of performance as agreed or as the nature of the transaction requires. If one party prevents the other from performing, the contract becomes voidable at the option of the party prevented (s.53).

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the rule
pairs: Pay if the ship returns; ship sinks
Pay if a person does not marry X; X dies
Cannot be done by legal representatives

quiz.q: An insurance contract is an example of
quiz.why: Payment depends on an uncertain collateral event such as fire or death.

quiz.q: A valid tender must be
options: unconditional and of the whole obligation
quiz.why: Tender must be unconditional, complete, and at the proper time and place.

quiz.q: If time is not of the essence and delivery is late, the buyer can
quiz.why: Section 55 allows compensation but not avoidance when time is not essential.

scenes.text: A family books a marriage hall in Jaipur for 12 December.
On 1 December the hall burns down without anyone's fault.
Is the hall owner in breach, or is the contract discharged?

steps.title: Modes of discharge
steps.body:
1 Performance (actual or attempted).
2 Mutual agreement (s.62–63): novation, rescission, alteration, remission, waiver, merger.
3 Impossibility (s.56).
4 Lapse of time (Limitation Act, 1963; generally 3 years for contract suits).
5 Operation of law: death, insolvency, merger, unauthorised material alteration.
6 Breach: actual or anticipatory.

steps.title: Frustration (s.56)
steps.body: A contract to do an act which, after it is made, becomes impossible or unlawful, without the promisor's fault, becomes void. Examples: destruction of subject matter (Taylor v Caldwell, music hall burned), death or incapacity in personal contracts, change of law, outbreak of war, non-occurrence of the very basis of contract. The Supreme Court in Satyabrata Ghose v Mugneeram Bangur (1954) read 'impossible' as including impracticable in the light of the contract's object.

steps.title: Not frustration
steps.body: Mere difficulty, higher cost, commercial hardship, strikes or riots (usually), or failure of one of several purposes.

steps.title: Anticipatory breach
steps.body: When a party refuses before the due date to perform, the other may treat the contract as ended and sue at once, or wait for the due date (s.39).

steps.title: The hall case
steps.body: Destruction of the subject matter without fault frustrates the contract; any advance must be refunded under s.65.

activity.prompt: Frustrated or not?

New law bans the goods to be supplied

quiz.why: Novation replaces the existing contract with a new one, possibly between different parties.

quiz.why: Section 39 deals with refusal before performance is due.

story.title: Money sent to the wrong account

scenes.text: Ritu sends ₹40,000 by UPI to a mistyped account belonging to a stranger.
The stranger says: we had no contract, I owe you nothing.
The law creates an obligation anyway.

steps.title: Idea
steps.body: Quasi-contracts are obligations imposed by law to prevent unjust enrichment, even without an agreement. The Contract Act calls them 'certain relations resembling those created by contract'.

steps.title: Sections 68–72
steps.body:
- s.68: necessaries supplied to a person incapable of contracting: recoverable from their property.
- s.69: payment by an interested person of money another is bound to pay (e.g. paying arrears of revenue to save your property).
- s.70: non-gratuitous act: a person who lawfully does something for another, not intending it gratuitously, where the other enjoys the benefit.
- s.71: finder of goods has the responsibilities of a bailee.
- s.72: money paid or thing delivered by mistake or under coercion must be repaid or returned.

steps.title: Ritu's case
steps.body: Money paid by mistake falls under s.72; the recipient must repay.

steps.title: Quantum meruit
steps.body: 'As much as is earned': a claim for reasonable payment for work done when a contract is discovered void, is discharged by breach by the other party, or when work is accepted though not fully as agreed.

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the section
pairs: Food supplied to a person of unsound mind
Tenant pays landlord's overdue tax to prevent auction
Trader leaves goods at a house by mistake; owner uses them

quiz.q: Quasi-contracts are based on
quiz.why: Law imposes the obligation so no one is unjustly enriched at another's expense.

quiz.q: A finder of goods is treated as a
quiz.why: Section 71 gives the finder the responsibilities of a bailee.

quiz.q: Quantum meruit means
quiz.why: It allows reasonable payment for work actually done.

lessons.title: Remedies for breach: damages and equitable relief

scenes.text: A mill's crankshaft breaks and is sent for repair by a carrier, who delays delivery.
The mill stays idle; it claims its lost profits.
Hadley v Baxendale (1854) set the test for which losses can be claimed.

steps.title: Section 73 and Hadley v Baxendale
steps.body: Compensation for loss which naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or which the parties knew when they made the contract to be likely to result. Remote and indirect losses are not recoverable. In Hadley, the carrier did not know the mill would be idle, so lost profits were too remote.

steps.title: Kinds of damages
steps.body: Ordinary (general), special (with notice of special circumstances), exemplary (rare in contract; e.g. dishonour of a cheque by a bank with sufficient funds in older cases, breach of promise to marry), nominal (no real loss), and damages for inconvenience. Duty to **mitigate** loss applies.

steps.title: Measuring damages
steps.body: Contract to buy 100 quintals of wheat at ₹2,400/quintal for delivery on 1 March. Seller fails; market price on 1 March is ₹2,650. Ordinary damages = (2,650 − 2,400) × 100 = **₹25,000**.

steps.title: Liquidated damages and penalty (s.74)
steps.body: Where a sum is named in the contract as payable on breach, the injured party can recover reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount named, whether it is a genuine pre-estimate or a penalty. Indian law does not strictly separate the two as English law does.

steps.title: Other remedies
steps.body: Rescission, specific performance (under the Specific Relief Act, 1963, where damages are inadequate, e.g. unique property), injunction (prohibitory or mandatory), quantum meruit, and suit for price.

activity.prompt: Match the remedy
pairs: Buyer of a unique painting wants the painting itself
Stop a singer performing for a rival in breach of a negative covenant
Loss that arises naturally from breach

quiz.q: Contract price ₹500/unit for 200 units; market price on delivery date ₹560. Seller defaults. Damages =

courses.title: Unit 4 · Special Contracts: Indemnity, Guarantee, Bailment, Pledge and Agency

scenes.text: Anil takes a ₹5 lakh business loan from a bank. His friend Vinod signs as guarantor.

steps.title: Indemnity (s.124)
steps.body: A contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused by the conduct of the promisor or any other person. Two parties: indemnifier and indemnity holder. Rights of the indemnity holder (s.125): recover damages, costs of suits and sums paid under a compromise, if acting prudently and within authority.

steps.title: Guarantee (s.126)
steps.body: A contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. Three parties: **surety**, **principal debtor** and **creditor**. May be oral or written. Anything done for the benefit of the principal debtor may be sufficient consideration for the surety (s.127).

steps.title: Surety's liability
steps.body: **Coextensive** with that of the principal debtor unless the contract provides otherwise (s.128). The creditor can sue the surety directly without first suing the debtor. A **continuing guarantee** (s.129) extends to a series of transactions and can be revoked for future transactions by notice (s.130).

steps.title: Indemnity vs guarantee
steps.body: Indemnity: 2 parties, primary liability, one contract, liability arises on loss. Guarantee: 3 parties, secondary liability, three contracts, liability arises on default; surety has right of subrogation (s.140).

Lend him ₹50,000; if he doesn't pay, I will

steps.title: Modes of discharge of surety
steps.body:
- Revocation by notice (continuing guarantee, s.130) or death of surety (s.131) for future transactions.
- **Variance** in terms without surety's consent (s.133).
- Release or discharge of principal debtor (s.134).
- Composition, extension of time or promise not to sue the debtor without surety's consent (s.135).
- Creditor's act or omission impairing surety's eventual remedy (s.139).
- Loss of security by creditor (s.141).

steps.title: Rights of surety
steps.body:
- Against the principal debtor: **subrogation** (s.140) and **indemnity** (s.145).
- Against the creditor: benefit of securities held by creditor (s.141), set-off.
- Against co-sureties: contribution equally or proportionately (s.146–147).

steps.title: Co-sureties
steps.body: A, B and C are co-sureties for ₹3,00,000 with no other agreement. Debtor defaults fully. Each contributes ₹1,00,000. If their limits were ₹1,00,000, ₹2,00,000 and ₹3,00,000 respectively and the default is ₹3,00,000, they contribute in proportion 1 : 2 : 3, i.e. ₹50,000, ₹1,00,000 and ₹1,50,000, within their limits (s.147).

steps.title: Bailment (s.148)
steps.body: Delivery of goods by one person (bailor) to another (bailee) for some purpose, on a contract that they shall be returned or disposed of as directed when the purpose is accomplished. Essentials: delivery of possession, purpose, return of the specific goods. Money and immovable property are not subjects of bailment.

steps.title: Duties
steps.body:
- Bailee: take reasonable care like a person of ordinary prudence (s.151); no unauthorised use (s.154); not mix goods (s.155–157); return goods (s.160); return accretions (s.163).
- Bailor: disclose known faults (s.150); bear necessary expenses in gratuitous bailment (s.158).

steps.title: Lien
steps.body: **Particular lien** (s.170): bailee who renders services involving skill or labour can retain the goods until paid for those services. **General lien** (s.171): bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court and policy brokers may retain goods for a general balance of account.

steps.title: Pledge (s.172)
steps.body: Bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise. Pawnor and pawnee. On default (s.176) the pawnee may sue on the debt and retain the goods, or sell after giving reasonable notice; any surplus goes to the pawnor and any shortfall remains recoverable.

steps.title: Pawnee's sale
steps.body: Loan due ₹1,00,000 plus ₹6,000 expenses. After reasonable notice, coins sold for ₹1,20,000. Surplus to pawnor = 1,20,000 − 1,06,000 = **₹14,000**. If sold for ₹90,000, pawnor still owes **₹16,000**.

steps.title: Definition (s.182)
steps.body: An agent is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in dealings with third persons. The person represented is the principal. Consideration is not necessary to create agency (s.185). Any person of majority and sound mind may be a principal; anyone can be an agent, but a minor agent is not personally liable to the principal.

steps.title: Creation of agency
steps.body: Express, implied (including by estoppel or holding out), by necessity, and by **ratification** (s.196). Valid ratification requires: principal in existence and competent when the act was done, act done on behalf of the principal, full knowledge of facts, ratification of the whole transaction, within reasonable time, and act must be lawful (not void ab initio).

steps.title: Agent's duties
steps.body: Follow instructions or custom (s.211), act with reasonable skill and diligence (s.212), render accounts (s.213), not deal on own account without consent (s.215–216), pay sums received, not delegate except as allowed (s.190).

steps.title: Termination (s.201)
steps.body: By revocation by principal, renunciation by agent, completion of business, death or insanity of either, insolvency of principal, or expiry of time. An agency coupled with interest cannot be revoked to the agent's prejudice (s.202).

steps.title: Neha's case
steps.body: The broker dealt on his own account (through his cousin) without disclosure and sold below her minimum. She may repudiate the sale and claim from him any benefit he made (s.215–216) and damages for disobeying instructions.

courses.title: Unit 5 · The Sale of Goods Act, 1930
courses.summary: Sale vs agreement to sell, goods and price, conditions and warranties with implied terms and caveat emptor, transfer of property and risk, sale by non-owners (nemo dat) and its exceptions, rights of the unpaid seller (lien, stoppage in transit, resale), and auction sales.
outcomes: Distinguish a sale from an agreement to sell and from hire-purchase

lessons.title: Contract of sale: essentials and kinds of goods

scenes.text: A farmer in Punjab pays ₹50,000 to book a tractor that will be delivered next month.
Before delivery, the dealer's yard catches fire.
Whose loss is it? It depends on whether this was a sale or an agreement to sell.

steps.title: Section 4
steps.body: A contract of sale is a contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price. If property passes immediately, it is a **sale**; if it is to pass in future or on a condition, it is an **agreement to sell**, which becomes a sale when the time elapses or conditions are fulfilled.

steps.title: Essentials
steps.body: Two parties, goods (movable property, excluding actionable claims and money; includes stock and shares, growing crops attached to land agreed to be severed), price in money, transfer of property (ownership), and the general essentials of a valid contract.

steps.title: Kinds of goods
steps.body:
- **Existing**: specific (identified and agreed at the time), ascertained, unascertained (generic).
- **Future**: to be manufactured or acquired after the contract.
- **Contingent**: acquisition depends on an uncertain event.
A present sale of future goods operates only as an agreement to sell (s.6).

steps.title: Sale vs hire-purchase
steps.body: In hire-purchase, the hirer gets possession and pays instalments, with an option to buy; ownership passes on the last payment. In a sale, ownership passes as agreed, usually at once for specific goods.

steps.title: Back to the tractor
steps.body: If the tractor was not yet identified (unascertained), there was only an agreement to sell; ownership and risk remained with the dealer, who bears the loss.

activity.prompt: Sale or agreement to sell?

Ordering a sofa to be made next month

scenes.text: Imran tells a shopkeeper he needs a watch for swimming. The shopkeeper recommends one.

steps.title: Condition vs warranty (s.12)
steps.body:
- **Condition**: stipulation essential to the main purpose; breach gives the right to **reject** goods and treat the contract as repudiated.
- **Warranty**: collateral to the main purpose; breach gives a claim for **damages** only.
A buyer may waive a condition or treat its breach as a breach of warranty (s.13).

steps.title: Implied conditions
steps.body:
- s.14 title: seller has the right to sell.
- s.15 sale by description: goods correspond with description.
- s.16(1) fitness for purpose: when buyer makes the purpose known and relies on seller's skill.
- s.16(2) merchantable quality: when bought by description from a dealer.
- s.17 sale by sample: bulk corresponds to sample, reasonable chance to compare, free from hidden defects.
Implied warranties: quiet possession, freedom from encumbrances, disclosure of dangerous nature.

steps.title: Caveat emptor (s.16)
steps.body: 'Let the buyer beware': in general there is no implied condition about quality or fitness. Exceptions: fitness for a made-known purpose relied on, merchantable quality, usage of trade, sale by sample, seller's fraud, and conditions under consumer protection law.

steps.title: Imran's case
steps.body: He made his purpose known and relied on the seller's skill; the implied condition of fitness under s.16(1) was breached, so he may reject the watch and recover the price.

Goods fit for a disclosed purpose

quiz.why: Warranties are collateral, so breach allows damages but not rejection.

quiz.why: Generally the buyer must satisfy himself about quality and fitness.

lessons.title: Transfer of property, risk and sale by non-owners

scenes.text: Rahul buys a scooter at a fair price from a stranger who had stolen it.
The real owner finds it and demands it back.

steps.title: When property passes
steps.body:
- Specific goods in a deliverable state: when the contract is made (s.20), even if payment or delivery is postponed.
- Specific goods to be put in deliverable state: when done and buyer has notice (s.21).
- Specific goods to be weighed or measured to fix price: when done and buyer has notice (s.22).
- Unascertained goods: when goods are ascertained and unconditionally appropriated to the contract (s.23).
- Sale or return: on approval, retention beyond time, or act adopting the transaction (s.24).

steps.title: Risk follows property (s.26)
steps.body: Unless otherwise agreed, goods remain at the seller's risk until property passes, whether or not delivery has been made. If delivery is delayed by the fault of either party, that party bears the risk of loss caused by the delay.

steps.title: Nemo dat quod non habet (s.27)
steps.body: No one can give a better title than he has. Exceptions: sale by mercantile agent in ordinary course, by one of joint owners in sole possession, under a voidable contract not yet rescinded (s.29), by seller or buyer in possession after sale (s.30), by estoppel, by finder or pawnee in specified cases.

steps.title: Rahul's case
steps.body: A thief has no title, so Rahul acquires none; the owner can recover the scooter. Rahul's remedy is against the thief. (Contrast: goods obtained under a voidable contract can pass good title to a bona fide buyer before rescission.)

steps.title: Unpaid seller (s.45)
steps.body: A seller who has not been paid or tendered the whole price, or who received a negotiable instrument that has been dishonoured.

steps.title: Rights against the goods
steps.body:
- **Lien** (s.47): retain goods in possession until paid, when goods sold without credit, credit expired, or buyer insolvent. Lost on delivery to carrier without reserving disposal, buyer obtaining possession lawfully, or waiver.
- **Stoppage in transit** (s.50): when the buyer is insolvent and goods are with a carrier, the seller can resume possession.
- **Resale** (s.54): if goods are perishable, or after notice of intention to resell and buyer fails to pay within reasonable time.

steps.title: Rights against the buyer personally
steps.body: Suit for price (s.55), damages for non-acceptance (s.56), interest and special damages (s.61), and suit for repudiation before the due date.

steps.title: Auction sales (s.64)
steps.body: Each lot is a separate contract; sale is complete on the fall of the hammer; a bid may be withdrawn before then; seller may reserve the right to bid only if notified; pretended bidding to raise the price makes the sale voidable at the buyer's option.

steps.title: The trader's case
steps.body: The buyer is insolvent and goods are in transit, so the trader can exercise stoppage in transit by notice to the carrier.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Negotiable Instruments, Company and LLP Law, and Consumer Protection
courses.summary: Promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques; holder and holder in due course; crossing; dishonour of cheques under section 138 and its procedure; companies under the Companies Act, 2013 (features, kinds, MoA, AoA, indoor management); LLPs under the LLP Act, 2008; and consumer rights, commissions and product liability under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

lessons.title: Negotiable instruments: notes, bills and cheques

scenes.text: A Kanpur leather supplier receives a post-dated cheque of ₹2 lakh from a shoe maker.
He endorses it to his own creditor to settle a debt.
The cheque is a negotiable instrument: it passes from hand to hand like money.

steps.title: Section 13 and the three instruments
steps.body:
A negotiable instrument means a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable either to order or to bearer.
- **Promissory note (s.4)**: unconditional written promise, signed by the maker, to pay a certain sum to a certain person or order. Two parties: maker, payee. Cannot be made payable to bearer (RBI Act s.31 restriction).
- **Bill of exchange (s.5)**: unconditional written order, signed by the drawer, directing a certain person to pay. Three parties: drawer, drawee, payee; needs acceptance.
- **Cheque (s.6)**: bill drawn on a specified banker, payable on demand; includes electronic cheque and truncated cheque.

steps.title: Holder and holder in due course
steps.body: **Holder (s.8)**: person entitled in his own name to possession and to receive the amount. **Holder in due course (s.9)**: holder for consideration, who became holder before maturity, without sufficient cause to believe any defect in the title of the transferor. An HDC gets a good title free from prior defects.

steps.title: Crossing
steps.body:
- **General crossing (s.123)**: two parallel transverse lines, with or without '& Co.' or 'not negotiable': payable only through a bank account.
- **Special crossing (s.124)**: name of a banker added: payable only through that bank.
- **Account payee**: banking practice requiring credit only to the payee's account.
- **Not negotiable (s.130)**: transferee gets no better title than transferor.

steps.title: Negotiation
steps.body: Bearer instruments are negotiated by delivery; order instruments by endorsement and delivery.

activity.prompt: Match the instrument or term
pairs: Unconditional promise to pay, signed by maker
Unconditional order to pay, needs acceptance
Bill drawn on a banker, payable on demand

quiz.why: Maker and payee are the two parties to a promissory note.

quiz.why: Section 6 defines a cheque as a bill payable on demand.

quiz.q: Writing 'not negotiable' on a crossed cheque means
options: the transferee gets no better title than the transferor
quiz.why: Section 130 limits the transferee's title to that of the transferor.

scenes.text: The ₹2 lakh cheque is returned: 'funds insufficient'.
The supplier's lawyer sends a legal notice to the shoe maker.
Strict time limits apply at every step.

steps.title: Ingredients of the offence
steps.body:
1 Cheque drawn for discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability.
2 Presented within its validity (3 months from date under current RBI directions).
3 Returned unpaid for insufficient funds or exceeding arrangement.
4 Payee gives written **notice within 30 days** of receiving the bank's information.
5 Drawer fails to pay **within 15 days** of receiving the notice.

steps.title: Timeline example
steps.body: Cheque dated 1 June, presented 10 July (within 3 months), return memo received 12 July. Notice must be sent by 11 August (30 days). Notice received by drawer 16 July; 15 days end 31 July. Cause of action arises 1 August. Complaint to be filed within **one month** of that date (s.142), i.e. by about 31 August; courts may condone delay for sufficient cause.

steps.title: Punishment and interim relief
steps.body: Imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both. The court may order interim compensation up to 20% of the cheque amount (s.143A). The offence is compoundable (s.147). Companies: persons in charge may be liable (s.141).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: A cheque given as a gift or for a debt not legally enforceable does not attract s.138. There is a presumption in favour of the holder (s.139) that the cheque was for a debt, which the drawer may rebut.

activity.prompt: Match the step to its time limit

Within 1 month of cause of action

quiz.q: The maximum fine under section 138 is
quiz.why: Section 138 allows a fine up to twice the amount of the cheque.

quiz.q: Interim compensation under section 143A can be up to
quiz.why: The court may order up to 20% of the cheque amount as interim compensation.

quiz.q: A cheque given as a birthday gift bounces. Section 138
quiz.why: Section 138 requires a legally enforceable debt or liability, which a gift is not.

scenes.text: Three friends run a successful bakery as a partnership.
An investor offers funding but wants limited liability and shares.
They consider a private company or an LLP.

steps.title: Company: meaning and features
steps.body: Company means a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 or a previous company law (s.2(20)). Features: separate legal entity (Salomon v Salomon & Co, 1897), limited liability, perpetual succession, common seal (now optional), transferability of shares (restricted in private companies), separate property, capacity to sue and be sued.

steps.title: Kinds
steps.body:
- **Private company (s.2(68))**: restricts share transfer, maximum 200 members (excluding employee members), minimum 2 members and 2 directors.
- **Public company (s.2(71))**: not private; minimum 7 members and 3 directors.
- **One Person Company (s.2(62))**: single member, natural person who is an Indian citizen.

uni-bba-business-research-methods.description: Business research methods for BBA: research process, problem and hypothesis formulation, research designs, sampling and sample size, measurement and scaling, questionnaire design, primary and secondary data, descriptive statistics, z, t and chi-square tests, report writing and research ethics, with worked examples. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BBA programmes.

lessons.title: Meaning and types of business research

scenes.text: A Jaipur beverage brand sees a 12% fall in sales in two districts.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: Business research is a systematic, objective inquiry that provides information to guide managerial decisions. Features: systematic, logical, empirical, replicable, objective. The scientific method moves from observation → problem → hypothesis → data → analysis → conclusion, open to revision.

steps.title: Types
steps.body: By purpose: **basic (pure)** builds theory; **applied** solves a specific problem. By objective: **exploratory** (clarify vague problems: interviews, focus groups, secondary data), **descriptive** (who, what, how many: surveys), **causal/explanatory** (cause and effect: experiments). By data: **quantitative** vs **qualitative**. By time: **cross-sectional** vs **longitudinal**.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body:
Exploratory: depth interviews with retailers on why the drink is not reordered.
Descriptive: survey of 400 consumers on brand awareness by age.
Causal: test whether a ₹5 price cut raises sales in matched test and control towns.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a survey 'causal': surveys show association, not cause.
- Skipping exploratory work when the problem is vague.

steps.title: Steps

The process is iterative: findings can send you back to redefine the problem.

steps.title: Research proposal
steps.body: Contents: title, background, problem statement, objectives, hypotheses, scope, methodology (design, sampling, tools, analysis), timeline, budget, expected outcomes, references. It is the contract between researcher and sponsor.

steps.title: Value of information
steps.body: Do research only if the expected value of better information exceeds its cost and time; for small, reversible decisions, a quick pilot may be enough.

steps.title: Management vs research problem
steps.body: **Management dilemma/decision problem**: what should the manager do? (e.g. Should we cut price?) **Research problem**: what information is needed? (e.g. What are the reasons for declining repeat purchase in districts X and Y?) Then derive **research questions** and **investigative questions**. A good problem statement is specific, researchable, relevant and ethical.

steps.title: Worked example: from dilemma to questions
steps.body:
Dilemma: sales down 12%.
Research problem: identify factors behind lower repeat purchase among 18–30 consumers in two districts.
Research questions: (1) Has awareness fallen? (2) Is availability lower at outlets? (3) How is price perceived versus rivals? (4) Has taste preference shifted?

steps.title: Literature review
steps.body: Purpose: avoid repetition, find theories and variables, identify gaps, choose methods. Sources: journals (via Google Scholar, J-Gate, EBSCO, ProQuest), books, industry reports, government data (MoSPI, RBI). Write it thematically, not as a list of summaries; end with the research gap. Cite consistently (APA style is common in management).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the problem as a solution ('to prove that price cuts work').
- A literature review that only summarises papers one by one with no synthesis.

scenes.text: An insurer asks whether its 3-day sales training improves agents' monthly premium collection.

steps.title: Variables
steps.body: **Independent (IV)**: presumed cause (training). **Dependent (DV)**: outcome (premium collected). **Moderating**: changes the strength of the IV-DV link (agent experience). **Mediating (intervening)**: explains how the IV affects the DV (product knowledge). **Extraneous/control**: other influences held constant (territory).

steps.title: Hypotheses
steps.body: A hypothesis is a testable statement of relationship between variables. **Null (H₀)**: no effect or no difference (μ_trained = μ_untrained). **Alternative (H₁)**: the effect exists (μ_trained > μ_untrained: one-tailed; ≠: two-tailed). Good hypotheses are clear, specific, testable, and based on theory or prior evidence.

steps.title: Errors
steps.body: **Type I error (α)**: rejecting a true H₀ (concluding training works when it does not). **Type II error (β)**: failing to reject a false H₀. Power = 1 − β. Lowering α increases β for a given sample size; larger samples reduce both.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing H₀ as the claim you hope is true.
- 'Accepting' H₀: correctly, we fail to reject it.

story.title: Will the new shelf display work?

scenes.text: A supermarket chain in Chennai wants to know if an end-of-aisle display raises biscuit sales.
Comparing a store before and after is not enough: Diwali might have caused the rise.

steps.title: Design as a blueprint
steps.body: Research design is the plan for collecting and analysing data to answer the research question within constraints of time and cost. Exploratory designs are flexible (secondary data, expert interviews, pilot studies, case studies). Descriptive designs are structured (cross-sectional surveys, panels). Causal designs are experiments with manipulation, control and randomisation.

steps.title: Validity
steps.body: **Internal validity**: the observed change is due to the treatment. Threats: history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, selection, mortality (dropout), regression to the mean. **External validity**: results generalise to other people, places and times. Lab experiments have high internal validity; field experiments have higher external validity.

steps.title: Basic layouts (O = observation, X = treatment, R = random)
steps.body: One-shot case study: X O (weak). One-group pre-post: O₁ X O₂ (history threat). **Pre-test post-test control group**: R O₁ X O₂ / R O₃ O₄. Effect = (O₂ − O₁) − (O₄ − O₃). Post-test-only control group: R X O₁ / R O₂.

steps.title: Worked example: treatment effect
steps.body:
Test stores: weekly biscuit sales 500 before, 620 after. Control stores: 480 before, 540 after.
Effect = (620 − 500) − (540 − 480) = 120 − 60 = **60 units per week**. The 60-unit rise in control stores reflects the festival season.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a one-group pre-post design and calling the whole change the treatment effect.
- Assigning the best stores to the treatment (selection bias).

scenes.text: An IT firm in Pune wants to survey job satisfaction among its 2,000 employees.

steps.title: Process and terms
steps.body: Population (all elements of interest) → sampling frame (list of elements, e.g. HR database) → sampling unit → method → sample size → execution. Census = study every element. Sample statistic estimates population parameter.

steps.title: Probability methods
steps.body: Every element has a known, non-zero chance of selection. **Simple random**: lottery or random numbers. **Systematic**: every kth element after a random start, k = N/n. **Stratified**: divide into homogeneous strata (department, grade) and sample from each, proportionally or disproportionately. **Cluster**: randomly select whole groups (branches) and survey all or some within them; cheaper but less precise. **Multistage**: clusters at several levels (state → district → village).

steps.title: Worked example 1: systematic
steps.body: N = 2,000, n = 100 → k = **20**. Random start between 1 and 20, say 7: select 7, 27, 47, … 1,987.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Systematic sampling from a list with a periodic pattern (e.g. every 20th is a team lead).
- Confusing strata (sample within each) with clusters (sample whole groups).

steps.title: Methods
steps.body: Selection chance is unknown. **Convenience**: easiest to reach. **Judgement (purposive)**: expert picks typical cases. **Quota**: fill fixed quotas by characteristics (e.g. 50% women), but selection within quota is non-random. **Snowball**: respondents refer others (rare populations such as gig workers). Useful for exploratory work and pilots; not for statistical generalisation.

steps.title: Errors
steps.body: **Sampling error**: difference between sample statistic and parameter due to chance; falls as n rises. **Non-sampling errors**: frame error, non-response, interviewer bias, response bias (social desirability), measurement and processing errors; they do not fall with larger n and can be larger than sampling error.

steps.title: Worked example: response rate
steps.body: Questionnaires sent 800; usable returned 240. Response rate = 240 ÷ 800 = **30%**. If non-respondents differ (e.g. busier executives), results may be biased; send reminders and compare early vs late respondents.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling quota sampling 'stratified random'.
- Believing a very large online poll is unbiased.

scenes.text: A food-delivery app wants to measure customer satisfaction, delivery time and preferred cuisine.
Each needs a different kind of scale, and that decides which statistics are allowed.

steps.title: Four levels
steps.body: **Nominal**: categories only (gender, city); mode, frequency, chi-square. **Ordinal**: order without equal intervals (rank of brands); median, percentiles, rank correlation. **Interval**: equal intervals, arbitrary zero (temperature in °C, rating scales treated as interval); mean, SD, t-test. **Ratio**: true zero (income, delivery time, age); all statistics including ratios ('twice as long').

steps.title: Attitude scales
steps.body: **Likert**: agreement with statements on 5 or 7 points (strongly disagree to strongly agree). **Semantic differential**: bipolar adjectives (slow — fast) on 7 points. **Stapel**: unipolar −5 to +5 around one adjective. **Rank order**: rank brands 1 to n. **Constant sum**: allocate 100 points across attributes. **Paired comparison**: n(n − 1)/2 pairs.

steps.title: Worked example: paired comparisons
steps.body: Comparing 5 brands two at a time needs 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = **10 pairs**. For 8 brands, 28 pairs: respondent fatigue grows fast.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing a mean of nominal codes (e.g. average city = 2.4).
- Calling a ranking 'ratio' data.

quiz.q: Which level has a true zero?
quiz.why: Ratio scales have an absolute zero, so statements like 'twice as much' are meaningful.

quiz.why: Respondents divide a fixed total, revealing relative importance.

quiz.why: With order but unequal intervals, the median is the meaningful centre.

story.title: Does the scale measure what it claims?

scenes.text: A bathroom scale that always shows 2 kg too much is consistent but wrong.
Research scales need both consistency (reliability) and accuracy (validity).

steps.title: Reliability
steps.body: Consistency of measurement. **Test-retest**: same respondents, two occasions. **Parallel forms**. **Internal consistency**: split-half, **Cronbach's α = [k/(k − 1)] × [1 − Σσᵢ² ÷ σ_T²]**, where k = items, σᵢ² = item variances, σ_T² = variance of total score. α ≥ 0.7 is commonly treated as acceptable.

steps.title: Worked example: Cronbach's alpha
steps.body:
k = 4 items; sum of item variances = 6; variance of total = 15.
α = (4/3) × (1 − 6/15) = 1.333 × 0.6 = **0.80** → acceptable reliability.

steps.title: Validity
steps.body: **Content (face) validity**: items cover the concept (expert judgement). **Criterion validity**: correlates with an external criterion, concurrent or predictive. **Construct validity**: convergent (correlates with related measures) and discriminant (does not correlate with unrelated ones). A measure can be reliable without being valid, but not valid without being reliable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating reliability with validity.
- Applying α to a single-item measure.

quiz.why: It reflects how closely items in a scale move together.

quiz.why: Measures of the same or related concepts should agree.

steps.title: Primary data methods
steps.body: **Surveys**: personal interview, telephone, mail, online (cheap, fast, frame and response issues). **Observation**: structured/unstructured, participant/non-participant, human/mechanical (footfall counters, eye tracking); records actual behaviour but not motives. **Depth interviews** and **focus groups** (6–10 people, moderator, 60–90 minutes) for qualitative insight. **Experiments** for causal data.

steps.title: Secondary data
steps.body: Collected earlier for another purpose. Internal: sales records, CRM, accounts. External: Census of India, NSSO/MoSPI surveys, RBI database, company annual reports, industry associations, CMIE Prowess, journals. Evaluate: purpose, accuracy, recency, definitions, source credibility. Advantages: cheap and fast; limitations: may not fit, may be outdated.

steps.title: Rule of thumb
steps.body: Start with secondary data; collect primary data only for the gap that remains.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using secondary data without checking definitions (e.g. 'urban' differs across sources).
- Using focus groups to estimate market share.

steps.title: Design steps
steps.body: Specify information needed → decide method of administration → decide question content → choose structure (open, multiple choice, dichotomous, scale) → wording → sequence (funnel: general to specific; sensitive and demographic questions at the end) → layout → pre-test (pilot with 15–30 respondents) → revise.

steps.title: Wording rules
steps.body: Avoid **leading** questions ('Don't you agree…'), **double-barrelled** questions (fast *and* cheap), ambiguous words (often, regularly), jargon, assumptions ('How much do you spend on your car?' to non-owners), and burdensome recall. Make categories mutually exclusive and exhaustive (e.g. age 18–24, 25–34, …, include 'other').

steps.title: Worked example: rewriting
steps.body:
Bad: 'Don't you agree our fast and cheap delivery is great?'
Good: Q1 'How satisfied are you with delivery speed?' (1 = very dissatisfied … 5 = very satisfied). Q2 'How satisfied are you with delivery charges?' (same scale).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Overlapping categories (₹0–10,000 and ₹10,000–20,000).
- Skipping the pilot test.

lessons.title: Lab: z and t tests for a mean

story.title: Is average waiting time really 50 minutes?

scenes.text: A hospital claims average OPD waiting time is 50 minutes. A sample of 25 patients shows 52.
Is 2 minutes a real difference or just chance?

steps.title: Testing procedure
steps.body: 1 State H₀ and H₁ · 2 Choose α (usually 0.05) · 3 Choose test statistic · 4 Compute it · 5 Compare with critical value (or p-value with α) · 6 Decide and interpret in business terms. **z test**: σ known or n large (n ≥ 30): z = (x̄ − μ) ÷ (σ/√n). **t test**: σ unknown, small n: t = (x̄ − μ) ÷ (s/√n), df = n − 1.

steps.title: Worked example 1: z test
steps.body:
μ₀ = 100, σ = 15, n = 36, x̄ = 105, two-tailed α = 0.05 (critical ±1.96).
SE = 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5. z = 5 ÷ 2.5 = **2.0** > 1.96 → **reject H₀**: the mean differs from 100.

steps.title: Worked example 2: t test
steps.body:
μ₀ = 50, x̄ = 52, s = 5, n = 25, two-tailed α = 0.05, df = 24 (critical t = 2.064).
SE = 5 ÷ 5 = 1. t = 2 ÷ 1 = **2.0** < 2.064 → **fail to reject H₀**: the evidence is not strong enough to dispute the 50-minute claim.

steps.title: p-value
steps.body: The probability, if H₀ is true, of a result at least as extreme as observed. Reject H₀ if p ≤ α. For z = 2.0 two-tailed, p ≈ 0.046.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using z when σ is unknown and n is small.
- Saying 'p = 0.046 means a 4.6% chance H₀ is true'.

quiz.why: Estimating σ from a small sample adds uncertainty, captured by the t distribution.

story.title: Do men and women prefer different plans?

scenes.text: A telecom firm cross-tabulates gender against preference for Plan A or Plan B among 100 users.
The chi-square test checks whether preference depends on gender.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: H₀: the two categorical variables are independent. Expected frequency **E = (row total × column total) ÷ grand total**. **χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E**. df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1). Reject H₀ if χ² > critical value. Condition: expected counts should generally be at least 5.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Observed: Male A 30, B 20; Female A 20, B 30. Row totals 50, 50; column totals 50, 50; N = 100.
Each E = 50 × 50 ÷ 100 = 25.
Each (O − E)²/E = 25/25 = 1 → χ² = **4.0**. df = 1; critical at 5% = 3.841.
4.0 > 3.841 → **reject H₀**: preference is associated with gender.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using percentages instead of counts.
- Concluding causation from a significant chi-square.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Title page · Acknowledgement · Table of contents · **Executive summary** (problem, method, key findings, recommendations in 1–2 pages) · Introduction (background, problem, objectives, hypotheses) · Literature review · Research methodology (design, sample, instrument, analysis) · Data analysis and interpretation · Findings · Conclusions and recommendations · Limitations and scope for further research · References · Appendices (questionnaire, raw tables).

steps.title: Presenting data
steps.body: Number and title every table and figure; state units and source; put the key message in the title ('Table 3: 62% of 18–24 users prefer Plan B'). Use bar charts for comparisons, line charts for trends, pie charts only for few parts of a whole. Interpret every table in text below it.

steps.title: Style
steps.body: Write in clear, impersonal, past tense for methods and findings; separate findings (what the data shows) from recommendations (what to do).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- An executive summary that only describes the method.
- Tables without interpretation, or interpretation without data.

steps.title: Ethical principles
steps.body: **Informed consent** (respondents know purpose and can refuse or withdraw), **voluntary participation**, **confidentiality and anonymity**, no deception or harm, honest reporting (no fabrication or falsification), conflict-of-interest disclosure, and sponsor ethics (not misusing findings). Personal data handling should respect India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

steps.title: Citation in APA style
steps.body: In text: (Kotler & Keller, 2016) or Kotler and Keller (2016). Reference list: Author, A. A., & Author, B. B. (Year). *Title of book* (edition). Publisher. Journal: Author, A. (Year). Title of article. *Journal Name, volume*(issue), pages. https://doi.org/…

steps.title: Plagiarism
steps.body: Presenting others' words or ideas as your own, including self-plagiarism and patchwriting. UGC's 2018 regulations on academic integrity for higher education set graded penalties based on similarity levels. Avoid by quoting with marks, paraphrasing genuinely and citing every source.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking paraphrased text needs no citation.

courses.title: Principles of Management
courses.summary: Management as a discipline: Taylor, Fayol and Weber, the planning-organising-leading-controlling cycle, delegation, span of control, MBO and motivation theories, applied to realistic Indian workplace cases.
outcomes: Learners can contrast scientific, administrative and bureaucratic schools

lessons.title: Lab: Classical thinkers and what they got right

story.title: Two bosses at a Pune packaging unit

scenes.text: Plant head Sunil times every packing motion with a stopwatch and pays a bonus for beating the standard time.
Regional manager Neha instead asks what functions the plant needs: planning, organising, commanding, coordinating, controlling.
Both are borrowing from classical management theory, from different ends of the organisation.

steps.title: Scientific management (F. W. Taylor, 1911)
steps.body: Taylor looked at **the shop floor**: study each task, find the one best method, select and train workers scientifically, and link pay to output (differential piece rate). Strength: big productivity gains. Weakness: treats people as machines and ignores motivation beyond money.

steps.title: Administrative theory (Henri Fayol)
steps.body: Fayol looked at **top management**. He listed five functions (planning, organising, commanding, coordinating, controlling) and 14 principles, including division of work, authority and responsibility, unity of command, unity of direction, scalar chain, esprit de corps and initiative. Modern textbooks compress the functions into planning, organising, leading, controlling.

steps.title: Bureaucracy (Max Weber)
steps.body: Weber described an ideal bureaucracy: fixed hierarchy, written rules, specialised roles, impersonal relations, hiring on qualification. It gives predictability and fairness in large bodies such as government offices; the risk is red tape.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Taylor and Fayol are the same: Taylor is operations-level, Fayol is whole-organisation level.
- Calling unity of command and unity of direction the same: the first is one boss per employee, the second is one plan per group of activities.

activity.prompt: Match the thinker to the idea
pairs: One best method and piece-rate pay
Chain of authority from top to bottom

quiz.why: Fayol, a mining engineer and executive, published the 14 principles in his administrative theory.

quiz.q: Differential piece-rate wages come from
quiz.why: Taylor proposed paying a higher rate to workers who beat the standard output.

quiz.q: An employee who gets orders from two bosses breaks the principle of
quiz.why: Unity of command means one superior per employee.

quiz.q: Weber's bureaucracy mainly relies on
quiz.why: An ideal bureaucracy runs on formal rules, defined roles and a clear hierarchy.

lessons.title: Lab: Plan with SMART objectives and MBO

scenes.text: Kavya manages a 6-person sales team at a mobile accessories distributor. Her director says: do better this year.
Nobody knows what better means. Kavya converts it into numbers with each person.
They agree objectives, review quarterly and appraise against results: Management by Objectives.

steps.title: Planning in one line
steps.body: Planning decides **what to achieve and how**, ahead of time. Types: strategic (long term, top level), tactical (middle level, 1-3 years), operational (day-to-day). Steps: set objectives, scan the environment, develop alternatives, evaluate, choose, implement, review.

steps.title: MBO (Peter Drucker, 1954)
steps.body: Superior and subordinate **jointly** set objectives, define results expected, then use them to run the unit and appraise performance. Cycle: set organisational goals, set individual goals, monitor, evaluate, reward and reset. Works best with measurable goals; fails when goals are imposed or when it ignores quality.

steps.title: Worked example: a SMART objective
steps.body: Weak: increase sales. SMART: **Increase monthly sales of accessories in Zone B from 40 lakh to 46 lakh by 31 March**. Specific (zone, product), Measurable (lakh), Achievable (15% rise), Relevant (company growth), Time-bound (31 March). Growth = (46-40)/40 = 15%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing activities (hold meetings) instead of results.
- Setting a goal the employee had no say in; that is not MBO.

scenes.text: Rohit, finance head, hands the vendor audit file to analyst Meera and goes on leave.
A wrong figure goes to the auditors. Rohit says it was Meera's job.

steps.title: Authority, responsibility, accountability
steps.body:
- **Authority**: right to decide and command.
- **Responsibility**: duty to perform the assigned task.
- **Accountability**: answerability for the outcome. Authority and responsibility can be delegated; **accountability cannot be passed down** entirely, the superior stays answerable.

steps.title: Delegation steps and span of control
steps.body: Steps: assign duties, grant authority, create obligation, follow up. Span of control = number of subordinates a manager supervises directly. Narrow span gives tight control and tall hierarchy; wide span gives flat structure and faster decisions. Typical effective spans are 5-8 at senior levels and larger for routine work.

steps.title: Worked example: management layers
steps.body: An organisation has 500 operatives; each supervisor handles 10 people. Supervisors = 500/10 = 50. If each manager has a span of 5, managers = 50/5 = 10. If those 10 report to one head with span of 10, total levels above operatives = 3 (supervisor, manager, head).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Delegating authority without resources.
- Believing the delegate alone is blamed if things fail.

steps.title: Diagnosis

- Answering with a pay rise when pay is not the problem.
- Treating hygiene factors as motivators.

scenes.text: Aman starts Crumb and Co. with 5,00,000 of his own money and borrows 2,00,000 from a bank.

steps.title: The equation
steps.body: **Assets = Liabilities + Owner's equity**. Every transaction changes at least two items and keeps both sides equal. Assets are resources owned (cash, stock, machinery); liabilities are obligations (loans, creditors); equity is the owner's claim (capital plus profits minus drawings).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
1. Capital 5,00,000 + loan 2,00,000: cash 7,00,000 = loan 2,00,000 + capital 5,00,000.
2. Oven bought for cash 3,00,000: cash 4,00,000 + oven 3,00,000 = 7,00,000 assets. Total unchanged.
3. Flour on credit 40,000: stock +40,000 and creditors +40,000. Assets 7,40,000 = liabilities 2,40,000 + equity 5,00,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a loan received as income; it is a liability.
- Treating drawings as an expense; drawings reduce equity directly.

steps.title: Price elasticity of demand
steps.body: Ed = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price (use absolute value). |Ed| > 1 elastic, = 1 unitary, < 1 inelastic. If demand is elastic, a price cut **raises** total revenue; if inelastic, a price cut lowers it.

steps.title: Cost concepts
steps.body: TC = FC + VC. AC = TC/Q. **MC = change in TC / change in Q.** In the short run MC cuts AC at the minimum of AC. A firm should accept extra output when price exceeds MC.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: TC = 5000 + 8Q. At Q = 500: TC = 9,000; AC = 18. At Q = 1000: TC = 13,000; AC = 13. MC = (13000 - 9000)/500 = **8**. A bulk order at 10 per brochure beats MC, so it adds profit.

lessons.title: What cost and management accounting do

scenes.text: A Ludhiana hosiery unit shows a profit in its annual accounts.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **Cost accounting** records, classifies and allocates costs to products, jobs, processes or services to ascertain and control cost. **Management accounting** uses cost and financial data to help managers plan, control and decide.

steps.title: Objectives
steps.body: Ascertain cost per unit, fix selling prices, control cost (standards, budgets), reduce waste, provide information for decisions (make or buy, shut down), value inventory.

steps.title: Financial vs cost accounting
steps.body: Financial accounting: statutory, whole business, historical, for outsiders. Cost accounting: largely internal (though cost records and cost audit are required for specified industries under the Companies Act, 2013), detailed by product or department, includes estimates and standards.

steps.title: Cost unit and cost centre
steps.body:
- **Cost unit**: unit of output for which cost is measured (per tonne of steel, per passenger-km, per room-night, per 1,000 bricks).
- **Cost centre**: location, person or equipment for which costs are gathered (machine shop, canteen). Production vs service cost centres.

steps.title: By element
steps.body: Material, labour, expenses; each **direct** (traceable to the unit) or **indirect** (overheads).

steps.title: By behaviour
steps.body:
- **Fixed**: total constant within relevant range (rent); per-unit falls as output rises.
- **Variable**: total varies in proportion to output (raw material); per-unit constant.
- **Semi-variable**: part fixed, part variable (phone, electricity with fixed charge).
- **Step costs**: fixed over ranges then jump (supervisor salaries).

steps.title: By function and for decisions
steps.body: Production, administration, selling, distribution, R&D. Decision costs: **relevant** (future, differ between options), **sunk** (already incurred, ignore), **opportunity** (benefit forgone), **controllable** vs **uncontrollable**, **marginal** cost.

steps.title: Methods (by industry)
steps.body:
- **Job costing**: customer orders (printing, repair).
- **Batch costing**: batches of identical items (biscuits, medicines).
- **Contract costing**: long-duration construction projects.
- **Process costing**: continuous stages (chemicals, sugar, cement).
- **Unit/output costing**: single uniform product (bricks, mining).
- **Operating/service costing**: transport, hotels, hospitals.
- **Multiple costing**: assembled products (cars).

steps.title: Techniques
steps.body: Historical, standard, marginal, absorption, uniform costing, and activity-based costing (ABC) which traces overheads using cost drivers.

steps.title: Cost control vs cost reduction
steps.body: Cost control keeps costs within standards and budgets. Cost reduction lowers costs permanently below standards without hurting quality, through value engineering or better methods.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Method answers 'which industry'; technique answers 'which approach to measure and control'. Marginal costing is a technique, process costing is a method.

steps.title: EOQ formula
steps.body: EOQ = √(2AO / C), where A = annual demand (units), O = cost per order, C = carrying cost per unit per year (often a % of unit price).

steps.body:
- **A items**: about 10% of items, about 70% of value: tight control.
- **B items**: about 20% of items, 20% of value.
- **C items**: about 70% of items, 10% of value: simple control.
Percentages are typical, not fixed rules.
