scenes.text: The pump maker uses 200–400 castings a week.
The supplier takes 4 to 6 weeks to deliver.
The storekeeper sets levels to avoid both stock-outs and overstocking.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Reorder level (ROL)** = maximum usage × maximum reorder period.
- **Minimum level** = ROL − (normal usage × normal reorder period).
- **Maximum level** = ROL + reorder quantity − (minimum usage × minimum reorder period).
- **Average stock** = (minimum + maximum) / 2, or minimum + ½ ROQ.
- **Danger level** = normal usage × emergency lead time.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Normal usage 300/week, minimum 200, maximum 400. Reorder period 4–6 weeks (normal 5). ROQ 3,000.
ROL = 400 × 6 = **2,400**.
Minimum = 2,400 − 300 × 5 = **900**.
Maximum = 2,400 + 3,000 − 200 × 4 = **4,600**.
Average = (900 + 4,600) / 2 = **2,750**.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Use maximum usage and maximum period for ROL, but minimum usage and minimum period inside the maximum-level formula.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: Usage 100–150 per day, lead time 5–7 days (normal 6), ROQ 1,000, normal usage 125. Find ROL (150 × 7 = 1,050) and maximum level (1,050 + 1,000 − 100 × 5 = 1,550).

scenes.text: Standard time for a pump assembly is 10 hours; Suresh finishes in 8.

steps.title: Time and piece wages
steps.body: Time rate: hours × rate (guaranteed, no output incentive). Piece rate: units × rate per unit. Taylor's differential piece rate pays a higher rate above standard.

steps.title: Halsey plan (50%)
steps.body:
Time allowed TA = 10, time taken TT = 8, rate R = ₹50. Time saved = 2.
Bonus = 50% × 2 × 50 = ₹50. Earnings = 8 × 50 + 50 = **₹450**.

steps.title: Rowan plan
steps.body: Bonus = (TT / TA) × time saved × R = (8/10) × 2 × 50 = ₹80. Earnings = 400 + 80 = **₹480**. Rowan pays more than Halsey when less than half the time is saved; the two are equal when exactly half is saved.

steps.title: Labour turnover
steps.body:
Workers at start 380, at end 420 → average 400. Separations 20, replacements 16.
- Separation method = 20/400 × 100 = **5%**.
- Replacement method = 16/400 × 100 = **4%**.
- Flux method = (separations + replacements)/average = 36/400 = **9%**.

steps.title: Idle time and overtime
steps.body: Normal idle time (tea breaks, set-up) is included in labour cost; abnormal idle time (power failure, strikes) goes to costing profit and loss. Overtime premium is usually overhead unless caused by a specific customer's urgent order.

steps.title: Three terms
steps.body:
- **Allocation**: charging a whole item to one cost centre (machining supervisor's salary to machining).
- **Apportionment**: sharing a common cost among centres on a fair basis.
- **Absorption**: charging overheads from cost centres to cost units using a rate.

steps.title: Common bases
steps.body: Rent, rates, building insurance → floor area. Power → horsepower × machine hours or kWh. Lighting → number of light points or floor area. Canteen, welfare → number of employees. Depreciation, machinery insurance → value of machinery. Supervision → direct labour hours or employees.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Do not apportion an item that can be traced directly; allocate it.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
- **Direct redistribution**: service costs go straight to production departments, ignoring services between service departments.
- **Step (non-reciprocal)**: close service departments in order.
- **Reciprocal**: repeated distribution, trial-and-error, or simultaneous equations.

steps.title: Simultaneous equations
steps.body:
S1 = ₹10,000 + 20% of S2; S2 = ₹8,000 + 10% of S1.
S1 = 10,000 + 0.2(8,000 + 0.1 S1) = 11,600 + 0.02 S1 → 0.98 S1 = 11,600 → **S1 = ₹11,836.73**.
S2 = 8,000 + 1,183.67 = **₹9,183.67**. These totals are then shared among production departments in the remaining percentages.

scenes.text: At the start of the year the firm budgets ₹4,00,000 overhead and 20,000 labour hours.

steps.title: Absorption bases
steps.body: % of direct material cost, % of direct labour cost, % of prime cost, direct labour hour rate, machine hour rate, rate per unit. Labour hour and machine hour rates are usually the most accurate because overheads accrue with time.

steps.title: Predetermined rate
steps.body:
Rate = budgeted overhead / budgeted base = 4,00,000 / 20,000 = **₹20 per labour hour**.
Absorbed = 21,000 × 20 = ₹4,20,000. Actual = ₹4,05,000.
Over-absorbed = 4,20,000 − 4,05,000 = **₹15,000**.

steps.title: Labour cost percentage
steps.body: Budgeted factory OH ₹3,00,000; budgeted direct labour ₹6,00,000 → rate = **50% of direct labour**. A job with ₹8,000 labour absorbs ₹4,000.

steps.title: Treatment
steps.body:
- Small amounts: transfer to costing P&L.
- Large amounts due to estimation errors: supplementary rate to adjust WIP, finished goods and cost of sales.
- Abnormal causes (strike, idle capacity): costing P&L.
- Carry forward only in seasonal businesses within the year.

steps.title: The core difference
steps.body: Under **absorption costing**, fixed production overhead is included in product cost and stock. Under **marginal costing**, fixed overhead is a period cost written off in full; stock is valued at variable cost.

steps.title: Reconciliation
steps.body:
Production 12,000, sales 10,000, no opening stock. Fixed production overhead ₹1,20,000 → ₹10 per unit. Closing stock 2,000 units carries 2,000 × 10 = ₹20,000 of fixed cost under absorption.
Absorption profit − Marginal profit = **₹20,000**.

steps.title: General rule
steps.body:
- Production > sales (stock rises): absorption profit higher.
- Production < sales (stock falls): marginal profit higher.
- Production = sales: profits equal.

steps.title: Merits and limits of marginal costing
steps.body: Merits: simple, avoids under/over-absorption, useful for decisions and CVP. Limits: hard to split semi-variable costs, stock undervalued for financial reporting (not accepted for external stock valuation), ignores fixed costs in long-run pricing.

courses.summary: Setting standards, material, labour, variable overhead and sales variances with full reconciliation, budgets and budgetary control, functional and master budgets, fixed vs flexible budgets, cash budgets, and zero-based and performance budgeting.

scenes.text: A Tiruppur garment unit buys cotton at ₹9/kg instead of the standard ₹10.
But it uses 1,100 kg instead of the standard 1,000 kg for the month's output.
Was the cheaper cotton really a saving?

steps.title: Standard costing
steps.body: A standard cost is a predetermined cost under efficient conditions. Variance = standard cost − actual cost; **Favourable (F)** if actual is lower, **Adverse (A)** if higher. Types of standards: ideal, basic, currently attainable (most used).

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **MCV** (cost) = SQ × SP − AQ × AP
- **MPV** (price) = (SP − AP) × AQ
- **MUV** (usage/quantity) = (SQ − AQ) × SP
MCV = MPV + MUV. SQ = standard quantity for actual output.

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.body: Cheaper, lower-quality cotton may have caused the extra wastage. Purchasing earns a favourable price variance while production bears an adverse usage variance, so investigate them together.

steps.title: Variable overhead
steps.body:
Standard VOH ₹10 per labour hour; actual VOH ₹5,500.
- **Expenditure** = AH × SR − actual = 5,200 − 5,500 = **₹300 A**.
- **Efficiency** = (SH − AH) × SR = (500 − 520) × 10 = **₹200 A**.
- **Total** = 500 × 10 − 5,500 = **₹500 A**.

steps.title: Idle time variance
steps.body: If paid hours include abnormal idle hours, idle time variance = idle hours × SR (always adverse), and efficiency is measured on hours actually worked.

steps.title: Budget and budgetary control
steps.body: A budget is a quantitative plan for a future period. Budgetary control sets budgets, compares actuals, investigates variances and takes corrective action. Needs: budget committee, budget manual, budget period, key (principal) budget factor (often sales).

steps.title: Types
steps.body: By function: sales, production, materials, labour, overhead, cash, capital expenditure → **master budget**. By flexibility: fixed vs flexible. By time: long-term, short-term, current.

steps.title: Flexible budget
steps.body:
Fixed overhead ₹50,000; variable overhead ₹12 per unit.
At 8,000 units: 50,000 + 96,000 = **₹1,46,000**.
At 10,000 units: 50,000 + 1,20,000 = **₹1,70,000**.
Actual ₹1,68,000 at 10,000 units → **₹2,000 favourable**. The manager did well; the fixed budget comparison (₹22,000 adverse) was misleading.

steps.title: Semi-variable item
steps.body: Maintenance ₹30,000 at 60% capacity and ₹36,000 at 80%. Variable part = 6,000 per 20% = ₹300 per 1%. At 100%: 36,000 + 20 × 300 = **₹42,000**.

steps.title: Receipts and payments method
steps.body: Opening cash + receipts (cash sales, collections from debtors, other income) − payments (creditors, wages, expenses, capital items, tax) = closing cash. Compare with minimum cash balance to plan borrowing or investment.

steps.title: Borrowing need
steps.body: Opening ₹20,000 + receipts ₹1,50,000 − payments ₹1,60,000 = closing **₹10,000**. Minimum balance ₹15,000 → borrow **₹5,000**.

steps.title: Zero-based and performance budgeting
steps.body: **Zero-based budgeting (ZBB)**: every activity is justified from zero each period, using decision packages ranked by priority. **Performance budgeting**: links spending to outputs and outcomes, used in government. **Rolling budgets** add a new period as one ends.

steps.title: Non-cash items
steps.body: Depreciation and provisions do not enter a cash budget because they involve no cash flow.

uni-bba-entrepreneurship.title: BBA · Entrepreneurship Development
uni-bba-entrepreneurship.description: Entrepreneurship for BBA: entrepreneurial traits and theories, intrapreneurship, idea generation and opportunity assessment, feasibility and business plans, business model canvas, start-up finance and valuation, Indian support schemes, MSMEs, legal forms, scaling, family and social enterprise, with worked numericals and cases. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BBA programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Entrepreneur, entrepreneurship and theories
courses.summary: Meaning of entrepreneur and entrepreneurship, functions and traits, types of entrepreneurs, intrapreneurship, major theories (Schumpeter, McClelland, Weber, Kirzner), entrepreneurial ecosystem, barriers, and entrepreneurship development programmes in India.
outcomes: Define entrepreneur, entrepreneurship and enterprise
Describe key traits and functions of entrepreneurs
Classify entrepreneurs by Danhof and other typologies
Explain major theories of entrepreneurship
Describe the purpose and phases of an EDP

scenes.text: Ravi started a tea stall near a Hyderabad IT park, then added filter coffee, then an app for office delivery.
Within five years he ran 14 outlets. What made him an entrepreneur rather than just a shopkeeper?

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: An **entrepreneur** identifies an opportunity, mobilises resources and bears risk to create a new venture or value. **Entrepreneurship** is the process of doing so. The **enterprise** is the resulting organisation. The word comes from the French *entreprendre*, 'to undertake'. Richard Cantillon emphasised risk bearing; J. B. Say emphasised combining factors of production.

steps.title: Functions
steps.body: Opportunity recognition, innovation, risk and uncertainty bearing, resource mobilisation, organisation and management, decision making, and creating jobs and wealth. Economic role: capital formation, balanced regional development, exports, import substitution.

steps.title: Traits
steps.body: Need for achievement, risk tolerance (calculated, not reckless), internal locus of control, creativity, persistence and resilience, tolerance for ambiguity, vision, leadership, and opportunity orientation. Traits help but skills (sales, finance, team building) can be learned.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating every small business owner with an innovator: many replicate existing models (still valuable, but 'imitative').
- Thinking entrepreneurs love any risk: they prefer moderate, calculated risk.

activity.prompt: Is each a typical entrepreneurial trait or a myth?

items.text: You need huge capital to start

quiz.q: The economist who linked entrepreneurship to risk bearing early was
quiz.why: Cantillon described the entrepreneur as one who buys at certain prices and sells at uncertain ones.

quiz.q: Internal locus of control means believing
options: outcomes depend largely on one's own actions
quiz.why: Entrepreneurs tend to believe their effort shapes results, which drives initiative.

quiz.q: Entrepreneurs typically prefer
quiz.why: McClelland found high achievers choose challenging but attainable goals.

quiz.q: Which is a macro-economic role of entrepreneurship?
quiz.why: New ventures in smaller towns spread jobs and incomes beyond big cities.

scenes.text: One invents a new battery chemistry; one copies a successful café concept in a new town; one only runs the family flour mill as it always was.
Inside a large IT firm, an employee builds a new product line with company resources.

steps.title: Danhof's classification
steps.body: **Innovative**: introduce new products or methods (Schumpeterian). **Imitative (adoptive)**: copy successful innovations, common in developing economies. **Fabian**: cautious, change only when failure to change threatens survival. **Drone**: refuse change even at a loss.

steps.title: Other typologies
steps.body: By ownership: private, state, joint. By motivation: pure, induced (by incentives), motivated, spontaneous. By area: rural, urban. By gender: women entrepreneurs. Others: technopreneur, social entrepreneur, serial entrepreneur, lifestyle entrepreneur, first-generation entrepreneur.

steps.title: Intrapreneurship
steps.body: Gifford Pinchot coined 'intrapreneur': an employee who acts like an entrepreneur within an organisation, using its resources and bearing less personal financial risk. Firms foster it through innovation labs, hackathons, internal venture funds and tolerance of failure. Examples: product teams that launch new lines inside large firms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing Fabian (cautious) with Drone (refuses change).
- Saying intrapreneurs bear the same financial risk as founders.

activity.prompt: Match the type with the description
pairs: Introduces a new product or method
Adopts a proven idea in a new market
Changes only when forced by survival

quiz.q: Danhof's classification is based on
quiz.why: He grouped entrepreneurs by how readily they adopt innovations.

quiz.q: An imitative entrepreneur is most common in
quiz.why: Adapting proven technologies is efficient where innovation infrastructure is limited.

quiz.q: An intrapreneur's personal financial risk is generally
quiz.why: The organisation funds the project, so the employee risks reputation more than capital.

quiz.q: A serial entrepreneur
options: starts several ventures one after another
quiz.why: Serial founders build, exit and start again, reusing experience and networks.

story.title: Why do some communities produce more founders?

scenes.text: Historians note trading communities that produce many businesses across generations.
Economists, psychologists and sociologists each offer an explanation.

steps.title: Economic theories
steps.body: **Schumpeter (innovation theory)**: the entrepreneur is an innovator who causes 'creative destruction' through new products, new methods, new markets, new sources of supply and new organisation. **Kirzner**: entrepreneurs are alert to unnoticed profit opportunities and move markets towards equilibrium. **Knight**: profit is the reward for bearing uninsurable uncertainty.

steps.title: Psychological theories
steps.body: **McClelland**: need for achievement (n-Ach) drives entrepreneurship; also need for power and affiliation; achievement motivation can be developed through training (his Kakinada experiment in India in the 1960s). **Hagen**: withdrawal of status respect leads groups to seek recognition through enterprise.

steps.title: Sociological theories
steps.body: **Max Weber**: religious beliefs (the Protestant ethic) shaped attitudes to work and saving that supported capitalism. **Thomas Cochran**: cultural values and social sanctions shape entrepreneurial supply. Modern **ecosystem** view: finance, markets, policy, culture, human capital and support institutions together determine entrepreneurial activity (Isenberg).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Attributing 'creative destruction' to Kirzner instead of Schumpeter.
- Listing only one theory in a 10-mark answer; compare across economic, psychological and sociological schools.

activity.prompt: Match each theorist with the idea

quiz.q: Which is not one of Schumpeter's five types of innovation?
quiz.why: Schumpeter listed new products, methods, markets, supply sources and organisation, not tax changes.

quiz.q: McClelland's training experiment in India was conducted in
quiz.why: His achievement-motivation training with businessmen in Kakinada showed n-Ach could be developed.

quiz.q: Hagen's theory relates entrepreneurship to
quiz.why: Groups that lose social status may seek recognition through economic achievement.

quiz.q: Knight distinguished risk from
quiz.why: Measurable risk can be insured; true uncertainty cannot, and profit rewards bearing it.

lessons.title: Entrepreneurship development programmes and ecosystem in India

scenes.text: Sunita wants to start a food-processing unit but has no business background.
A six-week EDP helps her with a project report, bank linkage and market contacts.

steps.title: EDP: meaning and phases
steps.body: An Entrepreneurship Development Programme develops entrepreneurial motivation and competencies. Phases: **pre-training** (identify and select trainees, assess needs), **training** (achievement motivation, business opportunity guidance, project report preparation, managerial skills, plant visits), **post-training follow-up** (finance linkage, approvals, handholding).

steps.title: Support institutions
steps.body: Entrepreneurship Development Institute of India (EDII), Ahmedabad; National Institute for Entrepreneurship and Small Business Development (NIESBUD); state industrial development and technical consultancy organisations; District Industries Centres (DICs); SIDBI; Startup India (DPIIT); Atal Innovation Mission (incubators, tinkering labs); technology business incubators at institutes.

steps.title: Barriers
steps.body: Access to finance and collateral, regulatory compliance, limited market access, skill gaps, social attitudes to failure, and for women entrepreneurs mobility and family constraints. Ecosystem improvements: digital public infrastructure (UPI, GST network), credit guarantee schemes, incubators.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring the post-training phase: many EDP outcomes depend on follow-up.
- Listing schemes without explaining what each provides.

items: Opportunity guidance and project report preparation
Follow-up support for finance and approvals

quiz.why: Trainees often need help converting plans into funded, approved units.

quiz.why: Without family assets or contacts, raising credit and finding customers is harder.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Ideas, opportunity assessment and the business plan
courses.summary: Sources of ideas and creativity techniques, screening ideas into opportunities, market sizing with TAM-SAM-SOM, feasibility analysis (market, technical, financial, organisational), lean start-up and MVP, business model canvas, and the structure of a business plan or project report.
outcomes: Generate ideas using structured creativity techniques
Screen ideas and size a market with TAM, SAM and SOM
Conduct a four-part feasibility study including break-even

scenes.text: Ananya notices working parents in Kochi struggle to find trusted home-cooked tiffin services.
Her friends brainstorm ten possible solutions in one evening.

steps.title: Sources of ideas
steps.body: Personal experience and frustrations, hobbies, customer complaints, changes in technology, demographics, regulation and lifestyle (Drucker's sources of innovation), trade fairs, patents, research institutions, and existing products in other countries or cities.

steps.title: Creativity techniques
steps.body: **Brainstorming** (quantity first, no criticism), **mind mapping**, **SCAMPER** (Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other use, Eliminate, Reverse), **attribute listing**, **design thinking** (empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test), and the creative process (preparation, incubation, illumination, verification).

steps.title: Worked example: SCAMPER on a tiffin service
steps.body: Substitute: steel dabbas → returnable insulated boxes. Combine: tiffin + nutrition tracking app. Adapt: dabbawala-style route batching. Eliminate: daily ordering → weekly subscription. Reverse: customers' own recipes cooked by home chefs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Judging ideas during brainstorming, which kills volume.
- Falling in love with a solution before validating the problem.

activity.prompt: Match the SCAMPER letter to an example for a bicycle

quiz.q: The first rule of brainstorming is
options: defer judgement and go for quantity
quiz.why: Suspending criticism encourages more and wilder ideas, which can later be refined.

quiz.q: Design thinking begins with
quiz.why: Understanding users' needs deeply comes before defining the problem and ideating.

quiz.q: 'Illumination' in the creative process is
quiz.why: After incubation, the solution often appears as a flash of insight.

quiz.q: Drucker listed changing demographics as
quiz.why: Shifts in age, income and education create new needs and markets.

story.title: Is the tiffin market big enough?

scenes.text: An investor asks Ananya: how many customers, how much money, how much can you capture?
She answers with TAM, SAM and SOM.

steps.title: Idea vs opportunity
steps.body: An opportunity is an idea with a real customer need, willingness to pay, a viable market size, a feasible way to deliver and a window of time. Screening criteria: market (size, growth), economics (margins, capital needs), competition (barriers, advantage), management fit, and fatal flaws.

steps.title: TAM, SAM, SOM
steps.body: **TAM** (total addressable market): total demand for the solution. **SAM** (serviceable available market): the part you can reach with your model and geography. **SOM** (serviceable obtainable market): realistic share in 3–5 years. Top-down uses published data; bottom-up multiplies target customers × price × frequency and is more credible.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
2 crore urban working professionals in target metros spending ₹1,200 a year on tiffin: TAM = 2,00,00,000 × 1,200 = **₹2,400 crore**.
SAM: only Kochi and Bengaluru, 25% → **₹600 crore**.
SOM: 2% of SAM in 3 years → **₹12 crore** a year.

steps.title: Competitive check
steps.body: Use Porter's five forces and a competitor grid (price, quality, delivery time, variety). Identify the unique value proposition (UVP).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming '1% of India' as a plan.
- Confusing TAM with revenue forecast.

activity.prompt: 50 lakh target users × ₹600 a year = TAM. SAM is 30% of TAM; SOM is 5% of SAM. SOM in ₹ crore?

quiz.q: SOM represents
quiz.why: SOM is the slice of SAM a start-up can plausibly win within a few years.

quiz.q: Bottom-up market sizing is preferred because
options: it builds from customers, price and frequency
quiz.why: Starting from concrete units and prices makes the estimate verifiable.

quiz.q: A 'fatal flaw' in screening means
options: a problem that makes the venture unworkable
quiz.why: Examples are illegal activity, no willingness to pay or impossible cost structure.

quiz.q: An opportunity differs from an idea because it has
quiz.why: An opportunity is an idea that can create value for customers profitably.

lessons.title: Feasibility analysis, lean start-up and the business model canvas

scenes.text: Ananya runs a two-week pilot with 40 customers using a WhatsApp group and Google Forms.
She maps her model on a one-page canvas.

steps.title: Feasibility
steps.body: **Market**: demand, customers, competition, pricing. **Technical**: technology, location, equipment, raw materials, capacity. **Financial**: project cost, means of finance, profitability, break-even, cash flow, payback. **Organisational/legal**: team, form of ownership, licences (FSSAI for food, GST, Udyam). Also environmental and social feasibility.

steps.title: Worked example: break-even
steps.body:
Monthly fixed cost ₹3,00,000; price per meal ₹150; variable cost ₹90.
Contribution = ₹60. BEP = 3,00,000 ÷ 60 = **5,000 meals a month** (≈ 167 a day). Margin of safety at 7,000 meals = (7,000 − 5,000)/7,000 = **28.6%**.

steps.title: Lean start-up
steps.body: Eric Ries: build–measure–learn loop. Launch a **minimum viable product (MVP)**, measure actual behaviour, then **persevere or pivot**. Use validated learning and actionable metrics (repeat orders) rather than vanity metrics (app downloads).

steps.title: Business model canvas (Osterwalder)
steps.body: Nine blocks: customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partnerships, cost structure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Building a full app before testing demand.
- Tracking vanity metrics.

activity.prompt: Fixed cost ₹2,40,000/month, price ₹200, variable cost ₹120. Break-even units per month?

quiz.q: An MVP is
options: the simplest version that tests key assumptions
quiz.why: It gathers real customer learning with minimum effort and cost.

quiz.q: Which is not one of the nine canvas blocks?
quiz.why: The canvas covers how value is created, delivered and captured, not market valuation.

quiz.q: FSSAI registration relates to
options: technical/legal feasibility of a food business
quiz.why: Food businesses in India need FSSAI registration or licence to operate legally.

quiz.q: A pivot means
options: changing a key element of the model based on learning
quiz.why: Pivoting changes direction, such as target customer or channel, while keeping the venture alive.

story.title: A plan for the bank and for investors

scenes.text: The bank needs a project report with costs and repayment. The angel investor wants growth and team.
One plan, tailored executive summary.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Executive summary · Company description and mission · Problem and solution · Market analysis (TAM-SAM-SOM, customers, competitors) · Marketing and sales plan (4Ps, channels) · Operations plan (location, process, suppliers) · Management team and organisation · Financial plan (project cost, means of finance, projected P&L, cash flow, balance sheet, break-even, ratios such as DSCR) · Funding ask and use of funds · Risks and mitigation · Appendices.

steps.title: Worked example: means of finance
steps.body:
Project cost ₹20 lakh: kitchen equipment 9, vehicles 5, deposits 2, working capital margin 4.
Means: promoter's contribution 25% = ₹5 lakh; term loan ₹12 lakh; working capital loan ₹3 lakh. Debt-equity = 15 : 5 = **3 : 1**.

steps.title: Pitch deck (10–12 slides)
steps.body: Problem, solution, market, product demo, business model, traction, competition, go-to-market, team, financials, the ask.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Hockey-stick projections with no assumptions listed.
- Ignoring working capital in project cost.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Financing the venture
courses.summary: Bootstrapping, debt and equity sources, angel investors, venture capital stages and term sheets, pre- and post-money valuation and dilution, unit economics (CAC, LTV, burn and runway), and Indian schemes such as Startup India, MUDRA, Stand-Up India and the credit guarantee scheme for MSEs.
outcomes: Compare bootstrapping, debt, angel and VC funding
Compute pre-money and post-money valuation and founder dilution

lessons.title: Sources of finance across the venture life cycle

scenes.text: Ananya starts with ₹3 lakh of savings and a friend's loan.
As revenue grows she meets a bank, an angel and finally a VC fund.

steps.title: Stages and sources
steps.body: **Pre-seed/idea**: own savings, family and friends, grants, competitions, incubator support. **Seed**: angels, angel networks, seed funds, accelerators, crowdfunding. **Early (Series A/B)**: venture capital. **Growth**: late-stage VC, private equity, venture debt, strategic investors. **Mature**: bank loans, IPO (e.g. SME exchange platforms of BSE and NSE).

steps.title: Bootstrapping
steps.body: Funding growth from own savings and customer revenue: advance payments, lean operations, deferring salaries, using co-working spaces. Keeps control, forces discipline; may slow growth.

steps.title: Debt vs equity
steps.body: Debt: interest and repayment obligations, collateral, no ownership loss, suits stable cash flows. Equity: no repayment, investors share ownership and upside, bring networks and governance, suits high-risk, high-growth ventures. Quasi-equity: convertible notes, compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS, common in Indian VC deals).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Raising VC for a business that cannot grow rapidly; VCs need large exits.
- Taking short-term loans for long-term assets.

activity.prompt: Match the stage with a typical source
pairs: Public issue on a stock exchange

quiz.q: Bootstrapping means
options: funding through own resources and revenue
quiz.why: Founders rely on savings and customer cash rather than outside investors.

quiz.q: A key disadvantage of equity finance for founders is
quiz.why: New shareholders take part of the ownership and often board rights.

quiz.q: Debt is best suited to firms with
quiz.why: Fixed repayments need dependable cash inflows.

quiz.q: CCPS in Indian VC deals are
quiz.why: They give investors preference rights that later convert into equity shares.

lessons.title: Lab: Valuation, dilution and the term sheet

scenes.text: An angel offers ₹2 crore for 20% of Ananya's company.
What does that say the company is worth, and how much will she own after the next round?

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: **Post-money valuation = investment ÷ investor's stake**. **Pre-money = post-money − investment**. After a round where new investors get x%, each existing holder's stake is multiplied by (1 − x).

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: ₹2 crore for 20% → post-money = 2 ÷ 0.20 = **₹10 crore**; pre-money = **₹8 crore**.

steps.title: Worked example 2: dilution over rounds
steps.body: Founders start at 100%. Seed: 20% sold → founders 80%. Series A: 25% sold → founders 80% × 0.75 = **60%**. ESOP pool of 10% created after that → 60% × 0.9 = **54%**.

steps.title: Term sheet clauses
steps.body: Valuation and amount; instrument (equity, CCPS, convertible note); **liquidation preference** (e.g. 1× non-participating: investors first get their money back on exit); **anti-dilution** (full ratchet or weighted average) for down rounds; board seats; **pro-rata** rights; **ROFR/tag-along/drag-along**; vesting of founder shares (commonly 4 years with a 1-year cliff); ESOP pool; information rights.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding dilution percentages (20% + 25% ≠ 45% dilution).
- Focusing only on valuation and ignoring liquidation preference.

activity.prompt: An investor puts ₹3 crore for 15%. Pre-money valuation in ₹ crore?

quiz.q: ₹5 crore for 25% gives a post-money of
quiz.why: 5 ÷ 0.25 = ₹20 crore; pre-money is then ₹15 crore.

quiz.q: Founders own 70%; a new round sells 20%. Founders now own
quiz.why: 70% × (1 − 0.20) = 56%, because everyone is diluted proportionally.

quiz.q: A 1× liquidation preference means investors on exit get
options: their investment back before common shareholders
quiz.why: It protects investors if the exit value is low.

quiz.q: Vesting with a one-year cliff means
options: no founder shares vest before 12 months
quiz.why: It protects the company if a founder leaves early.

scenes.text: The tiffin start-up spends ₹5 lakh more than it earns every month.
With ₹60 lakh in the bank, how long can it survive, and does each customer make money?

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **CAC** (customer acquisition cost) = sales and marketing spend ÷ new customers. **LTV** (lifetime value) ≈ ARPU × gross margin × average customer lifetime; lifetime ≈ 1 ÷ churn rate. **LTV/CAC** of about 3 or more is widely seen as healthy. **Payback** of CAC = CAC ÷ (ARPU × gross margin). **Burn rate** = net cash outflow per month. **Runway** = cash ÷ burn.

steps.title: Worked example 1: unit economics
steps.body:
Marketing ₹2,50,000 brings 500 customers → CAC = **₹500**.
ARPU ₹200/month, gross margin 60%, monthly churn 5% → lifetime 20 months.
LTV = 200 × 0.6 × 20 = **₹2,400**. LTV/CAC = **4.8**. CAC payback = 500 ÷ 120 = 4.2 months.

steps.title: Worked example 2: runway
steps.body: Cash ₹60 lakh; monthly burn ₹5 lakh → runway = **12 months**. Fundraising usually takes 4–6 months, so start raising by month 6.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using revenue rather than gross margin in LTV.
- Ignoring churn: high churn shrinks lifetime and LTV dramatically.

activity.prompt: ARPU ₹300/month, gross margin 50%, monthly churn 10%, CAC ₹750. LTV/CAC ratio?

quiz.q: Monthly churn of 4% implies an average lifetime of about
quiz.why: Lifetime ≈ 1 ÷ churn = 1 ÷ 0.04 = 25 months.

quiz.q: Runway for cash ₹90 lakh and burn ₹6 lakh
quiz.why: 90 ÷ 6 = 15 months before cash runs out at the current burn.

quiz.q: An LTV/CAC ratio below 1 means
options: each customer costs more to acquire than they return
quiz.why: Growth then destroys value until acquisition cost or retention improves.

quiz.q: Gross margin is used in LTV because
options: it reflects the profit each rupee of revenue contributes
quiz.why: Only revenue after direct costs is available to repay acquisition spending.

scenes.text: Sunita's food unit, Ananya's tech start-up and a Dalit woman entrepreneur in Pune each qualify for different schemes.
Knowing eligibility saves months.

steps.title: Startup India (2016)
steps.body: DPIIT recognition for entities up to 10 years from incorporation with annual turnover not exceeding ₹100 crore in any year, working on innovation or scalable models. Benefits include self-certification for certain labour and environmental laws, faster patent examination with fee rebates, Fund of Funds for Startups (managed by SIDBI) investing via SEBI-registered AIFs, and eligibility to apply for income-tax exemption under Section 80-IAC subject to conditions.

steps.title: MUDRA loans (PMMY, 2015)
steps.body: Collateral-free loans to non-farm micro enterprises through banks, NBFCs and MFIs: **Shishu** up to ₹50,000; **Kishore** ₹50,000–₹5 lakh; **Tarun** ₹5–10 lakh; **Tarun Plus** ₹10–20 lakh for borrowers who have repaid Tarun loans (announced in the 2024 Budget).

steps.title: Other schemes
steps.body: **Stand-Up India**: bank loans of ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore for greenfield enterprises of SC/ST and women entrepreneurs. **CGTMSE**: credit guarantee for collateral-free loans to micro and small enterprises. **PMEGP**: subsidy-linked credit for new micro units via KVIC. **Atal Innovation Mission**: incubators and tinkering labs. Many states run their own start-up policies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating MUDRA as a grant: it is a loan.
- Assuming every new company is a 'start-up' for Startup India benefits; DPIIT recognition is required.

Subsidy-linked credit for new micro units

quiz.why: Kishore is the middle category for growing micro units.

quiz.why: Each bank branch is expected to support at least one SC/ST and one woman borrower.

quiz.why: SIDBI invests the fund into SEBI-registered alternative investment funds.

scenes.text: Sunita's food unit has ₹80 lakh of plant and machinery and ₹4 crore turnover.
Its MSME category decides which schemes and priority-sector loans it can access.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body: Since July 2020, MSMEs are classified on a composite criterion of investment in plant and machinery (or equipment) **and** turnover, the same for manufacturing and services. The limits were raised with effect from 1 April 2025: **Micro**: investment up to ₹2.5 crore and turnover up to ₹10 crore; **Small**: up to ₹25 crore and ₹100 crore; **Medium**: up to ₹125 crore and ₹500 crore. (Earlier 2020 limits were ₹1/5, ₹10/50 and ₹50/250 crore.) Exports are excluded from turnover for classification.

steps.title: Udyam registration
steps.body: Free, online, paperless registration on the Udyam portal using Aadhaar and PAN; data is linked with GST and income-tax systems. Benefits: priority-sector lending, CGTMSE guarantees, protection against delayed payments (buyers must pay within 45 days where agreed, under the MSMED Act, 2006), public procurement preferences, and scheme eligibility.

steps.title: Role of MSMEs
steps.body: MSMEs contribute close to 30% of India's GDP, a large share of exports and employ well over 10 crore people, making them second only to agriculture in employment.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using only investment (the pre-2020 rule) to classify.
- Different limits for manufacturing and services (no longer applicable).

quiz.why: Since 2020 a unit must satisfy both limits; exceeding either moves it up a category.

steps.title: Forms compared
steps.body: **Sole proprietorship**: easiest, unlimited liability, no separate entity. **Partnership** (Indian Partnership Act, 1932): 2+ partners, unlimited liability, deed recommended. **LLP** (LLP Act, 2008): separate entity, limited liability, flexible, fewer compliances, but cannot issue equity shares to investors. **Private limited company** (Companies Act, 2013): separate entity, limited liability, can issue shares and ESOPs, preferred by VCs, more compliance. **One Person Company (OPC)**: single-member company with limited liability.

steps.title: Common registrations
steps.body: PAN and TAN, GST registration (mandatory above threshold turnover or for inter-state supply of goods and e-commerce cases), Udyam, Shops and Establishments licence (state), FSSAI for food, trade licence from the municipality, Import Export Code for exporters, EPF/ESI once employee thresholds are crossed, trademark registration for brand protection.

steps.title: Choice rules
steps.body: Small local business with low risk → proprietorship or partnership. Professional services with partners → LLP. Plans for outside equity, ESOPs and scale → private limited company.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting as a partnership and later finding investors require a company (conversion costs time).
- Ignoring trademark search before branding.

steps.title: Growth strategies
steps.body: Ansoff matrix: market penetration, market development, product development, diversification. Routes: organic expansion, franchising, licensing, strategic alliances, acquisitions. Greiner's growth model: each phase of growth ends in a crisis (leadership, autonomy, control, red tape) that demands new structures.

steps.title: Causes of failure and sickness
steps.body: No market need, running out of cash, wrong team, poor unit economics, competition, premature scaling, weak financial control, regulatory issues. For MSMEs, sickness indicators include continued losses, erosion of net worth, overdue loans; RBI frameworks address revival and restructuring, and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 provides a resolution process.

steps.title: Worked example: franchise economics
steps.body:
Franchisee pays a one-time fee of ₹5 lakh and 6% royalty on sales. Outlet sales ₹40 lakh a year.
Franchisor's yearly royalty per outlet = 0.06 × 40 = **₹2.4 lakh**. With 20 outlets: ₹48 lakh a year plus fees, with limited capital invested.

- Scaling before unit economics are positive in the first market.
- Diversifying into unrelated businesses too early.

scenes.text: A third-generation textile family in Surat debates who should run the business next.
A woman entrepreneur in rural Maharashtra organises self-help groups to sell millet snacks; a social enterprise brings solar lamps to off-grid villages.

steps.title: Family business
steps.body: Strengths: long-term orientation, trust, quick decisions, patient capital. Challenges: succession, family conflict, nepotism, professionalisation. Tools: family constitution, family council, independent directors, succession planning and grooming of next generation or professional CEOs.

steps.title: Women entrepreneurship
steps.body: Barriers: access to finance and collateral, mobility, networks, family responsibilities, social attitudes. Support: Stand-Up India, MUDRA, Mahila e-Haat, state women entrepreneurship programmes, SHG-bank linkage (DAY-NRLM). Examples of cooperative success include Lijjat Papad, a women's cooperative started in Mumbai in 1959.

steps.title: Social entrepreneurship
steps.body: Uses business methods to solve social problems; success is measured by social impact as well as financial sustainability. Models: non-profit, for-profit social enterprise, hybrid. Indian examples often cited: Amul (dairy cooperative), SELCO (solar energy for low-income households), Aravind Eye Care (high-volume affordable surgery). Measurement: social return on investment, impact metrics.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating social entrepreneurship as charity: it aims for sustainable revenue.
- Ignoring succession until a crisis in family firms.

uni-bba-financial-management.title: BBA · Financial Management
uni-bba-financial-management.description: Financial management for BBA: goals of the firm, time value of money, risk and return, capital budgeting (NPV, IRR, payback, PI), cost of capital, leverage and capital structure, working capital, cash and receivables, and dividend policy, with fully solved numericals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BBA programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Foundations, time value of money and risk-return
courses.summary: What financial management is, the three finance decisions, wealth versus profit maximisation, agency problems, compounding and discounting, annuities, effective rates, and expected return and standard deviation.
outcomes: Explain investment, financing and dividend decisions
Argue why wealth maximisation beats profit maximisation
Compute future and present values of single sums and annuities
Convert nominal rates into effective annual rates

lessons.title: Scope and goals of financial management

scenes.text: Meera runs a Nagpur snack brand. Her CA asks three questions: what to buy, how to pay for it, and how much profit to give back to owners.
Her investor says: maximise profit this year. Her mentor says: maximise the value of the shares. They are not the same thing.

steps.title: Definition and the three decisions
steps.body: Financial management is the planning, raising, allocating and controlling of a firm's funds. Its core decisions are: **investment decision** (which long-term assets to buy: capital budgeting; plus how much current assets to hold), **financing decision** (mix of debt and equity: capital structure), and **dividend decision** (how much profit to pay out versus retain). A fourth, **liquidity decision**, manages working capital.

steps.title: Profit maximisation vs wealth maximisation
steps.body: Profit maximisation is vague (which profit: gross, net, per share?), ignores the **timing** of returns and ignores **risk**. Wealth (value) maximisation aims to maximise the market value of shareholders' equity, i.e. the present value of expected future cash flows discounted at a rate reflecting risk. It therefore accounts for timing, risk and cash flows, and is the accepted goal in modern finance.

steps.title: Agency problem
steps.body: Managers (agents) may pursue perks, empire building or safe jobs instead of shareholders' (principals') wealth. Agency costs include monitoring (audits, independent directors), bonding and residual loss. Remedies: performance-linked pay, ESOPs, board oversight, market for corporate control.

steps.title: Finance manager's role
steps.body: Estimating fund requirements, choosing sources, investing surplus, managing cash and credit, dealing with banks and markets, and financial control through budgets and ratios. In large Indian firms this is the CFO's office, with treasury and controllership as sub-functions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that wealth maximisation ignores profit: it uses cash flows from profits but adds timing and risk.
- Confusing the financing decision (sources) with the investment decision (uses).

activity.prompt: Which finance decision is each action?

items.text: Take a term loan from SBI
Open a new plant in Indore

quiz.q: The main weakness of profit maximisation is that it
options: ignores timing and risk of returns
quiz.why: Profit maximisation treats ₹1 today and ₹1 in five years alike and ignores uncertainty, which wealth maximisation corrects.

quiz.q: Deciding the debt-equity mix is the
quiz.why: The financing decision chooses sources of funds and therefore the capital structure.

quiz.q: An ESOP mainly helps reduce

lessons.title: Compounding: future value and effective rates

scenes.text: Rahul puts ₹10,000 in a 3-year deposit at 10% a year compounded annually.
Interest earns interest. He wants to know the maturity value and whether monthly compounding is better.

steps.title: Why money has time value
steps.body: ₹1 today is worth more than ₹1 later because it can be invested to earn a return (opportunity cost), because of inflation, and because future cash is uncertain. Formulas: **FV = PV × (1 + r)ⁿ**. With m compounding periods a year: **FV = PV × (1 + r/m)^(m×n)**.

steps.title: Worked example 1: single sum
steps.body:
PV = ₹10,000, r = 10%, n = 3.
FV = 10,000 × 1.1³ = 10,000 × 1.331 = **₹13,310**.
Interest earned = ₹3,310 (simple interest would give only ₹3,000).

steps.title: Worked example 2: future value of an annuity
steps.body:
Deposit ₹5,000 at the end of each year for 5 years at 10%.
FVIFA = [(1.1)⁵ − 1]/0.1 = (1.61051 − 1)/0.1 = 6.1051.
FV = 5,000 × 6.1051 = **₹30,525.50**.
For an annuity due (deposits at the start), multiply by (1 + r): 30,525.50 × 1.1 = ₹33,578.05.

steps.title: Worked example 3: effective annual rate
steps.body:
Nominal 12% compounded monthly.
EAR = (1 + 0.12/12)¹² − 1 = 1.01¹² − 1 = 1.126825 − 1 = **12.68%**.
Compare loans on EAR, not on nominal rate.

steps.title: Rule of 72
steps.body: Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ interest rate in %. At 8%, about 9 years (exact: 9.01).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using r = 10 instead of 0.10.
- Forgetting to divide the rate by m and multiply n by m when compounding is not annual.
- Treating an annuity due like an ordinary annuity.

activity.prompt: ₹20,000 is invested at 8% compounded semi-annually for 2 years. Maturity value in ₹ (to nearest rupee)? Hint: 1.04⁴ = 1.16986.

quiz.why: 1,000 × 1.1² = 1,000 × 1.21 = ₹1,210, because the second year's interest is also earned on the first year's ₹100.

quiz.q: EAR of 12% compounded quarterly is about
quiz.why: (1.03)⁴ − 1 = 1.12551 − 1 = 12.55%, which is more than the nominal rate because of compounding.

quiz.q: By the rule of 72, money at 12% doubles in about
quiz.why: 72 ÷ 12 = 6 years, a quick approximation of ln 2 ÷ ln 1.12 ≈ 6.1 years.

quiz.q: An annuity due differs from an ordinary annuity because payments occur
options: at the start of each period
at the end of each period
quiz.why: Payments at the start of each period earn one extra period of interest, so FV due = FV ordinary × (1 + r).

lessons.title: Discounting: present value, annuities and perpetuities

scenes.text: Anjali wins a contest: take ₹24,000 now or ₹10,000 at the end of each of the next 3 years.
₹30,000 looks bigger, but she can earn 10% on her money. Discounting settles it.

steps.title: Present value formulas
steps.body: **PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ**. Present value of an ordinary annuity: **PV = A × [1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ] ÷ r** (the bracket ÷ r is the PVIFA). Perpetuity: **PV = A ÷ r**. Growing perpetuity: **PV = A₁ ÷ (r − g)**, valid only if r > g.

steps.title: Worked example 3: perpetuity and loan EMI
steps.body:
Preference share paying ₹12 a year forever, r = 10%: PV = 12 ÷ 0.10 = **₹120**.
Loan of ₹1,00,000 repaid in 3 equal year-end instalments at 10%: instalment = 1,00,000 ÷ 2.4869 = **₹40,211**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing undiscounted totals (₹30,000 vs ₹24,000).
- Using a growing perpetuity formula with g ≥ r: the value is not defined.
- Using A₀ instead of A₁ (next year's cash flow) in the growth formula.

activity.prompt: A dividend of ₹5 is expected next year and will grow at 5% forever. Required return 15%. Present value of the share in ₹?

quiz.why: 1,331 ÷ 1.1³ = 1,331 ÷ 1.331 = ₹1,000, the reverse of compounding.

quiz.q: A perpetuity of ₹500 a year at 8% is worth
quiz.why: PV = 500 ÷ 0.08 = ₹6,250 because a perpetuity's value is the annual cash flow divided by the rate.

quiz.q: As the discount rate rises, present value
quiz.why: A higher rate makes the denominator (1 + r)ⁿ larger, so each future rupee is worth less today.

quiz.q: The growing perpetuity formula requires
quiz.why: Only when the discount rate exceeds the growth rate does the infinite series converge to A₁ ÷ (r − g).

lessons.title: Risk and return of a single asset

scenes.text: Karan compares a steady FMCG share with a volatile tech share.
Both promise about 10% on average, but one swings far more. Standard deviation measures that swing.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: Return = (dividend + price change) ÷ beginning price. Expected return **E(R) = Σ pᵢRᵢ**. Variance **σ² = Σ pᵢ(Rᵢ − E(R))²**; standard deviation σ = √σ². Coefficient of variation **CV = σ ÷ E(R)** = risk per unit of return. Total risk = systematic (market, undiversifiable, measured by beta) + unsystematic (firm-specific, removable by diversification).

steps.title: Worked example 2: expected return and σ
CAPM in one line
steps.body: Required return **k = R_f + β(R_m − R_f)**. With R_f = 7%, R_m = 13%, β = 1.2: k = 7 + 1.2 × 6 = **14.2%**. Beta > 1 means the share moves more than the market.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to multiply squared deviations by probabilities.
- Saying diversification removes all risk: it removes only unsystematic risk.

activity.prompt: R_f = 6%, market return 12%, beta 1.5. Required return by CAPM in %?

quiz.q: Diversification can eliminate
quiz.why: Firm-specific shocks cancel out across many holdings, but economy-wide risk remains.

quiz.q: A share with beta 0.8 is
quiz.why: Beta below 1 means the share's returns move less than proportionately with the market.

quiz.q: Bought at ₹100, dividend ₹4, sold at ₹96. Return =
quiz.why: (4 + (96 − 100)) ÷ 100 = 0, because the dividend exactly offsets the capital loss.

lessons.title: Capital budgeting process and cash-flow estimation

scenes.text: Meera's snack company considers a ₹1 lakh oven line that will raise output for four years.
Her accountant shows profit figures; her CFO insists on cash flows after tax. Who is right?

steps.title: Meaning and process
steps.body: Capital budgeting is the process of evaluating and selecting long-term investments whose benefits extend beyond one year. Steps: idea generation, estimation of cash flows, evaluation by appraisal methods, selection, implementation and post-audit. Features: large outlays, long horizon, irreversibility, risk.

steps.title: Cash-flow principles
steps.body:
Use **incremental, after-tax cash flows**, not accounting profit. Include: initial outlay (cost + installation + working capital), operating cash flows, and terminal flows (salvage after tax + working-capital release). Ignore sunk costs; include opportunity costs; exclude interest (it is reflected in the discount rate).
**CFAT = PAT + Depreciation** or equivalently **(Revenue − Cash costs)(1 − t) + Depreciation × t**.

steps.title: Worked example: sunk and opportunity cost
steps.body: A market survey already paid (₹40,000) is sunk: ignore it. A warehouse that could be rented out for ₹60,000 a year is an opportunity cost: deduct ₹60,000 × (1 − t) each year from the project's cash flows.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Deducting interest from cash flows and then discounting at the cost of capital (double counting).
- Forgetting working capital recovery at the end.
- Including sunk costs.

activity.prompt: Revenue ₹8,00,000, cash costs ₹5,00,000, depreciation ₹1,20,000, tax 30%. CFAT in ₹?

quiz.q: In capital budgeting, interest on borrowed funds is

quiz.why: The cost of finance enters through the discount rate, so subtracting interest too would double count it.

quiz.why: Sunk costs cannot be recovered whichever way the decision goes, so they are irrelevant.

steps.title: Project data used in this unit
steps.body: Cost ₹1,00,000, life 4 years, no salvage, straight-line depreciation ₹25,000. CFAT: Year 1 ₹30,000; Year 2 ₹40,000; Year 3 ₹50,000; Year 4 ₹20,000. Cost of capital 10%.

steps.title: Worked example 1: payback
steps.body:
Cumulative: 30,000; 70,000; 1,20,000.
After 2 years ₹30,000 is still unrecovered, out of Year 3's ₹50,000.
Payback = 2 + 30,000/50,000 = **2.6 years**.
Merits: simple, favours liquidity. Demerits: ignores time value and cash flows after payback.

steps.title: Worked example 3: ARR
steps.body:
Accounting profit = CFAT − depreciation: 5,000; 15,000; 25,000; −5,000. Average = 40,000/4 = 10,000.
Average investment = (1,00,000 + 0)/2 = 50,000.
ARR = 10,000/50,000 = **20%**. (On initial investment it would be 10%; state which base you use.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using profit instead of CFAT for payback.
- Using CFAT instead of profit for ARR.

steps.title: NPV and PI
steps.body: **NPV = Σ CFₜ/(1 + k)ᵗ − C₀**. Accept if NPV > 0. NPV is consistent with wealth maximisation and is additive across projects. **PI = PV of inflows ÷ PV of outflows**; accept if PI > 1. PI is useful under capital rationing.

steps.title: Worked example 1: NPV of the unit project
Worked example 2: NPV with an annuity
Mutually exclusive projects
steps.body: When only one can be chosen, pick the higher NPV. For projects with unequal lives, compare equivalent annual annuity: EAA = NPV ÷ PVIFA(k, n).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Discounting the initial outlay at t = 0 (it is already a present value).
- Using PI to choose among mutually exclusive projects of very different size; NPV is the rule.

lessons.title: IRR, NPV-IRR conflicts and capital rationing

story.title: What return does the oven earn?

scenes.text: The board prefers a percentage it can compare with the bank rate.
The CFO searches for the rate at which NPV becomes exactly zero.

steps.title: Internal rate of return
steps.body: IRR is the discount rate at which NPV = 0. Accept if IRR > k. Find by trial and error, then linear interpolation: **IRR ≈ L + NPV_L ÷ (NPV_L − NPV_H) × (H − L)**.

steps.title: Worked example 1: IRR of the unit project
Worked example 2: IRR of an even annuity
Conflicts and rationing
steps.body: NPV and IRR can rank mutually exclusive projects differently because of **size** differences, **timing** of cash flows, or **unequal lives**. IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR; NPV assumes reinvestment at k (more realistic), so follow NPV. Non-conventional cash flows (sign changes) can give multiple IRRs; MIRR fixes this. Under **capital rationing**, rank divisible projects by PI and fill the budget; for indivisible projects, choose the feasible combination with the highest total NPV.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Interpolating between rates that do not bracket zero NPV.
- Choosing the higher-IRR project when it has the lower NPV.

quiz.why: Each sign change can create another root of the NPV equation (Descartes' rule of signs).

courses.summary: Specific costs of debt, preference and equity capital, weighted average cost of capital, operating, financial and combined leverage, EBIT-EPS analysis with the indifference point, and the NI, NOI, traditional and Modigliani-Miller theories of capital structure.
outcomes: Compute after-tax cost of irredeemable and redeemable debt

lessons.title: Cost of debt and preference capital

scenes.text: A Pune auto-parts firm can issue 10% debentures or 9% preference shares.
Interest saves tax; preference dividend does not. The real costs differ more than 1%.

steps.title: Concept
steps.body: Cost of capital is the minimum return a firm must earn on investments to keep its investors satisfied; it is the discount rate for capital budgeting. Specific costs: kd (debt), kp (preference), ke (equity), kr (retained earnings).

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
Irredeemable debt: **kd = I(1 − t) ÷ NP** (NP = net proceeds).
Redeemable debt (approximation): **kd = [I(1 − t) + (RV − NP)/n] ÷ [(RV + NP)/2]**.
Irredeemable preference: **kp = D ÷ NP**. Redeemable preference: [D + (RV − NP)/n] ÷ [(RV + NP)/2]. No tax adjustment for preference because dividends are paid from post-tax profit.

steps.title: Worked example 1: irredeemable debenture
steps.body:
₹100 face, 10% coupon, issued at par, tax 25%.
kd = 10 × 0.75 ÷ 100 = **7.5%**.
If issued at ₹95: kd = 7.5 ÷ 95 = 7.89%.

steps.title: Worked example 2: redeemable debenture
steps.body:
Face ₹100, coupon 10%, net proceeds ₹95, redeemable at par in 5 years, tax 25%.
Numerator = 7.5 + (100 − 95)/5 = 7.5 + 1 = 8.5.
Denominator = (100 + 95)/2 = 97.5.
kd = 8.5 ÷ 97.5 = **8.72%**.

steps.title: Worked example 3: preference share
steps.body:
9% preference share, face ₹100, net proceeds ₹95, irredeemable.
kp = 9 ÷ 95 = **9.47%**. Note it is higher than the 8.72% debt cost even though the coupon is lower, because there is no tax shield.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying (1 − t) to preference dividends.
- Using face value instead of net proceeds after flotation costs.

activity.prompt: 12% irredeemable debentures, face ₹100, issued at ₹96, tax 30%. kd in % (2 decimals)?

quiz.q: Debt is usually the cheapest source because

quiz.why: 10% × (1 − 0.25) = 7.5% because the government bears a quarter of the interest through lower tax.

quiz.q: Preference dividend is
quiz.why: It is an appropriation of post-tax profit, so no (1 − t) adjustment applies.

quiz.q: Flotation costs make the cost of a source
quiz.why: The firm receives less (net proceeds) for the same payments, which raises the effective cost.

scenes.text: Equity holders get no promised payment, yet they still expect a return.

steps.title: Cost of equity
steps.body: Dividend growth (Gordon) model: **ke = D₁ ÷ P₀ + g** (use net proceeds for a new issue). CAPM: **ke = R_f + β(R_m − R_f)**. Retained earnings: kr = ke (no flotation cost), adjusted for personal taxes only if the question asks.

steps.title: Worked example 1: Gordon model
steps.body:
Expected dividend D₁ = ₹4, share price ₹50, growth 6%.
ke = 4/50 + 0.06 = 0.08 + 0.06 = **14%**.
If D₀ = ₹4 is the dividend just paid, first compute D₁ = 4 × 1.06 = 4.24, giving ke = 8.48% + 6% = 14.48%.

steps.title: WACC
steps.body: **WACC = Σ wᵢkᵢ** where wᵢ = proportion of each source. Book-value weights use balance-sheet amounts; market-value weights use current market values and are theoretically better. Marginal cost of capital applies to new funds raised.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using D₀ in place of D₁ in the Gordon model.
- Using the pre-tax cost of debt in WACC.
- Weights that do not add to 1.

they reflect current investor opportunity costs
quiz.why: Investors' required returns relate to what their claims are worth today, not historical book values.

quiz.q: Retained earnings have a cost because
options: shareholders forgo dividends they could reinvest
quiz.why: Retaining profit has an opportunity cost equal to the return shareholders could earn elsewhere.

quiz.q: WACC is used as
options: the discount rate for average-risk projects
quiz.why: A project of average risk must earn at least WACC to leave all providers of capital satisfied.

story.title: A small rise in sales, a big jump in EPS

scenes.text: Sales of the auto-parts firm grow 10%, yet EBIT rises 20% and EPS rises about 27%.
Fixed costs and fixed interest act like levers that magnify changes.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
**DOL = Contribution ÷ EBIT** = % change in EBIT ÷ % change in sales (business risk, from fixed operating costs).
**DFL = EBIT ÷ EBT** (EBIT ÷ (EBIT − I), with preference dividend added as Dp/(1 − t) to interest) = % change in EPS ÷ % change in EBIT (financial risk, from fixed financing charges).
**DCL = DOL × DFL = Contribution ÷ EBT**.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
Sales ₹10,00,000; variable cost ₹6,00,000; fixed cost ₹2,00,000; interest ₹50,000.
Contribution = 4,00,000. EBIT = 2,00,000. EBT = 1,50,000.
DOL = 4/2 = **2**. DFL = 2/1.5 = **1.33**. DCL = 4/1.5 = **2.67**.
Meaning: a 10% rise in sales raises EBIT by 20% and EPS by about 26.7%.

steps.title: Worked example 2: verify
steps.body: Sales +10% → contribution 4,40,000; EBIT 2,40,000 (+20%); EBT 1,90,000 (+26.7%). With a constant tax rate and share count, EPS also rises 26.7%. ✔

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.body: High DOL and high DFL together are dangerous: a downturn hits EPS hard. Firms with high operating leverage (airlines, steel) usually keep financial leverage moderate. Operating break-even sales = Fixed cost ÷ P/V ratio = 2,00,000 ÷ 0.4 = ₹5,00,000 in the example.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using sales instead of contribution in DOL.
- Forgetting to gross up preference dividend by (1 − t) in DFL.

quiz.q: DFL = 1 means
quiz.why: With no interest or preference dividend, EBIT = EBT, so EBIT ÷ EBT = 1.

quiz.q: DCL equals
quiz.why: The two levers compound, so combined leverage is their product, equal to contribution ÷ EBT.

lessons.title: Capital structure: EBIT-EPS analysis and theories

scenes.text: The firm needs ₹10 lakh: all equity, or half equity and half 10% debt?
The answer depends on the EBIT it expects. Below a certain EBIT, equity wins; above it, debt wins.

steps.title: EBIT-EPS analysis
steps.body: **EPS = (EBIT − I)(1 − t) ÷ N** (subtract preference dividend before dividing if any). Indifference point: EBIT at which EPS of two plans is equal: (X − I₁)(1 − t)/N₁ = (X − I₂)(1 − t)/N₂.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body: **Net Income (Durand)**: kd and ke constant; more debt lowers WACC and raises value. **Net Operating Income**: WACC constant; ke rises with debt; value independent of structure. **Traditional**: moderate debt lowers WACC up to an optimum, then it rises. **MM without taxes (1958)**: value independent of capital structure, arbitrage keeps it so; ke rises linearly with D/E. **MM with taxes (1963)**: V_L = V_U + tD, so debt adds value through the tax shield; in practice, bankruptcy costs limit debt (trade-off theory). **Pecking order**: internal funds, then debt, then equity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking more debt always helps: higher EPS comes with higher financial risk.
- Mixing the NI and NOI assumptions about which rate is constant.

lessons.title: Working capital concepts and the operating cycle

scenes.text: A Tiruppur garment exporter shows good profit but cannot pay suppliers on time.
Its cash is stuck in fabric, half-stitched shirts and 60-day buyer credit.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: **Gross working capital** = total current assets. **Net working capital** = current assets − current liabilities. Permanent WC is the minimum level always needed; temporary (fluctuating) WC varies with seasons. Excess WC means idle funds and lower return; inadequate WC means missed discounts, stock-outs and loss of credit rating.

steps.title: Operating cycle
steps.body:
Time to convert cash into raw materials, WIP, finished goods, debtors and back to cash.
**Gross operating cycle = RMCP + WIPCP + FGCP + DCP**; **Net (cash) cycle = GOC − creditors' deferral period**. Each period = average balance ÷ (annual flow ÷ 365 or 360).

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
Raw material holding 30 days, WIP 15 days, finished goods 20 days, debtors 45 days, creditors 30 days.
GOC = 30 + 15 + 20 + 45 = **110 days**; NOC = 110 − 30 = **80 days**.

steps.title: Worked example 2: computing a period
steps.body:
Average debtors ₹3,00,000; annual credit sales ₹24,00,000; 360-day year.
Daily sales = 24,00,000 ÷ 360 = 6,666.67.
DCP = 3,00,000 ÷ 6,666.67 = **45 days**.

steps.title: Financing policies and determinants
steps.body: **Matching (hedging)**: permanent needs from long-term funds, temporary from short-term. **Conservative**: long-term funds also cover part of temporary needs (safe, costly). **Aggressive**: short-term funds finance part of permanent needs (cheap, risky). Determinants: nature of business, production cycle, credit policy, seasonality, growth, inflation. Sources: trade credit, bank overdraft and cash credit, commercial paper, factoring.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Subtracting creditors in the gross cycle.
- Mixing 360 and 365 days within one problem.

activity.prompt: RM 25 days, WIP 10, FG 15, debtors 40, creditors 35. Net operating cycle in days?

quiz.why: It is the part of current assets financed by long-term funds.

quiz.why: Using cheaper short-term funds for permanent needs raises refinancing risk.

quiz.why: A longer debtors' period lengthens the time before sales turn into cash.

lessons.title: Cash management and the Baumol model

story.title: Too much cash, too little cash

scenes.text: The exporter's treasurer keeps ₹10 lakh idle in current account, earning nothing.
Selling liquid funds every week costs fees. Is there an optimal balance?

steps.title: Motives and tools
steps.body: Keynes' motives for holding cash: transaction, precautionary, speculative (plus compensating balances for banks). Tools: cash budget, speeding collections (UPI, NEFT/RTGS, lockbox-style collection accounts), controlling disbursements, investing surplus in liquid mutual funds, treasury bills or short deposits.

steps.title: Baumol model
steps.body: Treats cash like inventory. Optimal transfer size **C* = √(2bT ÷ i)** where T = annual cash requirement, b = fixed cost per conversion, i = interest rate on securities. Average balance = C*/2. Total cost = (T/C)b + (C/2)i. The Miller-Orr model instead sets upper and lower limits for random cash flows.

steps.title: Worked example 2: cash budget line
steps.body:
Opening cash ₹50,000; receipts ₹3,20,000; payments ₹3,90,000; minimum balance ₹40,000.
Closing before financing = 50,000 + 3,20,000 − 3,90,000 = −20,000.
Borrowing needed = 40,000 − (−20,000) = **₹60,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 2 in the Baumol formula.
- Treating average cash as C* instead of C*/2.

activity.prompt: Baumol: T = ₹7,20,000, b = ₹50, i = 8%. Optimal transfer size in ₹?

quiz.q: The precautionary motive is holding cash for
quiz.why: It is a buffer against unforeseen outflows or delayed inflows.

quiz.q: In Baumol, if the interest rate rises, optimal cash transfer
quiz.why: i is in the denominator, so idle cash becomes costlier and smaller transfers are optimal.

quiz.q: A cash budget mainly shows
options: timing of cash surpluses and shortages
quiz.why: It forecasts receipts and payments period by period so financing can be arranged in time.

quiz.q: At the Baumol optimum, conversion cost equals
quiz.why: As in EOQ, total cost is minimised where the two opposing costs are equal.

scenes.text: The sales head wants 60-day credit instead of 30 to win a big retail chain.
Meanwhile the store manager orders fabric every week. Both decisions have hidden costs.

steps.title: Credit policy
steps.body: Elements: credit standards, credit period, cash discount, collection effort. Evaluate a change by **incremental contribution − incremental bad debts − cost of extra investment in receivables − extra collection cost**. Credit evaluation uses the 5 Cs: character, capacity, capital, collateral, conditions. Factoring sells receivables to a factor for immediate cash.

steps.title: Worked example 1: relaxing credit
steps.body:
Extra sales ₹2,00,000 a year; contribution 30%; bad debts 2% on extra sales; extra debtors carried at sales value for 60 days of a 360-day year; cost of funds 15%.
Contribution = 60,000. Bad debts = 4,000.
Extra debtors = 2,00,000 × 60/360 = 33,333; carrying cost = 33,333 × 0.15 = 5,000.
Net gain = 60,000 − 4,000 − 5,000 = **₹51,000** → relax credit. (Some texts carry debtors at cost; state your assumption.)

steps.title: Inventory: EOQ and ABC
steps.body: **EOQ = √(2DCo ÷ Ch)** where D = annual demand, Co = cost per order, Ch = holding cost per unit per year. Reorder level = lead-time usage + safety stock. **ABC analysis**: A items ≈ 10–20% of items but ≈ 70% of value (tight control); C items many items, little value. Also VED and JIT.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using monthly demand with annual holding cost.
- Ignoring bad-debt and carrying costs when judging a credit relaxation on sales growth alone.

lessons.title: Dividend policy: Walter, Gordon and MM

scenes.text: The board has EPS of ₹10. Shareholders want dividends; the CEO wants to fund expansion earning 15%.
Valuation models show when retaining profit raises the share price.

steps.title: Walter model
steps.body: **P = [D + (r/ke)(E − D)] ÷ ke**. r = return on investment, ke = cost of equity. If r > ke (growth firm): payout 0% maximises price. r = ke (normal): payout irrelevant. r < ke (declining): 100% payout maximises price.

steps.title: Gordon and MM
steps.body: Gordon: **P = E(1 − b) ÷ (ke − br)**, b = retention ratio, g = br. Gordon's 'bird-in-hand' argument: investors value near dividends more as uncertainty rises. **MM (1961)**: in perfect markets with no taxes, value depends on earning power, not dividend policy; a dividend is offset by a fall in share price or new issue. Real-world factors: taxes, signalling, clientele effect, legal limits, liquidity, stability.

steps.title: Forms of dividend
steps.body: Cash dividend (interim or final), bonus shares (stock dividend: capitalises reserves, no cash outflow), share buyback, and stable dividend policy (constant DPS or constant payout). Indian companies declare dividends under the Companies Act, 2013; final dividend needs shareholders' approval at the AGM.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- In Walter, using r/ke on D instead of on (E − D).
- In Gordon, using g ≥ ke.

quiz.why: Reserves move into share capital; total equity and cash are unchanged, and EPS falls as shares rise.

steps.title: Time value and risk
steps.body: FV = PV(1 + r)ⁿ · PV = FV/(1 + r)ⁿ · FVIFA = [(1 + r)ⁿ − 1]/r · PVIFA = [1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ]/r · Perpetuity = A/r · Growing perpetuity = A₁/(r − g) · EAR = (1 + r/m)ᵐ − 1 · E(R) = ΣpR · σ = √Σp(R − E)² · CAPM k = R_f + β(R_m − R_f).

steps.title: Capital budgeting

lessons.title: Lab: NPV and IRR in a spreadsheet

scenes.text: In the computer lab, students rebuild the oven project from Unit 2 in Excel or LibreOffice Calc.
The spreadsheet must agree with the hand answer: NPV ₹11,554 and IRR about 15.3%.

steps.title: Setup
steps.body: In A1:A5 type years 0–4; in B1:B5 type −100000, 30000, 40000, 50000, 20000. Put the rate 10% in D1.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
NPV: `=NPV(D1,B2:B5)+B1` → 11,554 (the NPV function assumes the first value is one period away, so add the year-0 outlay separately).
IRR: `=IRR(B1:B5)` → about 15.32%.
PI: `=NPV(D1,B2:B5)/-B1` → 1.12.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing `=NPV(D1,B1:B5)`: this discounts the outlay by one year and understates value.
- Entering 10 instead of 10% for the rate.

steps.title: Observation table
steps.body: Change the rate to 12%, 14%, 16% and record NPV. You should see NPV fall and cross zero between 15% and 16%, confirming the IRR. Viva: why does NPV fall as the rate rises? Because each future cash flow is divided by a larger (1 + k)ᵗ.

activity.prompt: Put the spreadsheet procedure in order
items: Enter years 0 to 4 in column A
Enter the cash flows with the outlay as a negative number
Enter the discount rate in a separate cell
Compute NPV with =NPV(rate, years 1–4) plus the year-0 cell
Vary the rate and record NPV in an observation table

quiz.why: NPV() discounts its first argument by one period, so a time-0 amount must be added undiscounted.

quiz.why: 16% exceeds the IRR of about 15.3%, so discounted inflows fall below the outlay.

scenes.text: Sharda Foods plans a ₹10 lakh expansion with expected EBIT of ₹2 lakh.
The CFO must pick a financing plan, check the project against WACC and set a dividend.

steps.title: Case data
steps.body: Plan A: all equity, 1,00,000 shares. Plan B: 50,000 shares + ₹5 L debt at 10%. Tax 25%. ke 14%, after-tax kd 7.5%. Project IRR 15.3%. ROI on retained funds 15%.

steps.title: Financing decision
steps.body: EPS A = 2,00,000 × 0.75 ÷ 1,00,000 = ₹1.50. EPS B = 1,50,000 × 0.75 ÷ 50,000 = ₹2.25. Indifference EBIT = ₹1 L; expected EBIT ₹2 L is well above it → Plan B raises EPS. DFL under B = 2,00,000 ÷ 1,50,000 = 1.33.

steps.title: Investment and dividend decisions
steps.body:
WACC under B (book weights 50/50) = 0.5 × 14 + 0.5 × 7.5 = 10.75%. IRR 15.3% > 10.75% → accept.
Dividend: r 15% > ke 14% → Walter favours low payout; balance with signalling by keeping a stable modest dividend.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Choosing debt only on expected EPS without testing a downside EBIT.

steps.body:

courses.title: Unit 1 · HRM Foundations, Human Resource Planning and Job Analysis

lessons.title: What HRM is and what HR does

scenes.text: A Gurugram start-up grows from 15 to 120 people in a year.
The founders are drowning in offer letters, payroll queries and complaints.
They hire an HR head. What exactly will she do?

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: HRM is the strategic and coherent approach to the management of an organisation's people: acquiring, developing, motivating and retaining them so they contribute to objectives while their needs are met.

steps.title: Functions (Flippo's classification)
steps.body:
- **Managerial**: planning, organising, directing, controlling HR.
- **Operative**: procurement (HRP, recruitment, selection, induction), development (training, career), compensation, integration (motivation, grievance, IR), maintenance (welfare, safety, health), separation.
- Advisory: advising top management and departments.

steps.title: Personnel management to SHRM
steps.body: Personnel management: administrative, reactive, rule-focused. HRM: people as assets, line managers involved. **Strategic HRM**: aligning HR policies with business strategy (e.g. a cost-leader stresses efficiency and standard roles; an innovator stresses creativity and learning).

steps.title: Ulrich's four HR roles
steps.body: Strategic partner, administrative expert, employee champion, change agent. Many firms now organise HR as business partners, centres of expertise and shared services.

scenes.text: An auto-parts maker in Chakan plans to raise output from 1 lakh to 1.2 lakh units next year.
It currently has 200 operators and expects some to leave or retire.
HR must work out how many to hire, and when.

steps.title: Process
steps.body:
1 Analyse organisational objectives and plans.
2 Forecast demand for HR.
3 Forecast supply (internal and external).
4 Estimate net requirement (gap).
5 Action plans: recruitment, training, redeployment, or downsizing.
6 Monitor and control.

steps.title: Workload analysis
steps.body: Planned output 1,20,000 units; standard time 2 hours per unit → 2,40,000 hours. Productive hours per worker per year = 2,000. Workers needed = 2,40,000 / 2,000 = **120**. Allowing 4% absenteeism: 120 / 0.96 = **125**.

steps.title: Net requirement
steps.body: Required next year: 230 (whole plant). Current: 200. Expected losses: attrition 10% (20), retirements 5, promotions out of the grade 5 → available = 200 − 30 = 170. Net hires needed = 230 − 170 = **60**.

steps.title: Forecasting techniques
steps.body: Demand: managerial judgement, Delphi, ratio-trend analysis, work-study, regression. Supply: skills inventories, replacement charts, succession planning, Markov analysis (transition probabilities).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Do not forget internal movements: promotions out of a grade reduce supply in that grade even though people stay in the company.

story.title: What does a store manager actually do?

scenes.text: A retail chain's store managers in different cities do very different work.

steps.title: Job analysis
steps.body: Systematic process of collecting information about the duties, responsibilities, working conditions and human requirements of a job. Output: **job description** (what the job is) and **job specification** (what the person needs).

steps.title: Methods
steps.body: Observation, interview, questionnaire (e.g. Position Analysis Questionnaire), diary/log, critical incident technique, technical conference, functional job analysis.

steps.title: Sample job description and specification
steps.body:
**Job title**: Store Manager. **Reports to**: Area Manager. **Purpose**: run a 6,000 sq ft store profitably. **Duties**: sales targets, staff rosters, inventory audits, customer complaints, cash control.
**Specification**: graduate; 4+ years retail with 1 year supervising; skills in Excel, inventory systems; traits: customer orientation, calm under pressure; local language fluency.

steps.title: Uses

steps.title: Job evaluation
steps.body: Determines the relative worth of jobs (not people) to build internal equity. Non-quantitative: **ranking**, **job classification/grading**. Quantitative: **point method**, **factor comparison**.

steps.title: Point method
steps.body:
Factors and maximum points: skill 300, effort 200, responsibility 300, working conditions 200 (total 1,000).
Supervisor: 180 + 150 + 200 + 160 = **690**. Accountant: 210 + 100 + 220 + 60 = **590**.
If pay = ₹50 per point per month, supervisor ₹34,500 and accountant ₹29,500, so the supervisors' complaint has merit under this scheme.

steps.body: Work simplification, job rotation, job enlargement, job enrichment, autonomous teams, ergonomics, flexible work arrangements.

courses.summary: Internal and external sources of recruitment, e-recruitment and employer branding, yield ratios and cost per hire, the selection process, tests and interviews, reliability and validity, reference and background checks, placement, induction and socialisation.
