scenes.text: A Hyderabad pharma company needs a new quality-control manager.
An experienced internal analyst wants the job; an outside candidate has a stronger regulatory background.
Each source has pros and cons.

steps.title: Recruitment
steps.body: Recruitment is the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply. It is a positive process (attracting many); selection is often called negative (rejecting most).

steps.title: Internal sources
steps.body: Promotions, transfers, internal job postings, employee referrals, re-hiring former employees. Pros: motivation, lower cost, known performance, faster. Cons: limited pool, inbreeding of ideas, resentment among those not chosen.

steps.title: External sources
steps.body: Campus placements, job portals, social media and professional networks, advertisements, placement consultants and executive search, walk-ins, employment exchanges, gig platforms. Pros: fresh ideas, wider talent, diversity. Cons: costlier, longer, adjustment risk.

steps.title: Employer branding
steps.body: Firms build an employee value proposition (learning, culture, flexibility, purpose) and showcase it on careers pages and social media to attract talent at lower cost per hire.

activity.prompt: Internal or external source?

quiz.why: Promotion opportunities motivate current employees.

quiz.why: It aims to attract as many suitable applicants as possible.

lessons.title: Recruitment metrics: yield ratios and cost per hire

scenes.text: An insurance company needs 10 new sales executives.
Past data: only half accept offers, and many applicants never reach interview.
HR works backwards to find how many applicants it needs.

steps.title: Recruitment yield pyramid
steps.body:
Target hires 10. Offer acceptance 50% → offers = 10 / 0.5 = **20**.
Interviews : offers = 3 : 1 → interviews = **60**.
Applicants : interviews = 5 : 1 → applicants = **300**.

steps.title: Cost per hire
steps.body: Advertising ₹2,00,000 + agency fees ₹2,50,000 + interview travel ₹50,000 + recruiter time ₹1,00,000 = ₹6,00,000. Hires = 20. **Cost per hire = ₹30,000**.

steps.title: Other metrics
steps.body: Time to fill, source of hire effectiveness, quality of hire (performance and retention after 6–12 months), offer acceptance rate, new-hire turnover.

steps.title: Comparing sources
steps.body: Referrals: 30 hires, ₹3,00,000 cost → ₹10,000 per hire, 90% still employed after a year. Portal: 40 hires, ₹8,00,000 → ₹20,000 per hire, 70% retained. Referrals are cheaper and retain better here.

steps.title: Don't optimise cost alone
steps.body: A cheap source that yields poor performers costs more later. Track quality of hire alongside cost.

lessons.title: The selection process, tests and interviews

scenes.text: Applications pour in for the sales role.
HR screens CVs, runs an aptitude test, then a role-play and panel interview.
Reference checks and a medical complete the process.

steps.title: Typical steps
steps.body: Preliminary screening → application blank → selection tests → interviews → reference and background checks → selection decision → medical examination → job offer → contract and joining. Not every firm uses every step, and the order can vary.

steps.title: Tests
steps.body: Aptitude, intelligence, personality, interest, achievement/trade tests, situational judgement, work samples, assessment centres (group discussion, in-basket, role play). Work samples and structured interviews tend to have high validity.

steps.title: Interviews
steps.body: Types: structured, unstructured, behavioural (tell me about a time…), situational (what would you do if…), panel, stress, video. Errors: halo, contrast, first impression, similar-to-me, leniency, central tendency.

steps.title: Reliability and validity
steps.body:
- **Reliability**: consistency of results (test–retest, inter-rater).
- **Validity**: measures what it claims and predicts job performance (criterion-related, content, construct).
A test can be reliable but not valid; it cannot be valid without being reliable.

steps.title: Fair and lawful selection
steps.body: Questions about religion, caste, marital plans or pregnancy are inappropriate and risk discrimination claims; keep questions job-related.

scenes.text: Kunal joins a bank branch; no one expects him and his login is not ready.

steps.title: Placement
steps.body: Assigning a selected candidate to the job for which he or she is best suited, matching job requirements with the person's qualifications and preferences.

steps.title: Induction (orientation)
steps.body: Welcoming and introducing new employees to the organisation, its people, policies and job. Contents: company history, products, structure, policies (leave, conduct, POSH policy), facilities, safety, team introductions, first-week plan, buddy assignment.

steps.title: Onboarding
steps.body: A longer process (often 90 days or more) that includes pre-joining contact, day-one readiness (laptop, ID), role clarity, early wins, check-ins at 30-60-90 days, and feedback.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Early turnover is costly because the recruiting cost is lost before the hire becomes productive. Structured onboarding is associated with better retention and faster productivity.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Training, Development and Career Management
courses.summary: Training vs development, training needs analysis at three levels, on-the-job and off-the-job methods, e-learning, Kirkpatrick's four levels of evaluation and training ROI, management development, career planning and succession planning.
outcomes: Distinguish training, education and development
Conduct organisational, task and individual needs analysis
Select suitable training methods for a given need
Evaluate training with Kirkpatrick's model and compute ROI
Explain career stages and succession planning

story.title: Rising complaints at the call centre

scenes.text: Customer complaints at a telecom call centre jump 40% in a quarter.
Managers want to send everyone for a two-day soft-skills course.
HR first asks: is training really the answer, and for whom?

steps.title: Training vs development
steps.body: **Training**: improving specific job skills for current jobs, short-term, task-focused. **Development**: growth of the person for future roles, long-term, broader. **Education**: general knowledge and understanding.

steps.title: Three levels of TNA (McGehee & Thayer)
steps.body:
- **Organisational analysis**: where training is needed given strategy, resources and climate.
- **Task (operations) analysis**: what skills each job requires.
- **Individual (person) analysis**: who needs training, using appraisals, tests and observations.
Training need = required competence − present competence.

steps.title: Is it a training problem?
steps.body: Performance gaps may come from poor tools, unclear goals, wrong incentives or bad processes. Training only fixes gaps in knowledge, skill or attitude.

steps.title: Call centre diagnosis
steps.body: Complaint analysis shows 70% relate to a new billing system that only 30% of agents were trained on. Focused system training for the untrained 70% of agents is better than generic soft skills for all.

activity.prompt: Match the TNA level to the question it answers
pairs: Where in the company is training needed?
What skills does this job need?
Is the problem tools or incentives?

quiz.q: Which level of TNA uses appraisal data on specific employees?
quiz.why: Individual analysis identifies which people need training.

quiz.q: Development is mainly
quiz.why: Development prepares people for future roles.

quiz.q: A gap caused by a broken machine is solved by
quiz.why: Not every performance gap is a skill gap; fix the environment first.

scenes.text: A quick-commerce firm hires 500 riders across five cities.
They need app skills, road safety and customer etiquette within a week.
HR mixes short videos, shadowing and a classroom safety module.

steps.title: On-the-job methods
steps.body: Job instruction training (JIT: prepare, present, try out, follow up), coaching, mentoring, job rotation, apprenticeship, understudy, internship.

steps.title: Off-the-job methods
steps.body: Lectures, case studies, role plays, simulations (flight or driving simulators), vestibule training (replica of the work area), business games, sensitivity training, conferences, e-learning and microlearning.

steps.title: Choosing a method
steps.body: Consider learning objective (knowledge, skill, attitude), number of trainees, cost, transfer to the job, safety risk, and time. Skills with safety risks suit simulation or vestibule training; attitude change suits role plays and coaching.

steps.title: Apprenticeships in India
steps.body: The Apprentices Act, 1961 and government schemes such as the National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme support structured on-the-job training with stipends in many trades.

quiz.why: Role plays let trainees practise behaviour with feedback.

scenes.text: A manufacturer spends ₹5 lakh on a quality-improvement programme.
Six months later, defect costs and output are compared.

steps.title: Kirkpatrick's four levels
steps.body:
1 **Reaction**: did participants like it? (feedback forms)
2 **Learning**: did they gain knowledge or skill? (tests)
3 **Behaviour**: do they apply it on the job? (observation, 360° feedback)
4 **Results**: did business outcomes improve? (quality, sales, safety)
Phillips adds a fifth level: **ROI**.

steps.title: Training ROI
steps.body:
Cost: ₹5,00,000. Benefits over a year: lower defect cost ₹3,00,000 + extra output contribution ₹4,00,000 = ₹7,00,000.
Net benefit = ₹2,00,000. **ROI = 2,00,000 / 5,00,000 × 100 = 40%**.
Benefit–cost ratio = 7 / 5 = **1.4**.

steps.title: Isolating the effect
steps.body: Other factors (new machines, market demand) may also improve results. Use control groups or trend comparison to isolate training's contribution.

steps.title: Transfer of training
steps.body: Learning transfers to the job when supervisors support it, there is opportunity to practise soon, and the content is relevant.

Level 3 of Kirkpatrick measures
quiz.why: Behaviour shows whether learning transfers to work.

quiz.q: Who added ROI as a fifth level?
quiz.why: Jack Phillips extended Kirkpatrick's model with ROI.

steps.title: Management development methods
steps.body: Coaching, mentoring, job rotation, understudy, special projects, action learning, executive education programmes, assessment and development centres, 360° feedback.

steps.title: Career planning
steps.body: Career stages (exploration, establishment, maintenance, disengagement), career paths and ladders (including dual ladders for technical experts), career counselling, individual development plans (IDPs).

steps.title: Succession planning
steps.body: Identify critical positions → define competencies → assess internal talent (e.g. 9-box grid of performance vs potential) → develop successors → review regularly. Distinguish ready-now, ready in 1–2 years and long-term successors.

steps.body: 12 critical roles; 9 have at least one ready-now successor. **Bench strength = 9/12 = 75%**.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Performance Appraisal and Compensation Management
courses.summary: Purpose and process of performance management, traditional and modern appraisal methods (ranking, paired comparison, forced distribution, BARS, MBO, 360°), rating errors, components of pay and CTC, incentives, compa-ratio, and statutory benefits such as provident fund, gratuity and bonus, with worked calculations.
outcomes: Choose and apply appraisal methods including paired comparison and forced distribution
Recognise and reduce rating errors
Build a CTC from salary components
Compute gratuity and compa-ratio
Explain incentive plans and statutory benefits in India

scenes.text: In a services firm, 85% of employees are rated 'exceeds expectations'.
The bonus pool cannot reward that many people.
HR rethinks the appraisal method.

steps.title: Performance management cycle
steps.body: Plan (set goals and KPIs) → monitor and coach (continuous feedback) → review (appraisal) → reward and develop. Appraisal is one step; performance management is the whole cycle.

steps.title: Traditional methods
steps.body: Straight ranking, **paired comparison**, **forced distribution**, graphic rating scales, checklists, critical incidents, essay/free-form, confidential reports (common in government).

steps.title: Paired comparison and forced distribution
steps.body:
Paired comparison: with n employees, pairs = n(n − 1)/2. For 6 employees: 6 × 5 / 2 = **15 comparisons**.
Forced distribution 10-20-40-20-10 for 50 employees: **5, 10, 20, 10, 5** across the five categories.

steps.title: Modern methods
steps.body:
- **MBO**: jointly set measurable objectives, review against results.
- **BARS**: behaviourally anchored rating scales: each point on the scale is anchored to a specific behaviour example.
- **360° feedback**: from supervisor, peers, subordinates, customers and self.
- **OKRs** and continuous check-ins in many tech firms.

steps.title: Forced distribution risks
steps.body: In small or uniformly strong teams it forces artificial low ratings and can hurt collaboration.

activity.prompt: Match the method
pairs: Every employee compared with every other
Fixed percentage in each rating band
Scale points tied to behaviour examples
Feedback from boss, peers, reports and customers

quiz.why: 8 × 7 / 2 = 28 comparisons.

BARS improves rating accuracy by
quiz.why: Behavioural anchors make each rating level concrete and less subjective.

scenes.text: Arun struggled for nine months but closed a huge deal in March.
His manager rates him outstanding for the year.
Was the rating fair to the whole year?

steps.title: Common errors
steps.body:
- **Halo / horn effect**: one trait colours all ratings.
- **Recency effect**: recent events dominate.
- **Leniency / strictness**: ratings too high or too low.
- **Central tendency**: everyone rated average.
- **Similar-to-me** and **personal bias** (gender, caste, region).
- **Contrast effect**: comparing with others instead of standards.

steps.title: Remedies
steps.body: Clear criteria and KPIs, rater training, behavioural anchors, documentation of critical incidents throughout the year, multiple raters, calibration meetings, appeal mechanisms.

steps.title: Appraisal interview
steps.body: Prepare evidence, start with strengths, discuss gaps with specific examples, agree an improvement and development plan, and document it. Tell-and-sell, tell-and-listen and problem-solving styles exist; problem-solving suits most knowledge workers.

activity.prompt: Name the rating error
pairs: Strong year-end deal outweighs nine weak months
Punctuality makes manager rate everything high
Manager rates all team members 3 out of 5
Manager rates everyone generously to avoid conflict

quiz.q: Keeping a log of critical incidents all year reduces
quiz.why: Records of the whole year counter over-weighting of recent events.

quiz.q: Calibration meetings help by
quiz.why: Managers compare and adjust ratings to apply consistent standards.

quiz.q: Rating a person low on everything because of one weakness is the
quiz.why: The horn effect is the negative counterpart of the halo effect.

scenes.text: Priya gets an offer of '₹7 lakh CTC' from a Bengaluru firm.
Her monthly in-hand pay seems much lower than ₹7 lakh ÷ 12.
She breaks the CTC into its parts.

steps.title: Components
steps.body: Fixed: basic pay, dearness allowance (common in public sector), HRA, special/other allowances. Variable: performance bonus, incentives, commission. Benefits: employer PF contribution, gratuity, insurance, meal cards. Statutory deductions from employee pay: employee PF, professional tax (in some states), income tax (TDS).

steps.title: Worked CTC (simplified)
steps.body:
Monthly: basic ₹30,000; HRA 40% of basic = ₹12,000; special allowance ₹13,000 → gross ₹55,000.
Annual gross = 55,000 × 12 = ₹6,60,000. Employer PF 12% of basic = ₹3,600/month = ₹43,200/year.
**CTC = 6,60,000 + 43,200 = ₹7,03,200** (excluding gratuity and insurance for simplicity).
In-hand is lower because employee PF (₹3,600/month), professional tax where applicable and TDS are deducted. Assumption: PF computed on full basic; many firms cap the PF wage at ₹15,000.

steps.title: Compa-ratio
steps.body: Compa-ratio = actual salary / midpoint of the pay range. Salary ₹54,000; range midpoint ₹60,000 → **0.90**: paid below midpoint, possibly due to low tenure or a retention risk.

steps.title: Pay-setting factors
steps.body: Job evaluation (internal equity), market surveys (external equity), individual performance and seniority (individual equity), ability to pay, legal minimum wages, collective bargaining, cost of living.

activity.prompt: Fixed pay, variable pay or benefit?

A compa-ratio well below 1 may indicate
options: underpayment relative to the range midpoint
quiz.why: Below 1 means pay is under the midpoint of the range.

scenes.text: Suman retires after 10 years with a last-drawn basic plus DA of ₹52,000 a month.
She asks HR what gratuity she will receive.

steps.title: Incentive plans
steps.body: Individual: piece rate, commission, Halsey/Rowan, merit pay, spot awards. Group: team bonus, gain-sharing (Scanlon, Rucker), profit sharing. Organisation-wide: ESOPs, ESPPs. Effective plans are simple, linked to controllable performance, and paid soon after results.

steps.title: Gratuity
steps.body:
For employees covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act (5+ years of continuous service, with exceptions such as death or disablement): gratuity = last drawn wages (basic + DA) × 15/26 × completed years.
52,000 × 15/26 × 10 = 30,000 × 10 = **₹3,00,000** (statutory ceiling ₹20 lakh).

steps.title: Other statutory benefits
steps.body:
- **Provident fund** (EPF): employer and employee each typically contribute 12% of basic + DA, with mandatory coverage up to a wage ceiling of ₹15,000.
- **Statutory bonus**: minimum 8.33% and maximum 20% of salary/wages for eligible employees (Payment of Bonus Act).
- **ESI**: health and cash benefits for employees under the wage ceiling.
- **Maternity benefit**: up to 26 weeks paid leave for eligible women (first two children).

steps.title: Labour codes
steps.body: India consolidated 29 central labour laws into four codes: Code on Wages (2019), Industrial Relations Code (2020), Code on Social Security (2020) and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code (2020). Check the latest notified rules for exact thresholds, which can change.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Industrial Relations, Grievance, Discipline, Welfare and HR Analytics
courses.summary: Industrial relations and trade unions, collective bargaining and dispute settlement, grievance handling, discipline and domestic enquiry, employee welfare, health and safety and prevention of sexual harassment, separation and exit, and HR analytics metrics such as attrition and absenteeism rates.
outcomes: Explain the parties and approaches to industrial relations
Describe collective bargaining and dispute settlement machinery
Design a grievance procedure and apply the hot-stove rule of discipline
Outline the POSH Act's Internal Committee requirements
Compute attrition, absenteeism and other HR metrics

lessons.title: Industrial relations, unions and collective bargaining

scenes.text: A tyre plant's union demands a 15% wage rise; management offers 6%.
Weeks of talks follow, with a threat of strike.
They sign a three-year settlement at 9% plus a productivity bonus.

steps.title: Industrial relations
steps.body: Relations between employers, employees/unions and the State. Approaches: unitary (common interests, conflict is abnormal), pluralist (different interests, conflict managed through institutions), Marxist (conflict rooted in class). Dunlop's systems approach: actors, context, ideology, rules.

steps.title: Trade unions
steps.body: Associations of workers to protect and promote their interests. Functions: collective bargaining, welfare, representation, political voice. Registration under the Trade Unions Act, 1926, now being subsumed in the Industrial Relations Code, 2020. Indian challenges: multiplicity of unions, political affiliation, outside leadership, low membership in the informal sector.

steps.title: Collective bargaining
steps.body: Negotiation between employer and union representatives on wages and conditions, producing an agreement or settlement. Process: preparation, presenting demands, negotiation, agreement, implementation and administration. Types: distributive, integrative, attitudinal structuring, intra-organisational bargaining (Walton & McKersie).

steps.title: Dispute settlement
steps.body: Bipartite negotiation, conciliation (by conciliation officers), voluntary arbitration, adjudication by labour courts and tribunals. Strikes and lockouts in public utility services require notice. Workers' participation in management via works committees and joint councils.

activity.prompt: Match the term
pairs: Third party helps the sides reach agreement without imposing a decision
Parties agree to accept an outsider's binding decision
Labour court or tribunal decides the dispute
Employer shuts the workplace in a dispute

quiz.q: The pluralist approach sees conflict as
quiz.why: Pluralists accept differing interests and rely on bargaining institutions.

quiz.q: Walton and McKersie's bargaining type that expands joint gains is
quiz.why: Integrative bargaining seeks win–win solutions.

quiz.q: In conciliation, the third party
options: helps parties reach their own agreement
quiz.why: Conciliators facilitate but do not decide.

scenes.text: Machinist Raju says he was denied overtime for months while others got it.
His supervisor brushes it off; he raises it formally.
Elsewhere, a worker is caught sleeping on night shift. How should each case be handled?

steps.title: Grievance
steps.body: Any dissatisfaction or feeling of injustice connected with employment, expressed or not. Causes: pay, working conditions, supervision, promotion, discipline. A typical step ladder: immediate supervisor → department head → grievance committee → top management → voluntary arbitration. Each step has a time limit (e.g. 48 hours to 1 week). The IR Code, 2020 requires a Grievance Redressal Committee in establishments with 20 or more workers.

steps.title: Discipline
steps.body: Positive discipline builds self-control and compliance through clear rules and coaching; negative discipline relies on penalties. **Progressive discipline**: oral warning → written warning → suspension → dismissal.

steps.title: McGregor's hot-stove rule
steps.body: Discipline should be like touching a hot stove: **immediate**, with **advance warning**, **consistent**, and **impersonal**.

steps.title: Domestic enquiry (principles of natural justice)
steps.body: For misconduct: charge sheet with specific allegations → reply → enquiry by an impartial officer → employee may cross-examine witnesses and present defence (often with a co-worker) → findings → show-cause on proposed punishment → order. Natural justice: no one should be a judge in their own cause; hear the other side.

activity.prompt: Match the hot-stove principle
pairs: Stove glows red before you touch it
Burns every time anyone touches it
Burns regardless of who touches it

quiz.q: The first step in most grievance procedures is
quiz.why: Grievances are best resolved closest to where they arise.

quiz.q: Progressive discipline means
options: increasingly serious penalties for repeated misconduct
quiz.why: It escalates gradually, giving chances to improve.

quiz.q: Which is a principle of natural justice in a domestic enquiry?
quiz.why: Audi alteram partem requires hearing the employee's defence.

lessons.title: Welfare, safety and a respectful workplace

scenes.text: A BPO arranges safe cab drops for women working night shifts.
A chemical plant runs monthly safety drills and health check-ups.
Both are part of employee welfare and safety.

steps.title: Employee welfare
steps.body: Statutory welfare (drinking water, canteens, crèches, first aid, washrooms, rest rooms as required by law) and voluntary welfare (transport, housing, education support, counselling, wellness, recreation).

steps.title: Health and safety
steps.body: Causes of accidents: unsafe conditions and unsafe acts. Prevention: safety committees, training, PPE, machine guarding, audits, near-miss reporting. Metrics: frequency rate = injuries × 10,00,000 / man-hours worked.

steps.title: Frequency rate
steps.body: 6 lost-time injuries in a year; 500 workers × 2,400 hours = 12,00,000 man-hours. Frequency rate = 6 × 10,00,000 / 12,00,000 = **5.0** per million man-hours.

steps.title: POSH Act, 2013
steps.body: The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act requires every employer with 10 or more employees to constitute an **Internal Committee** headed by a senior woman employee, with at least half its members women and one external member from an NGO or familiar with the issue. Complaints generally within 3 months of the incident; inquiry to be completed within 90 days.

activity.prompt: Statutory or voluntary welfare (typical classification)?

quiz.q: 4 injuries; 8,00,000 man-hours. Frequency rate =
Under the POSH Act an Internal Committee is required where an employer has at least
quiz.why: Employers with 10 or more employees must constitute an Internal Committee.

quiz.q: Most workplace accidents are attributed to
quiz.why: Safety management targets both risky behaviours and hazardous conditions.

scenes.text: An IT services firm sees many first-year engineers resign.
HR analyses exit data by manager, location and pay band.
Most exits cluster under three managers with low engagement scores.

steps.title: Separation
steps.body: Voluntary (resignation, voluntary retirement) and involuntary (dismissal, discharge, layoff, retrenchment, retirement on superannuation, death). Good practice: exit interviews, clear full-and-final settlement, knowledge transfer, alumni networks.

steps.title: Attrition rate
steps.body:
Headcount 400 at start and 440 at end of the year → average 420. Separations 36.
**Annual attrition = 36 / 420 × 100 = 8.57%**.
Monthly view: 4 exits in a month with average headcount 400 → 1% per month, roughly 12% annualised.

steps.title: Absenteeism rate
steps.body:
100 workers scheduled for 25 days = 2,500 man-days. Man-days lost to absence = 150.
**Absenteeism = 150 / 2,500 × 100 = 6%**.

steps.title: HR analytics levels
steps.body: Descriptive (what happened: attrition dashboard), diagnostic (why: drivers by manager or pay), predictive (who is likely to leave), prescriptive (what to do). Data from HRIS: headcount, hiring, performance, engagement surveys. Ethics: privacy, consent and fairness of algorithms; India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs personal data processing.

steps.title: Other useful metrics
steps.body: Revenue per employee, training hours per employee, offer acceptance rate, internal mobility rate, early (first-year) attrition, employee net promoter score.

uni-bba-international-business.title: BBA · International Business
uni-bba-international-business.description: International business for BBA: globalisation, trade theories from mercantilism to Porter's diamond, cultural, political and legal environments, trade policy, WTO and regional blocs, balance of payments, foreign exchange markets and parity conditions, entry modes, FDI, MNC strategies, and export-import procedures including Incoterms and letters of credit, with worked numericals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BBA programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Globalisation and theories of international trade
courses.summary: Meaning and scope of international business, drivers and debates of globalisation, mercantilism, absolute and comparative advantage with numerical examples, Heckscher-Ohlin and the Leontief paradox, product life cycle theory, new trade theory and Porter's diamond.
outcomes: Explain the scope and drivers of international business
Distinguish absolute and comparative advantage and compute opportunity costs
Explain factor endowment theory and the Leontief paradox
Apply Vernon's product life cycle theory
Use Porter's diamond to explain national competitive advantage

scenes.text: Cotton grown in Gujarat is spun in Tamil Nadu, stitched in Bangladesh and sold in a German store.
Designs come from Sweden; payment flows through banks in three countries.

steps.title: Meaning and scope
steps.body: International business (IB) covers all commercial transactions across national borders: trade in goods and services, foreign direct and portfolio investment, licensing and franchising, management contracts, and international finance. It differs from domestic business through multiple currencies, laws, cultures and political risks.

steps.title: Globalisation
steps.body: Increasing integration of markets and production worldwide. **Drivers**: falling trade barriers (GATT/WTO), technology (containers, internet), falling transport and communication costs, liberalisation (India's 1991 reforms), and global capital flows. Dimensions: globalisation of markets and of production (global value chains).

steps.title: Debate
steps.body: Benefits: efficiency, consumer choice, technology transfer, jobs in exporting sectors. Concerns: job losses in import-competing industries, inequality, environmental pressure, loss of policy autonomy, vulnerability to supply shocks. Recent trends include 'friend-shoring' and supply-chain diversification ('China plus one').

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating IB only with exports.
- Treating globalisation as purely economic; it also has cultural and political dimensions.

activity.prompt: Is each a driver of globalisation or a concern about it?

quiz.q: Which is part of international business?
options: Trade, FDI, licensing and finance across borders
quiz.why: IB includes all cross-border commercial transactions, not just goods exports.

quiz.q: India's major economic liberalisation began in
quiz.why: The 1991 reforms reduced licensing, tariffs and FDI restrictions.

quiz.q: Globalisation of production refers to
options: sourcing and making goods in different countries
quiz.why: Firms spread value-chain activities across locations to exploit cost and skill differences.

quiz.q: 'China plus one' describes
options: diversifying supply away from dependence on one country
quiz.why: Firms add other sourcing locations, such as India or Vietnam, to reduce concentration risk.

lessons.title: Lab: Mercantilism, absolute and comparative advantage

story.title: India and the UK: cloth and wheat

scenes.text: India needs 2 hours to make a unit of cloth and 4 hours for a unit of wheat; the UK needs 3 and 4.
Can both gain from trade even if one is never worse at anything?

steps.title: Mercantilism and absolute advantage
steps.body: **Mercantilism** (16th–18th c.): national wealth = gold; maximise exports, minimise imports; zero-sum view. **Adam Smith (1776)**: absolute advantage — each country should specialise in goods it produces with fewer resources than others; trade is positive-sum.

steps.title: Comparative advantage (Ricardo, 1817)
steps.body: Even if a country is more efficient in everything, both gain by specialising where their **opportunity cost** is lower. Opportunity cost of good X = labour for X ÷ labour for Y (units of Y forgone).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Hours per unit: India cloth 2, wheat 4; UK cloth 3, wheat 4.
Opportunity cost of cloth: India 2/4 = **0.5 wheat**; UK 3/4 = **0.75 wheat** → India has comparative advantage in cloth.
Opportunity cost of wheat: India 4/2 = 2 cloth; UK 4/3 = **1.33 cloth** → UK has comparative advantage in wheat.
Any terms of trade between 0.5 and 0.75 wheat per cloth benefit both.

steps.title: Assumptions and limits
steps.body: Two countries, two goods, labour only, constant costs, full employment, no transport costs. Real trade adds transport, scale economies and changing technology.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing hours directly (absolute advantage) when asked for comparative advantage.
- Inverting the opportunity-cost ratio.

activity.prompt: Country A: 6 hours per car, 3 hours per computer. Opportunity cost of one car in terms of computers?

quiz.why: They believed a trade surplus brought bullion and thus national power.

quiz.why: Ricardo showed specialisation by lower opportunity cost lets both countries consume more.

quiz.q: In the example, the UK should specialise in
quiz.why: UK gives up only 1.33 cloth per wheat versus India's 2 cloth.

quiz.q: Adam Smith's theory is
quiz.why: The Wealth of Nations argued for specialisation in goods made most efficiently.

lessons.title: Heckscher-Ohlin, Leontief paradox and product life cycle

story.title: Why India exports software and garments

scenes.text: India has abundant labour, including many engineers. It exports labour-intensive garments and skill-intensive IT services.
Factor endowments and product age both shape trade.

steps.title: Heckscher-Ohlin (factor endowment) theory
steps.body: Countries export goods that intensively use their **abundant** factors and import goods that use their scarce factors. Labour-abundant countries export labour-intensive goods; capital-abundant countries export capital-intensive goods.

steps.title: Leontief paradox (1953)
steps.body: Leontief found US exports were less capital-intensive than US imports, contradicting H-O for a capital-rich country. Explanations: US labour was highly skilled (human capital), demand differences, tariffs and natural resources.

steps.title: Product life cycle theory (Vernon, 1966)
steps.body: New product: produced and sold in the innovating (high-income) country. Maturing: exports grow, production starts in other advanced countries. Standardised: production moves to low-cost developing countries, which may export back to the innovator. Example: consumer electronics moving from the US and Japan to East and South Asia.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Leontief paradox disproved trade theory entirely; it led to refinements.
- Forgetting that PLC fits manufactured goods better than services or commodities.

items: Innovation and production in the home country
Production begins in other advanced countries

quiz.why: It specialises in goods using its abundant and relatively cheap factor.

quiz.q: The Leontief paradox found US exports were
quiz.why: This surprise prompted explanations based on skilled labour and human capital.

quiz.q: In the standardised stage of the PLC, production moves to
quiz.why: Once technology is mature, cost becomes the main competitive factor.

quiz.q: Vernon's PLC theory was proposed in
quiz.why: Raymond Vernon published it in 1966.

lessons.title: New trade theory and Porter's diamond

scenes.text: IT services cluster in Bengaluru; knitwear clusters in Tiruppur.
Porter's diamond explains why some nations and regions win in particular industries.

steps.title: New trade theory
steps.body: Krugman and others: with **economies of scale** and network effects, first movers can dominate world markets; trade can occur between similar countries in similar products (intra-industry trade, e.g. cars between Germany and France). Strategic trade policy may support such industries.

steps.title: Porter's diamond (1990)
steps.body: Four determinants: **factor conditions** (skilled labour, infrastructure; advanced factors matter more than basic), **demand conditions** (sophisticated home buyers), **related and supporting industries** (clusters, suppliers), **firm strategy, structure and rivalry** (domestic competition sharpens firms). Plus two external influences: **government** and **chance**.

steps.title: Applying the diamond to Indian IT services
steps.body: Factors: large English-speaking engineering workforce. Demand: initially driven by foreign clients more than domestic. Related industries: telecom, education and training institutes. Rivalry: intense competition among Indian IT firms. Government: software technology parks and telecom liberalisation. Chance: Y2K demand in the late 1990s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Listing government as one of the four core determinants (it is an external influence).
- Treating cheap labour as the only factor condition.

quiz.why: Scale economies can make the location of an industry depend on who moves first.

courses.summary: Political and legal environment and country risk, cultural environment with Hall's context and Hofstede's dimensions, tariff and non-tariff barriers with numericals, arguments for protection, dumping, GATT and WTO principles and agreements, and levels of regional economic integration.

story.title: An Indian pharma firm in a new market

scenes.text: A Hyderabad generics maker plans to enter a country with high growth but frequent policy changes.
Its board asks: what could go wrong, and how do we protect ourselves?

steps.title: Political environment and risk
steps.body: Political systems (democracy, authoritarian), stability, government role in business. **Political risk**: expropriation or nationalisation, confiscation, creeping restrictions (local content, profit repatriation limits), civil unrest, sanctions, contract repudiation. Management: risk assessment, insurance (e.g. MIGA, export credit agencies such as ECGC in India), joint ventures with local partners, local sourcing.

steps.title: Legal environment
steps.body: Legal systems: **common law** (precedent; India, UK, USA), **civil law** (codified; France, Germany), **religious law**, mixed systems. Issues: contracts, intellectual property protection, product liability, competition law, data protection, dispute resolution through international arbitration (e.g. under the New York Convention on enforcement of foreign arbitral awards).

steps.title: Economic environment
steps.body: Economic systems (market, mixed, command), GDP and GDP per capita (often at purchasing power parity), inflation, interest and exchange rates, income distribution, infrastructure, and stage of development. Indicators help estimate market size and risk.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating democracy with low business risk.
- Ignoring creeping expropriation, which is more common than outright seizure.

activity.prompt: Classify each risk

scenes.text: An Indian sales team in Tokyo presses for a quick yes; the Japanese hosts go quiet and change the topic.
Understanding culture would have changed the approach.

steps.title: Elements of culture
steps.body: Language (verbal and non-verbal), religion, values and attitudes, customs and etiquette, social structure, education, aesthetics. **Ethnocentrism** (judging others by one's own culture) and the **self-reference criterion** are common traps.

steps.title: Hall's context
steps.body: **High-context** cultures rely on implicit messages, relationships and setting (Japan, China, Arab countries, India to a large extent). **Low-context** cultures rely on explicit, written communication and contracts (Germany, USA, Scandinavia).

steps.title: Hofstede's dimensions
steps.body: **Power distance**, **individualism vs collectivism**, **masculinity vs femininity** (achievement vs care orientation), **uncertainty avoidance**, **long-term vs short-term orientation**, **indulgence vs restraint**. Use: design of HR policies, advertising, negotiation style and organisation structure. Limits: national averages hide variation; data partly dated.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stereotyping individuals from national scores.
- Translating brand names without checking meanings.

lessons.title: Lab: Tariffs, non-tariff barriers and dumping

story.title: What will the importer really pay?

scenes.text: A Chennai importer buys machine parts with a CIF value of $5,000.
Duty type and rate change the landed cost a lot.

steps.title: Tariffs
steps.body: **Ad valorem**: % of value (usually CIF for imports). **Specific**: fixed amount per unit. **Compound**: both. Effects: higher domestic price, lower imports, government revenue, protection to domestic producers, deadweight loss to consumers.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
CIF $5,000; ad valorem duty 10% → duty = **$500**; landed value = $5,500.
Compound duty: 5% + $2 per unit on 300 units of $10 each (CIF $3,000): 150 + 600 = **$750**.

steps.title: Non-tariff barriers and protection
steps.body: Quotas, voluntary export restraints, import licensing, subsidies, local content rules, technical standards (TBT), sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) measures, government procurement preferences, administrative delays. Arguments for protection: infant industry, national security, jobs, anti-dumping, retaliation; against: higher prices, inefficiency, retaliation.

steps.title: Dumping
steps.body: Exporting at a price below normal value (home price or cost). WTO allows **anti-dumping duty** if dumping causes material injury. Dumping margin = (normal value − export price) ÷ export price. E.g. normal value ₹120, export price ₹100 → margin = **20%**. In India, the Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR) investigates.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying duty on FOB when the rule specifies CIF.
- Confusing anti-dumping duty with countervailing duty (which offsets foreign subsidies).

activity.prompt: CIF value $8,000 for 400 units. Compound duty 7.5% ad valorem plus $1.50 per unit. Total duty in $?

quiz.why: It is a fixed amount per physical unit regardless of value.

quiz.q: Countervailing duty offsets
quiz.why: It neutralises the price advantage from subsidies given by the exporting government.

quiz.q: Normal value ₹150 and export price ₹120 give a dumping margin of
quiz.why: (150 − 120) ÷ 120 = 25% of the export price.

quiz.q: The infant industry argument supports
options: temporary protection for new domestic industries
quiz.why: Young industries may need time to reach scale before facing full competition.

story.title: Rules of the global trade game

scenes.text: An Indian exporter faces a sudden import ban on its shrimp in a foreign market.
WTO rules and trade agreements decide what can be done.

steps.title: GATT to WTO
steps.body: GATT (1947) reduced tariffs through rounds; the Uruguay Round (1986–94) created the **WTO (1 January 1995)**, headquartered in Geneva. India is a founding member. Functions: administer agreements, forum for negotiations, dispute settlement, trade policy review, technical assistance.

steps.title: Principles and agreements
steps.body: **Most-favoured-nation (MFN)**: no discrimination between trading partners. **National treatment**: imported goods treated like domestic goods once inside. Also transparency, predictability through bound tariffs, and special and differential treatment for developing countries. Agreements: GATT 1994 (goods), **GATS** (services), **TRIPS** (intellectual property), **TRIMs** (investment measures), Agreement on Agriculture, SPS and TBT.

steps.title: Regional integration (Balassa's levels)
steps.body: **Free trade area** (no internal tariffs, own external tariffs; e.g. SAFTA, ASEAN FTA), **customs union** (plus common external tariff), **common market** (plus free movement of labour and capital), **economic union** (plus harmonised economic policies and possibly a common currency; e.g. EU, euro area), **political union**. Effects: trade creation vs trade diversion (Viner).

steps.title: Indian agreements (examples)
steps.body: India has comprehensive agreements with the UAE (CEPA, 2022) and an economic cooperation and trade agreement with Australia (ECTA, 2022), and a trade and economic partnership agreement with EFTA countries (2024). India chose not to join RCEP in 2019.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the EU a free trade area only; it is a common market and economic union.
- Confusing MFN with preferential treatment.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Balance of payments and foreign exchange
courses.summary: Structure of the balance of payments and current account deficit, exchange-rate regimes, quotations, cross rates and spreads, spot and forward markets with premium and discount, interest rate parity and purchasing power parity, and hedging transaction exposure with forwards.
outcomes: Classify transactions into current, capital and financial accounts and compute the current account balance
Read direct and indirect quotes and compute cross rates and spreads
Compute annualised forward premium or discount
Apply interest rate parity and purchasing power parity
Hedge an export receivable with a forward contract

scenes.text: India imports more goods than it exports, yet software exports and remittances earn large surpluses.
The balance of payments records every rupee crossing the border.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: The BoP is a systematic record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world over a period. **Current account**: goods (merchandise trade), services (IT, travel, transport), primary income (interest, dividends, wages) and secondary income (remittances, grants). **Capital account**: capital transfers and non-produced, non-financial assets. **Financial account**: FDI, portfolio investment, loans (ECBs), banking capital, and changes in **reserve assets**. Errors and omissions balance the statistical discrepancy. Overall, BoP always balances in accounting terms.

steps.title: Worked example: current account
steps.body:
Merchandise exports $450 bn, imports $700 bn → trade balance = **−$250 bn**.
Net services +$150 bn, net primary income −$40 bn, net secondary income (remittances) +$70 bn → net invisibles = +$180 bn.
Current account balance = −250 + 180 = **−$70 bn** (deficit). If GDP is $3,500 bn, CAD = 2% of GDP.

steps.title: Correcting disequilibrium
steps.body: Expenditure-reducing policies (fiscal and monetary tightening), expenditure-switching policies (depreciation, tariffs), export promotion, attracting stable capital (FDI). Persistent deficits financed by short-term flows increase vulnerability, as in India's 1991 crisis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting FDI in the current account (it is in the financial account).
- Treating remittances as capital flows (they are secondary income in the current account).

activity.prompt: Exports $400 bn, imports $620 bn, net services +$140 bn, net primary income −$30 bn, net remittances +$60 bn. Current account balance in $ bn?

quiz.q: Remittances from Indians abroad are recorded in
quiz.why: They are unrequited transfers, part of secondary income in the current account.

quiz.q: FDI inflows appear in the
quiz.why: They are acquisitions of assets and liabilities, recorded in the financial account.

quiz.q: Trade balance for exports $450 bn and imports $700 bn
quiz.why: Exports minus imports = −$250 bn, a merchandise trade deficit.

quiz.q: An expenditure-switching policy is
quiz.why: Depreciation shifts demand from imports to domestic and export goods by changing relative prices.

lessons.title: Exchange-rate regimes, quotes and cross rates

scenes.text: The dealer's screen shows USD/INR 83.90/84.10 and EUR/USD 1.0800.
An importer wants euros. What rupee rate will she get?

steps.title: Regimes
steps.body: **Fixed/pegged** (currency board, hard peg), **floating** (market-determined), **managed float** (market-determined with central bank intervention; India's regime, with RBI smoothing volatility). Historical: gold standard, Bretton Woods (1944–71) with the IMF. Depreciation/appreciation under floating; devaluation/revaluation under fixed regimes.

steps.title: Quotations
steps.body: **Direct quote**: home currency per unit of foreign currency (₹84 per $ in India). **Indirect quote**: foreign currency per unit of home currency ($0.011905 per ₹). **Bid** = rate at which the dealer buys the base currency; **ask/offer** = rate at which the dealer sells. Spread = ask − bid; % spread = (ask − bid) ÷ ask × 100.

steps.title: Worked example 1: spread
steps.body: USD/INR 83.90/84.10. Spread = 0.20; % spread = 0.20 ÷ 84.10 × 100 = **0.238%**. An exporter selling dollars gets 83.90; an importer buying dollars pays 84.10.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the bid when the customer is buying foreign currency.
- Dividing instead of multiplying when chaining quotes.

activity.prompt: GBP/USD = 1.25 and USD/INR = 84.40. GBP/INR cross rate?

quiz.q: ₹84 per dollar in India is a
quiz.why: It states the home currency price of one unit of foreign currency.

quiz.q: An Indian importer buying dollars at 83.90/84.10 pays
quiz.why: The bank sells dollars at its ask (offer) rate.

quiz.q: India's exchange-rate regime is best described as
quiz.why: The rupee is market-determined, with RBI intervening to curb excessive volatility.

quiz.q: If USD/INR moves from 84 to 86, the rupee has
quiz.why: More rupees are needed per dollar, so the rupee has lost value.

story.title: Why is the forward rate higher?

scenes.text: The 3-month USD/INR forward is 84.84 while spot is 84.00.
Interest-rate differences explain the gap; inflation differences explain long-run trends.

steps.title: Forward premium/discount
steps.body: Annualised premium (+) or discount (−) on the foreign currency = **(F − S) ÷ S × (12 ÷ months) × 100**. If F > S, the foreign currency is at a premium.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
S = 84.00, 3-month F = 84.84.
Premium = 0.84 ÷ 84 × 4 × 100 = **4% p.a.** on the dollar.

steps.title: Interest rate parity (IRP)
steps.body: **F = S × (1 + i_home) ÷ (1 + i_foreign)** for the period. The higher-interest currency trades at a forward discount, eliminating covered interest arbitrage.

steps.title: Purchasing power parity (PPP)
steps.body: **Absolute PPP**: identical goods cost the same across countries after conversion: S = P_home ÷ P_foreign. **Relative PPP**: exchange rate changes offset inflation differences: S₁ = S₀ × (1 + π_home) ÷ (1 + π_foreign). PPP holds better in the long run. The Economist's Big Mac index is a popular illustration.

steps.title: Worked example 3: PPP
steps.body:
Absolute: a basket costs ₹250 in India and $5 in the US → implied rate ₹50/$; actual ₹84/$ → by this measure the rupee is undervalued by (50 − 84) ÷ 84 = **−40.5%**.
Relative: inflation India 5%, US 2%, S₀ = 84 → expected S₁ = 84 × 1.05 ÷ 1.02 = **₹86.47**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to annualise the premium.
- Swapping home and foreign rates in IRP.

activity.prompt: S = ₹84/$, 6-month forward = ₹85.26. Annualised forward premium on the dollar in %?

quiz.q: Under IRP, the currency with the higher interest rate trades at a
quiz.why: Higher interest is offset by expected depreciation in the forward rate.

quiz.q: Relative PPP links exchange-rate changes to
quiz.why: Currencies of high-inflation countries tend to depreciate to keep real prices aligned.

quiz.q: IRP 1-year forward for S 84, i_India 7%, i_US 4% is about
The Big Mac index illustrates
quiz.why: It compares prices of an identical product to judge currency valuation.

scenes.text: A Tiruppur garment exporter will receive $1,00,000 from a US buyer in three months.
If the rupee strengthens, her rupee income falls. Should she lock a forward rate?

steps.title: Exposure types
steps.body: **Transaction exposure**: known foreign-currency receivables/payables. **Translation (accounting) exposure**: restating foreign subsidiaries' accounts. **Economic exposure**: effect of exchange rates on future cash flows and competitiveness. Hedging tools: forwards, futures (exchange-traded, e.g. currency futures on NSE/BSE), options, money-market hedge, invoicing in home currency, netting, leading and lagging.

steps.title: Worked example: forward hedge
steps.body:
Receivable $1,00,000; 3-month forward bid 84.84.
Locked proceeds = **₹84,84,000**.
If spot after 3 months is 83.50: unhedged = ₹83,50,000; hedge benefit = **₹1,34,000**.
If spot is 86.00: unhedged = ₹86,00,000; hedge 'opportunity loss' = ₹1,16,000 — the price of certainty.

steps.title: Options vs forwards
steps.body: A forward removes both downside and upside. A **put option** on USD (right to sell at a strike) protects the downside while keeping upside, at the cost of a premium. Choice depends on risk appetite and cost.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Judging a hedge as 'bad' when spot moves favourably: its purpose is certainty.
- Using the ask rate for an exporter's forward sale of dollars.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Entry modes, FDI, MNC strategy and export-import procedures
courses.summary: Foreign market entry modes from exporting to wholly owned subsidiaries, theories and policy of FDI including India's routes, MNC strategies on the integration-responsiveness grid, and export-import procedure with documents, Incoterms 2020, letters of credit and export pricing.
outcomes: Compare entry modes on control, risk and resource commitment

story.title: How should an Indian brand enter the Gulf?

scenes.text: A south Indian restaurant chain wants to open in Dubai.
Export ready-to-eat mixes, franchise the brand, form a JV, or open its own outlets?

steps.title: Modes
steps.body: **Exporting** (indirect via merchant exporters/export houses, direct via own agents and distributors): low risk and control. **Contractual**: **licensing** (IP for royalty), **franchising** (business format plus brand, common in services), **management contracts**, **turnkey projects**, contract manufacturing. **Investment**: **joint venture** (shared ownership), **wholly owned subsidiary** (greenfield or acquisition/brownfield). Also strategic alliances.

steps.title: Choosing a mode
steps.body: Trade-off among **control**, **resource commitment**, **risk** and **speed**. Factors: market size and growth, country risk, legal limits on foreign ownership, cultural distance, need to protect technology, firm's international experience (Uppsala model: gradual increase in commitment).

steps.title: Worked example: licensing vs own plant
steps.body: Licensing: royalty 5% on licensee sales of $4 million a year = **$2,00,000** with little investment. Own plant: expected profit $6,00,000 a year on $3 million investment → 20% return but full risk. The choice depends on risk appetite and technology protection.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Licensing core technology to a partner who may become a competitor.
- Choosing a wholly owned subsidiary where the law caps foreign ownership.

story.title: A Korean electronics plant near Chennai

scenes.text: A foreign electronics maker builds a factory in Tamil Nadu to serve India and export.
Why invest abroad rather than export, and what rules apply in India?

steps.title: FDI vs FPI
steps.body: **FDI**: investment with a lasting interest and significant influence over management (commonly 10% or more of equity). **FPI**: portfolio investment in securities without control. Forms: greenfield, brownfield (M&A), horizontal and vertical FDI.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body: **Dunning's eclectic (OLI) paradigm**: firms invest abroad when they have **O**wnership advantages (technology, brands), the host offers **L**ocation advantages (markets, costs, resources), and it pays to **I**nternalise rather than license (protect knowledge, control quality). Also market imperfections (Hymer), product life cycle (Vernon).

steps.title: India's FDI policy
steps.body: Two routes: **automatic route** (no prior government approval, subject to sectoral caps and conditions) and **government route** (prior approval). Most sectors allow up to 100% under the automatic route. Some sectors have caps or require approval (e.g. defence beyond a threshold, print media); a few are prohibited (e.g. lottery, gambling, atomic energy). Investment from countries sharing a land border with India requires government approval (Press Note 3 of 2020). Policy is notified by DPIIT; FEMA governs foreign exchange aspects.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling FPI 'FDI'.
- Assuming every sector allows 100% automatic-route FDI.

quiz.why: FDI implies control or significant influence; FPI is a passive holding of securities.

options: need RBI licence first in all cases
quiz.why: They only make post-investment filings, subject to sectoral rules.

quiz.q: Dunning's 'I' advantage justifies
quiz.why: When markets for know-how are imperfect, firms internalise by owning operations.

quiz.q: Investments from countries sharing a land border with India require
quiz.why: Press Note 3 (2020) placed such investments under the government route.

lessons.title: MNC strategy: global integration vs local responsiveness

scenes.text: A global fast-food chain removes beef from its Indian menu and adds vegetarian items.
Yet its kitchen systems and brand are identical worldwide.

steps.title: Two pressures
steps.body: **Pressure for global integration/cost reduction** (standardised products, scale economies) vs **pressure for local responsiveness** (different tastes, regulations, distribution, infrastructure). Bartlett and Ghoshal's grid gives four strategies.

steps.title: Four strategies
steps.body: **International/export** (low on both: home-developed products sold abroad). **Multidomestic** (high responsiveness, low integration: local subsidiaries adapt fully). **Global** (high integration, low responsiveness: standardised products, centralised). **Transnational** (high on both: global efficiency, local adaptation and worldwide learning). Perlmutter's EPRG orientations: ethnocentric, polycentric, regiocentric, geocentric.

steps.title: Examples (illustrative)
steps.body: Global: semiconductors and commercial aircraft. Multidomestic: packaged foods and media. Transnational: fast-food chains adapting menus while keeping global systems; consumer goods firms with global brands and local variants.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 'global' means operating in many countries; it means standardisation.
- Confusing polycentric (host-country focus) with geocentric (world focus).

quiz.why: It balances integration with adaptation and spreads learning across units.

options: host-country nationals and practices dominate each subsidiary
quiz.why: Each subsidiary is run in the local way by local managers.

quiz.q: Global strategy fits industries where
options: customer needs are similar worldwide and scale matters
quiz.why: Standardisation then maximises cost advantages.

quiz.q: The integration-responsiveness grid is associated with
quiz.why: They developed the typology in Managing Across Borders (1989).

lessons.title: Lab: Export procedure, Incoterms and letters of credit

scenes.text: A Moradabad brassware maker receives an order from a German buyer, CIF Hamburg, payment by letter of credit.
Documents must match exactly or the bank will not pay.

steps.title: Export procedure (outline)
steps.body: Obtain **IEC** from DGFT and register with the relevant export promotion council (RCMC) → receive enquiry and send proforma invoice → confirm order and receive LC → arrange finance (pre-shipment credit) and produce goods → pre-shipment inspection if needed → book freight and insurance → customs clearance with **shipping bill** (via ICEGATE) → load goods, obtain **bill of lading** (sea) or **airway bill** → submit documents to bank → realisation of payment and post-shipment benefits.

steps.title: Key documents
steps.body: Commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading, certificate of origin (needed to claim FTA preference), insurance certificate, inspection certificate, shipping bill, bill of exchange (draft).

steps.title: Incoterms 2020 (ICC)
steps.body: 11 terms. Any mode: **EXW**, FCA, CPT, CIP, DAP, DPU, **DDP**. Sea and inland waterway only: FAS, **FOB**, CFR, **CIF**. FOB: risk passes when goods are on board at the port of shipment; seller does not pay main freight. CIF: seller pays cost, insurance and freight to the destination port, but risk still passes on board at origin.

steps.title: Worked example: CIF price
steps.body: Ex-works price ₹8,00,000; inland transport and port charges ₹40,000 → FOB = ₹8,40,000. Sea freight ₹60,000 → CFR = ₹9,00,000. Insurance at 0.5% on CIF value (commonly 110% of CIF in practice; here simply on CFR for illustration): 0.005 × 9,00,000 = ₹4,500 → **CIF ≈ ₹9,04,500**. At ₹90.72/€, CIF ≈ **€9,970**.

steps.title: Letter of credit
steps.body: A bank's undertaking to pay the exporter (beneficiary) on presentation of complying documents. Parties: applicant (importer), issuing bank, advising/confirming bank, beneficiary. Types: irrevocable, confirmed, sight vs usance, transferable, back-to-back. Governed by ICC's UCP 600. Other payment terms: advance, documents against payment (D/P), documents against acceptance (D/A), open account.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing CIF moves risk to the destination port.
- Minor discrepancies (spelling, dates) between LC and documents, which allow banks to refuse payment.

steps.title: Theories

steps.title: Document checklist
steps.body: Commercial invoice: description, quantity, value and Incoterm exactly as in the LC · Bill of lading: shipped on board date within the LC deadline, port names, consignee as required · Insurance certificate: coverage at least as required (often 110% of CIF), same currency, dated no later than shipment · Certificate of origin · Packing list · Bill of exchange drawn as per LC.

steps.title: Spot the discrepancies
steps.body: Invoice says '480 pcs' (LC: 500) → discrepancy. B/L on-board date 18 March (LC: by 15 March) → late shipment. Insurance dated 20 March, after shipment → discrepancy. Each can lead to refusal unless the applicant waives it.

steps.title: Viva questions

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Missing the presentation period after shipment.

lessons.title: Core concepts: needs, wants, demands and value

scenes.text: At 42°C, Ramesh is thirsty: a need.
He wants a cold lassi from his favourite shop: a want shaped by culture.
He has ₹40 and buys it: a demand, a want backed by ability to pay.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: Kotler defines marketing as a social and managerial process by which individuals and groups obtain what they need and want through creating and exchanging value with others. The AMA defines it as the activity, institutions and processes for creating, communicating, delivering and exchanging offerings that have value for customers, clients, partners and society.

steps.title: Needs, wants, demands
steps.body:
- **Need**: a state of felt deprivation (food, safety, belonging).
- **Want**: the form a need takes, shaped by culture and personality.
- **Demand**: a want backed by buying power.

steps.title: Value and satisfaction
steps.body: Customer perceived value = total customer benefit − total customer cost. Satisfaction depends on performance relative to expectations: below → dissatisfied, equal → satisfied, above → delighted.

steps.title: Customer lifetime value (simple)
steps.body: A customer spends ₹2,000 per month at a grocery app with 20% margin, and stays 3 years. Monthly margin = ₹400; CLV (undiscounted) = 400 × 12 × 3 = **₹14,400**. This explains why apps spend on retention.

steps.title: The five concepts
steps.body:
- **Production**: consumers want available, affordable products; focus on efficiency.
- **Product**: consumers favour quality and features; risk of marketing myopia.
- **Selling**: consumers won't buy enough unless pushed; inside-out.
- **Marketing**: know target customers' needs and deliver better than competitors; outside-in.
- **Societal marketing**: marketing plus long-run consumer and society well-being.

steps.title: Selling vs marketing
steps.body: Selling: starting point factory, focus existing products, means selling and promotion, end profit through sales volume. Marketing: starting point market, focus customer needs, means integrated marketing, end profit through customer satisfaction.

steps.title: Marketing myopia
steps.body: Theodore Levitt (1960) warned that firms defining themselves by product (railways) rather than need (transport) lose to new solutions.

steps.title: Holistic marketing
steps.body: Kotler's holistic view combines relationship marketing, integrated marketing, internal marketing and performance (socially responsible) marketing.

steps.title: Micro environment
steps.body: Actors close to the firm: the company itself, suppliers, marketing intermediaries, customers, competitors and publics (media, government, citizen groups).

steps.title: Macro environment: PESTEL
steps.body: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal forces. Example for EVs: P subsidies; E fuel prices, interest rates; S youth adoption; T battery chemistry; E pollution concerns; L battery safety standards.

steps.title: SWOT
steps.body: Strengths and weaknesses are **internal**; opportunities and threats are **external**. Strategies: SO (use strengths to seize opportunities), WO, ST, WT (TOWS matrix).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: A government subsidy is an opportunity (external), not a strength. A strong brand is a strength (internal).

Template: **For** (target) **who** (need), **our** (brand) **is a** (frame of reference) **that** (point of difference) **because** (reason to believe).

courses.title: Unit 3 · Product Decisions, Branding and the Product Life Cycle
courses.summary: Levels of product, classification of goods, product mix width and depth, new product development, the product life cycle and its strategies, branding decisions and brand equity, packaging and labelling, and the BCG matrix.

scenes.text: A guest pays for a night's rest: the core benefit.

steps.title: Kotler's five product levels
steps.body: Core benefit → basic product → expected product → augmented product → potential product (future transformations).

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
- **Consumer products**: convenience (staples, impulse, emergency), shopping, specialty, unsought (life insurance).
- **Industrial products**: materials and parts, capital items, supplies and services.
- By durability: non-durable, durable, services.

steps.title: Product mix dimensions
steps.body:
A company has 3 lines: soaps (4 brands), shampoos (3 brands), toothpaste (2 brands).
- **Width** = number of lines = **3**.
- **Length** = total items = 4 + 3 + 2 = **9**.
- **Average length** = 9/3 = **3**.
- **Depth**: if one soap brand comes in 3 sizes × 2 fragrances, its depth = **6**.

steps.title: Consistency
steps.body: Consistency is how closely lines relate in end use, production or distribution. Soaps, shampoos and toothpaste share retail channels, so consistency is high.

steps.title: Eight stages
steps.body: 1 Idea generation 2 Idea screening 3 Concept development and testing 4 Marketing strategy development 5 Business analysis 6 Product development 7 Test marketing 8 Commercialisation.

steps.title: Diffusion of innovation (Rogers)
steps.body: Adopter categories: innovators 2.5%, early adopters 13.5%, early majority 34%, late majority 34%, laggards 16%. Characteristics speeding adoption: relative advantage, compatibility, low complexity, divisibility (trialability), communicability (observability).

steps.title: Business analysis
steps.body: Expected annual sales 5 lakh units at ₹40 = ₹2 crore. Variable cost ₹25/unit; fixed cost ₹50 lakh. Profit = 5,00,000 × (40 − 25) − 50,00,000 = 75,00,000 − 50,00,000 = **₹25 lakh**.

steps.title: Screening errors
steps.body: A **drop error** kills a good idea; a **go error** lets a poor idea move ahead. Both are costly.

steps.title: PLC stages and strategies
steps.body:
- **Introduction**: low sales, high cost per customer, losses; build awareness, trial, basic product.
- **Growth**: rising sales and profits, more competitors; improve features, expand distribution.
- **Maturity**: peak sales, profits start to fall; modify market, product or mix.
- **Decline**: falling sales; maintain, harvest or drop.

steps.title: BCG growth-share matrix
steps.body:
Relative market share vs market growth rate:
- **Star**: high share, high growth: invest.
- **Cash cow**: high share, low growth: milk for cash.
- **Question mark**: low share, high growth: build or divest.
- **Dog**: low share, low growth: harvest or divest.

steps.title: Relative market share
steps.body: Our sales ₹60 crore, largest competitor ₹40 crore. RMS = 60/40 = **1.5** (high, we lead). If we had ₹20 crore, RMS = 20/40 = 0.5 (low).

steps.body: Market penetration (existing product, existing market), market development (new market), product development (new product), diversification (both new).

steps.title: Brand and brand equity
steps.body: A brand is a name, term, sign, symbol or design identifying a seller's goods. **Brand equity** is the differential effect brand knowledge has on customer response. Aaker's dimensions: brand awareness, perceived quality, brand associations, brand loyalty (plus other proprietary assets).

steps.title: Branding strategies
steps.body:
- **Line extension**: new flavours/sizes under existing brand.
- **Brand extension**: existing brand into a new category.
- **Multibrands**: several brands in the same category.
- **New brands**.
Also: individual vs family (umbrella) branding; manufacturer vs private label (store brands).

steps.title: Packaging and labelling
steps.body: Packaging protects, promotes and adds convenience (primary, secondary, shipping packaging). Labels identify, grade, describe and promote. In India, pre-packaged goods carry mandatory declarations such as MRP and net quantity under legal metrology rules, and food packs carry FSSAI licence details.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Pricing Decisions
courses.summary: Factors affecting price, price elasticity with calculations, cost-based methods (cost-plus, markup, target return, break-even), value- and competition-based pricing, new-product strategies (skimming and penetration), price adjustments and channel margins.
outcomes: List internal and external factors affecting price
Compute price elasticity and its revenue effect
Set prices with cost-plus, markup on price and target-return methods
Find break-even volume
Choose skimming or penetration and work back channel margins from MRP

scenes.text: A snack brand raises its pack price from ₹100 to ₹110.
Monthly packs sold fall from 1,000 to 850.
The brand manager checks whether revenue went up or down.

steps.title: Objectives and factors
steps.body: Objectives: survival, profit maximisation, market-share leadership, product-quality leadership. Internal factors: objectives, mix strategy, costs, organisation. External: demand, competition, economy, government regulation (e.g. MRP printing; price controls on some essential drugs), channel members.

steps.title: Price elasticity of demand
steps.body: PED = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price. |PED| > 1 elastic (revenue falls when price rises); |PED| < 1 inelastic (revenue rises when price rises); = 1 unitary.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Price ₹100 → ₹110: +10%. Quantity 1,000 → 850: −15%. PED = −15/10 = **−1.5** (elastic).
Revenue before = 100 × 1,000 = ₹1,00,000. After = 110 × 850 = **₹93,500**. Revenue fell by ₹6,500, as expected for elastic demand.

steps.title: What makes demand inelastic
steps.body: Few substitutes, necessity, small share of budget, perceived high quality, difficulty comparing.

activity.prompt: Elastic or inelastic demand?

items.text: One brand of potato chips among many

quiz.q: Price rises 5%, quantity falls 2%. PED is
quiz.why: −2 / 5 = −0.4, so demand is inelastic.

quiz.q: For inelastic demand, a price rise will
quiz.why: Quantity falls proportionally less than price rises, so revenue goes up.

quiz.q: Which objective suits a firm in heavy overcapacity and price wars?
quiz.why: When survival is at stake, prices may be set just to cover variable costs.

scenes.text: A steel bottle maker in Rajkot has variable cost ₹60 per bottle and fixed cost ₹4 lakh a year.
It expects to sell 20,000 bottles.
The owner tries three pricing methods.

steps.title: Markup on selling price
steps.body: Desired markup 20% on price: price = unit cost / (1 − 0.20) = 80 / 0.8 = **₹100**. Check: margin 20 is 20% of 100.

steps.title: Target-return pricing
steps.body: Investment ₹10 lakh, target ROI 20% → required profit ₹2,00,000. Price = unit cost + (ROI × investment)/units = 80 + 2,00,000/20,000 = 80 + 10 = **₹90**.

steps.title: Break-even
steps.body: At price ₹100: contribution per unit = 100 − 60 = ₹40. BEP = FC / contribution = 4,00,000 / 40 = **10,000 bottles**. BEP in value = 10,000 × 100 = ₹10 lakh.

steps.title: Limitation
steps.body: Cost-based methods ignore what customers will pay and what rivals charge; unit cost also depends on the volume you assume.

scenes.text: A premium phone launches at a high price for early enthusiasts, then cuts price over months.

steps.title: Value- and competition-based pricing
steps.body:
- **Customer value-based**: start with perceived value, then design costs (good-value pricing, value-added pricing).
- **Competition-based**: going-rate pricing, sealed-bid tendering.

steps.title: Skimming vs penetration
steps.body:
- **Skimming**: high initial price to skim revenue layer by layer. Works when quality and image support it, enough buyers want it at that price, and rivals cannot enter easily.
- **Penetration**: low price to gain share quickly. Works when market is price-sensitive, costs fall with volume, and low price deters competition.

steps.title: Product-mix pricing
steps.body: Product line pricing, optional-product, captive-product (printer cheap, ink costly), by-product, product bundle pricing.

steps.title: Psychological and other tactics
steps.body: Odd pricing (₹499), prestige pricing, reference prices, loss leaders, dynamic pricing (ride-hailing surge), geographical pricing (FOB origin, uniform delivered).

steps.title: Discounts and allowances

steps.title: Working back from MRP

steps.title: Cash discount value
steps.body: Invoice ₹50,000 on terms 2/10 net 30. Paying in 10 days saves 2% = **₹1,000**, so the buyer pays ₹49,000.

steps.title: Initiating and responding to price changes
steps.body: Price cuts can signal low quality or start a price war; increases can be softened by unbundling or smaller packs (shrinkflation is criticised by consumer groups). Responding: hold price, raise perceived value, cut price, or launch a low-price fighter brand.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Distribution, Integrated Marketing Communication and Digital Marketing
courses.summary: Channel functions, levels and intensity, retailing and wholesaling, logistics; the promotion mix, AIDA and IMC; advertising, sales promotion, PR and personal selling; and digital marketing metrics (CPM, CTR, CPC, conversion, ROAS) with calculations, plus rural marketing and ethics.
outcomes: Explain why intermediaries reduce transactions
Choose intensive, selective or exclusive distribution
Design an IMC plan using AIDA
Compute CPM, CTR, CPC, conversion rate and ROAS

scenes.text: A biscuit maker wants its packs in tiny kirana stores across India.
It cannot visit every store; it uses distributors, stockists and wholesalers.
Intermediaries make the reach possible.

steps.title: Why intermediaries
steps.body: They reduce the number of contacts, offer assortment, hold inventory, finance stock and share risk. Functions: information, promotion, contact, matching, negotiation, physical distribution, financing, risk taking.

steps.title: Contact efficiency
steps.body: 4 producers selling directly to 6 customers need 4 × 6 = **24** contacts. Through one distributor: 4 + 6 = **10** contacts.

steps.title: Channel levels
steps.body: Zero-level (direct: D2C website), one-level (manufacturer → retailer → consumer), two-level (+ wholesaler), three-level (+ jobber/stockist). Vertical marketing systems: corporate, contractual (franchise), administered.

steps.title: Distribution intensity
steps.body:
- **Intensive**: as many outlets as possible (soft drinks, soap).
- **Selective**: some outlets (appliances).
- **Exclusive**: few authorised dealers (luxury cars).
Also omnichannel and quick commerce in Indian cities.

steps.title: Logistics
steps.body: Order processing, warehousing, inventory management, transportation. Goal: right product, right place, right time at lowest total cost for the target service level.

quiz.why: 5 × 8 = 40, compared with 13 via one intermediary.

quiz.why: No intermediaries stand between manufacturer and consumer.

quiz.q: A franchise system is a
quiz.why: Franchising links independent members through contracts.

scenes.text: A paint brand launches a range for small apartments.
TV ads build awareness, dealers get contests, painters get training.
Every message says the same thing: bright rooms, small spaces.

steps.title: Promotion mix tools
steps.body:
- **Advertising**: paid, non-personal, identified sponsor.
- **Sales promotion**: short-term incentives (coupons, contests, BOGO, trade deals).
- **Public relations**: publicity, events, CSR stories.
- **Personal selling**: face-to-face, two-way.
- **Direct and digital marketing**: email, SMS, social, search.

steps.title: AIDA and push vs pull
steps.body: AIDA: Attention → Interest → Desire → Action. **Push** strategy targets channel members (trade discounts, dealer contests). **Pull** strategy targets consumers so they ask retailers for the product (mass advertising).

steps.title: IMC
steps.body: Integrated marketing communication coordinates all tools to deliver a clear, consistent, compelling message. Steps: identify audience, set objectives, design message, choose media, set budget, measure results.

steps.title: Budget methods
steps.body: Affordable, percentage-of-sales, competitive parity, objective-and-task (most logical: define objectives, determine tasks, cost them).

steps.title: Percentage-of-sales
steps.body: Forecast sales ₹80 crore; firm spends 5% of sales on promotion. Budget = **₹4 crore**.

steps.title: Channels
steps.body: SEO, search ads (SEM), social media marketing, content marketing, email, influencer and affiliate marketing, marketplaces. Owned, paid and earned media.

steps.title: ROAS is not profit
steps.body: A ROAS of 4.8 ignores product cost. If gross margin is 25%, gross profit = ₹36,000, leaving ₹6,000 after ad spend.

steps.title: Rules to know

scenes.text: A van with a loudspeaker and a demo stall visits the weekly haat in a Bihar village.
A promoter shows how a small sachet of detergent cleans a shirt.
Rural buyers trust what they see and what neighbours say.

steps.title: Rural marketing: the 4As

steps.body: SERVQUAL dimensions: reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy, responsiveness (RATER). The gap model highlights differences between customer expectations and perceptions.

steps.title: Ethics and consumerism
steps.body: Concerns: deceptive pricing and ads, high-pressure selling, dark patterns online, unsafe products, targeting children. Consumer rights under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 include the rights to safety, information, choice, being heard, redressal and consumer awareness; a Central Consumer Protection Authority handles issues such as misleading ads.

steps.title: Green marketing
steps.body: Claims like 'eco-friendly' must be specific and verifiable; vague claims risk accusations of greenwashing.
